items.title: MbedTLS Security Audit
items.summary: Introduction Mbed TLS is a widely deployed open-source TLS, DTLS, and X.509 library maintained by Trusted Firmware, targeting constrained and embedded environments. It is used as the cryptographic backbone of products across the IoT, automotive, and industrial sectors, and forms the TLS layer for projects such as the Trusted Firmware family. Version 4.0 represents the most significant architectural change in the project's history. The cryptographic layer has been extracted into a standalone library, TF-PSA-Crypto, which implements the PSA Cryptography API v1.2 as specified by Arm. The Mbed TLS repository now consumes TF-PSA-Crypto as a submodule, and the configuration space has been split across two header files: mbedtls_config.h for the TLS and X.509 options, and psa/crypto_config.h for the cryptographic primitives. All RNG callbacks have been removed in favor of a mandatory call to psa_crypto_init() before any operation. The Open Source Technology Improvement Fund (OSTIF) commissioned Quarkslab to perform a security audit of this new architecture. Scope The primary objectives of this audit are: Architectural transition review. Assess the security implications of the Mbed TLS 3.x to 4.0 split, focusing on the trust boundary between the TLS layer and TF-PSA-Crypto, the correctness of the PSA API integration, and whether the removal of the legacy crypto paths introduces new attack surface. PSA API usage correctness. Verify that key attributes (usage flags, permitted algorithms, lifetimes) are correctly set and enforced throughout the TLS and X.509 code paths, and that the mandatory psa_crypto_init() dependency is properly documented and enforced. Memory safety. Identify memory corruption vulnerabilities in the SSL/DTLS context management (in particular, session serialization and resumption), the X.509 parsing subsystem, and the PSA key store. Default configuration posture. Review the security of the default build configuration, including enabled cipher suites, protocol versions, key exchange algorithms, and compile-time options that may expose users to risk without explicit opt-in. Protocol compliance. Identify deviations from the TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246), TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446), and DTLS specifications that have security consequences. The engagement covers: Mbed TLS at commit 0fe989b6b514192783c469039edd325fd0989806 . TF-PSA-Crypto (integrated submodule) at commit 29160dd877d29658279fd683b2ae57b320ddcf09 . The complete technical report, including our findings and recommendations, is available in Quarkslab's public reports repository . Findings The table below summarizes the findings of the audit. A total of 5 vulnerabilities were identified: 1 of high severity, 1 of low severity, and 3 informational ones. ID Title Severity Perimeter HIGH-1 CID Buffer Overflow in `mbedtls_ssl_context_load()` High `library/ssl_tls.c:5002` LOW-4 `mbedtls_pk_verify()` accepts BER-encoded signatures Low `tf-psa-crypto/extras/pk.c` INFO-2 No Anti-Replay Protection for TLS 1.3 0-RTT Early Data Info `include/mbedtls/ssl.h:5166` INFO-3 Mismatch in CMAC cipher support between the documentation and the implementation. Info TF-PSA-Crypto documentation INFO-5 `compat.sh` DTLS 1.2 tests fail on the `mbedtls-test` Docker image due to IPv6 `localhost` resolution Info mbedtls-test Docker images, `compat.sh` Note: All relevant findings have since been resolved. Conclusion The audit identified a few vulnerabilities with only two non-informational ones, and the auditors were overall very satisfied with the quality of the product in general, and this version's changes in particular. The high and low vulnerabilities are related to a heap buffer overflow and potential signature malleability, respectively, with the second one being identified thanks to the integration of integration of Project Wycheproof test vectors into the test suite. An informational finding documents the absence of any anti-replay protection for TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data, a known limitation that is currently not surfaced in the public-facing documentation in a way that prevents inadvertent misuse. Auditors have proposed improvements to the existing fuzzing harnesses and corpora, along with an integration of the #anv test suite into the CI/CD pipeline. We would like to thank the Mbed TLS maintainers for their responsiveness and collaboration throughout the audit process, as well as the OSTIF team for their continuous support. Further details can be found in our report . Further reading OSTIF blog post
items.summary_html:
Introduction

Mbed TLS is a widely deployed open-source TLS, DTLS, and X.509 library maintained by Trusted Firmware, targeting constrained and embedded environments. It is used as the cryptographic backbone of products across the IoT, automotive, and industrial sectors, and forms the TLS layer for projects such as the Trusted Firmware family.

Version 4.0 represents the most significant architectural change in the project's history. The cryptographic layer has been extracted into a standalone library, TF-PSA-Crypto, which implements the PSA Cryptography API v1.2 as specified by Arm. The Mbed TLS repository now consumes TF-PSA-Crypto as a submodule, and the configuration space has been split across two header files: mbedtls_config.h for the TLS and X.509 options, and psa/crypto_config.h for the cryptographic primitives. All RNG callbacks have been removed in favor of a mandatory call to psa_crypto_init() before any operation.

The Open Source Technology Improvement Fund (OSTIF) commissioned Quarkslab to perform a security audit of this new architecture.

Scope

The primary objectives of this audit are:

  • Architectural transition review. Assess the security implications of the Mbed TLS 3.x to 4.0 split, focusing on the trust boundary between the TLS layer and TF-PSA-Crypto, the correctness of the PSA API integration, and whether the removal of the legacy crypto paths introduces new attack surface.

  • PSA API usage correctness. Verify that key attributes (usage flags, permitted algorithms, lifetimes) are correctly set and enforced throughout the TLS and X.509 code paths, and that the mandatory psa_crypto_init() dependency is properly documented and enforced.

  • Memory safety. Identify memory corruption vulnerabilities in the SSL/DTLS context management (in particular, session serialization and resumption), the X.509 parsing subsystem, and the PSA key store.

  • Default configuration posture. Review the security of the default build configuration, including enabled cipher suites, protocol versions, key exchange algorithms, and compile-time options that may expose users to risk without explicit opt-in.

  • Protocol compliance. Identify deviations from the TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246), TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446), and DTLS specifications that have security consequences.

The engagement covers:

  • Mbed TLS at commit 0fe989b6b514192783c469039edd325fd0989806.
  • TF-PSA-Crypto (integrated submodule) at commit 29160dd877d29658279fd683b2ae57b320ddcf09.

The complete technical report, including our findings and recommendations, is available in Quarkslab's public reports repository.

Findings

The table below summarizes the findings of the audit. A total of 5 vulnerabilities were identified: 1 of high severity, 1 of low severity, and 3 informational ones.

ID Title Severity Perimeter HIGH-1 CID Buffer Overflow in `mbedtls_ssl_context_load()` High `library/ssl_tls.c:5002` LOW-4 `mbedtls_pk_verify()` accepts BER-encoded signatures Low `tf-psa-crypto/extras/pk.c` INFO-2 No Anti-Replay Protection for TLS 1.3 0-RTT Early Data Info `include/mbedtls/ssl.h:5166` INFO-3 Mismatch in CMAC cipher support between the documentation and the implementation. Info TF-PSA-Crypto documentation INFO-5 `compat.sh` DTLS 1.2 tests fail on the `mbedtls-test` Docker image due to IPv6 `localhost` resolution Info mbedtls-test Docker images, `compat.sh`

Note: All relevant findings have since been resolved.

Conclusion

The audit identified a few vulnerabilities with only two non-informational ones, and the auditors were overall very satisfied with the quality of the product in general, and this version's changes in particular.

The high and low vulnerabilities are related to a heap buffer overflow and potential signature malleability, respectively, with the second one being identified thanks to the integration of integration of Project Wycheproof test vectors into the test suite.

An informational finding documents the absence of any anti-replay protection for TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data, a known limitation that is currently not surfaced in the public-facing documentation in a way that prevents inadvertent misuse. Auditors have proposed improvements to the existing fuzzing harnesses and corpora, along with an integration of the #anv test suite into the CI/CD pipeline.

We would like to thank the Mbed TLS maintainers for their responsiveness and collaboration throughout the audit process, as well as the OSTIF team for their continuous support.

Further details can be found in our report.

Further reading
  • OSTIF blog post

items.title: Large OS Disk Encryption is now generally available for Azure Confidential VM migrations
items.summary: Today, we are excited to announce the General Availability of Large OS Disk Encryption (LOSDE) for Azure Confidential VM migration scenarios. This capability removes a key adoption barrier for customers migrating sensitive workloads to Azure Confidential Virtual Machines by enabling confidential encryption for operating system disks larger than 127 GB. With LOSDE, organizations can securely migrate larger, more complex workloads to Azure while maintaining the confidentiality protections provided by Azure Confidential Computing. Why this matters For many enterprises, migrating existing workloads to the cloud is not simply a matter of redeployment. Business-critical applications often rely on large operating system disks and established operational configurations that must be preserved during migration. Until now, customers migrating workloads with operating system disks larger than 127 GB faced limitations when attempting to bring those workloads into Azure Confidential VMs while preserving confidential computing guarantees. This created an adoption challenge for organizations operating highly regulated or security-sensitive environments. Large OS Disk Encryption addresses this gap by extending confidential encryption support to larger operating system disks during migration workflows. With LOSDE, customers can: Enable upgrading virtual machines to Azure Confidential VMs through the migration process. Migrate workloads with OS disks larger than 127 GB to Azure Confidential VMs. Continue to use customer-managed keys (CMKs) aligned with their security and compliance requirements. Support migration scenarios for Windows, Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, and Rocky Linux. Check the Azure Migrate documentation for the support list. Accelerate adoption of Azure Confidential Computing for existing enterprise environments. Simplifying secure migration to Azure Confidential VMs The Large OS Disk Encryption feature integrates seamlessly into Azure migration workflows, enabling customers to move existing workloads into Azure Confidential VMs while continuing to benefit from hardware-backed protections and the trusted execution environment capabilities of Azure Confidential Computing. LOSDE helps close that gap by enabling customers to bring existing workloads into Azure Confidential Computing environments while preserving the confidentiality guarantees required for regulated, critical, and sensitive applications. The solution offers automation with Azure Migrate , enabling Windows, Ubuntu, RHEL, and Rocky Linux workloads to be encrypted before data leaves the customer boundary while preserving the confidentiality guarantees of Azure Confidential Computing and supporting customer-managed keys (CMKs). The result is a simpler path to cloud modernization, stronger protection for data in use, and expanded adoption opportunities for Azure Confidential Virtual Machines . This work reflects Microsoft's ongoing commitment to making advanced security capabilities easier to adopt without increasing operational complexity.

Today, we are excited to announce the General Availability of Large OS Disk Encryption (LOSDE) for Azure Confidential VM migration scenarios.

This capability removes a key adoption barrier for customers migrating sensitive workloads to Azure Confidential Virtual Machines by enabling confidential encryption for operating system disks larger than 127 GB. With LOSDE, organizations can securely migrate larger, more complex workloads to Azure while maintaining the confidentiality protections provided by Azure Confidential Computing.

Why this matters

For many enterprises, migrating existing workloads to the cloud is not simply a matter of redeployment. Business-critical applications often rely on large operating system disks and established operational configurations that must be preserved during migration.

Until now, customers migrating workloads with operating system disks larger than 127 GB faced limitations when attempting to bring those workloads into Azure Confidential VMs while preserving confidential computing guarantees. This created an adoption challenge for organizations operating highly regulated or security-sensitive environments. Large OS Disk Encryption addresses this gap by extending confidential encryption support to larger operating system disks during migration workflows. With LOSDE, customers can:

  • Enable upgrading virtual machines to Azure Confidential VMs through the migration process.
  • Migrate workloads with OS disks larger than 127 GB to Azure Confidential VMs.
  • Continue to use customer-managed keys (CMKs) aligned with their security and compliance requirements.
  • Support migration scenarios for Windows, Ubuntu, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, and Rocky Linux. Check the Azure Migrate documentation for the support list.
  • Accelerate adoption of Azure Confidential Computing for existing enterprise environments.
Simplifying secure migration to Azure Confidential VMs

The Large OS Disk Encryption feature integrates seamlessly into Azure migration workflows, enabling customers to move existing workloads into Azure Confidential VMs while continuing to benefit from hardware-backed protections and the trusted execution environment capabilities of Azure Confidential Computing.

LOSDE helps close that gap by enabling customers to bring existing workloads into Azure Confidential Computing environments while preserving the confidentiality guarantees required for regulated, critical, and sensitive applications. The solution offers automation with Azure Migrate , enabling Windows, Ubuntu, RHEL, and Rocky Linux workloads to be encrypted before data leaves the customer boundary while preserving the confidentiality guarantees of Azure Confidential Computing and supporting customer-managed keys (CMKs).

The result is a simpler path to cloud modernization, stronger protection for data in use, and expanded adoption opportunities for Azure Confidential Virtual Machines . This work reflects Microsoft's ongoing commitment to making advanced security capabilities easier to adopt without increasing operational complexity.

items.title: Cutting our inference bill by 68% by being obsessive about optimization
items.summary: When we previously blogged about our AI code reviewer in April , an average review cost a palatable $1.19. By the end of August, that figure had shot up to about $2.46. We hadn't made any significant architectural changes: the coordinator was still handing work to the same set of specialist reviewers, and the same risk tiers decided how intensive of a review we gave. Around mid-September we tasked our agents with working out where those tokens were going and cutting them — aggressively. With code quality at high effort, the average review now costs just $0.77, down 68% from the $2.43 it averaged over our two most expensive weeks before we started. Our main goal was to cut costs, but as part of this work we also managed to optimize the reviewer, so that the median review now takes just 1m 32s instead of the 4m 09s it took before. About 40% of the savings came from changes and optimizations to the reviewer's code, and the rest from experimenting with which models we use and how much effort they put in. How a review doubled in cost The chart below shows the cost of an average review on each weekday since March. It holds the mix of review tiers fixed, so a day with more large reviews doesn't skew the data. The cost per review steadily rose from $1.22 (March) → $1.44 (June) → $1.74 (July) and finally, to $2.32 (August). A small part of that is that more reviews landed in the most expensive tier (59% of reviews in March and then 65% in August). We believe there’s a simple answer for why: models are getting much better, and much more capable. Naturally, engineers are producing bigger, more complex changes which means more of them fall into our “full review” tier. We found that most of the cost increase actually came from model changes over those months, though. At the start of August we moved every reviewer onto Anthropic models, which raised the cost per job from $1.38 to $2.03. We made this choice because we found that during our evals, Anthropic models performed better on this specific workload than other models. Our internal standards reviewer, Codex , ended up on Claude Opus 4.7 due to a mix of performance and reliability. That took it from about $0.25 per review to $0.88 in August, which made it more expensive than the coordinator agent itself. The cache hit rate also increased, going from 85.7% in April to 97% by September, while the number of tokens per review more than tripled, from 0.91 million to 2.99 million. A high hit rate on three times as many tokens still costs a lot more, even with the low cache read cost. What else has changed since our last post? One of the biggest changes is that the reviewer now runs on OpenCode v2, which is a ground-up rewrite from v1. Before switching all reviews over from v1 to v2, we ran every review in every canary repo on both v1 and v2 in a comparative shadow mode. The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable . We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out! So, where were the tokens going? Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%, cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again. That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the context, and over the last few months we had slowly increased both. It’s worth taking a few minutes to read about how Anthropic's prompt cache works. It works by caching parts of the prompt that have already been computed by the large language model (LLM). These are known as prefixes, because they only work on the messages at the start of the conversation, not mid way through or the end. This means that a future request can reuse an earlier prefix, up to the part of the conversation that changes from what’s been cached. In our case, the harness tools, system prompt and messages at the start of our AI reviewer sessions rarely change, so they’re a great candidate for prefix caching. A prefix is only stored where a cache breakpoint ends it. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the normal input price and reading costs 0.1 times, and an entry expires after five minutes unless something reads it. That means we had two things to work on: make the first request of each session read from the cache instead of writing to it, and make each session use fewer calls. Sharing a cached prefix between every repository Beginning September 14, the reviewer recorded the token usage of each reviewer's first LLM call, plus a hash of the first system block exactly as it was sent to the provider. The data showed that the first request of a session found a cached prefix only 14% to 26% of the time. Every session starts with the same tool definitions and the same agent prompt, between 11k and 21k tokens that are identical in every repository we review, so almost all of them should have been cache hits. The problem ended up being in how OpenCode v1 constructed the system prompt: It built one block containing our agent prompt, followed by an environment section with the working directory and the date, and placed the only cache breakpoint at the end of that block. The shared part was never stored on its own, so a review in one repository could never reuse what a reviewer ran in another repository had written. On September 16, we added a marker to the end of every agent prompt and a plugin hook that split the block in two at that marker. The first half now ended on bytes that every job shares, and got its own breakpoint. To keep it that way we had to remove anything repository-specific from in front of it, so the list of available skills is disabled and tool descriptions can't change between jobs. The same day we also moved our internal standards (Codex) reviewer's reference index (a table of internal standards, a skill file and a list of reference files) into its prompt. Until then every session had spent its first three turns reading those files with tool calls. Its LLM calls per run decreased from 15.9 to 9.6, and its cost per run dropped from $1.12 to $0.72. Together these took the cost per review from $2.47 down to $2.02, and the drop was noticeable as soon as we kicked off the release. Fewer calls, fewer dollars The next set of changes went out on September 21 and 23. None of them were particularly impressive by themselves, but together they took about $0.20 off every review. Change What was happening Effect of change Removing tools that reviewers couldn't use Sub-reviewers could see the tool that posts the final review comment. In 57% to 76% of sessions they tried to call it, were rejected by a check on the server, and spent another call recovering. One wasted call gone, and about 2.9k fewer tokens of tool definitions in every sub-reviewer request Reading files in parallel In 64% of the code quality reviewer's turns, the model made exactly one tool call, usually to read a single file. Reviewers read the shared context and all of their patches in their first response, up to 150 KB Skipping reviewers on re-reviews About two-thirds of our jobs are a second or later review of the same merge request, and often three of the reviewers have nothing new to look at. On full-tier re-reviews, AGENTS.md reviews are skipped 56% of the time, performance reviews skipped 23% and documentation reviews skipped 13%. Stopping after the review is posted OpenCode passed the result back to the model for one more turn, which read the entire conversation again to write a summary nobody saw. About $0.07 saved per job Treating a slow reviewer differently from a broken provider A reviewer that hit its time limit was treated like a provider failure and started again with the same time limit. Together with longer time limits and lower effort, security reviewer timeouts went from 1.8% of runs to almost none Canceling canceled jobs GitLab's Kubernetes executor doesn't send a signal to a job's script when the job is cancelled. In a sample of 446 cancelled jobs, 358 kept running until the review was finished. Jobs check their own status every 15 seconds and stop if cancelled The most involved change was sharing one prefix between three reviewers. The code quality, security, and performance reviewers now send identical first requests with the same tools, a shared rules file, then the merge request with every patch included. Each reviewer's own instructions follow after that, and we make sure that one of them writes the cache and the other two read from it. A cache entry can't be read until the response that wrote it has started streaming, and the three reviewers start at the same time. So the second and third wait for the first one's response to begin, for up to 20 seconds, before sending their own first request. It slows them down slightly and saves about nine cents per reviewer. Changing models and effort The next chart shows the same line from the start of September, with each change marked. When we split the period at every release and every configuration change, the code changes turn out to be the smaller part of the saving. Code changes account for $0.65 of the $1.67, and model and effort changes for $1.06. Each step compares the weekday hours before a change with the hours after it, so this isn't a statistically sound controlled experiment. The coordinator had been running three model and effort combinations since August. On the same model, full-tier jobs on medium effort finished 20% sooner, so we dropped the other two. In a later randomized split, Opus 5.5 at medium showed no measurable change in review outcomes or critical findings compared with Opus 5, so we switched. Opus 5.5 at high effort cost more than Opus 5.5 at medium while not producing a meaningful increase in findings. Opus 5.5 is cheaper per token than Opus 5, but price is only responsible for about $0.20 of the drop. The rest comes from sending and generating fewer tokens. Since the start of September cache reads per review are down 82%, cache writes down 54%, and output down 67%. The most recent change was a new model. On October 3, we split every Sonnet reviewer 50/50 between Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5. After two and a half days, Sonnet 5.5 was 62% cheaper per run for code quality, 58% for performance and 47% for security. The two models cost the same per token, so all of that comes from using fewer tokens. On full-tier reviews, the 5.5 reviewers posted about as many critical and warning findings as the Sonnet 5 ones, so on October 5 we moved all of them to 5.5. On Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort, the code quality reviewer makes 1.7 LLM calls per run instead of 6.2, and more than half of its runs finish in a single call, which means they don't open any other file in the repository. At high effort it makes 3.4 calls per run. We were concerned that this made reviews shallower, which we cover in the quality section below. To see whether more effort brings findings back on the larger tiers, the code quality reviewer has been split 50/50 between medium and high effort on 5.5 since October 5. After one day, high effort costs 61% more per run and posts 58% more critical and warning findings. That's about two cents per review, and the quality section below shows those extra findings are worth having, so we're moving code quality to high effort. The cost figures in this post assume that. Latency We weren't aiming to make reviews faster, but fewer calls also means less waiting, which means faster reviews and happier engineers. The slowest reviews improved the most. In the four weeks before September 14, 37.9% of reviews took longer than five minutes and now just 0.7% do. The 99th percentile today is faster than three quarters of reviews were in April. Every tier got faster along the way with the median full-tier review going from 5m 16s to 1m 54s, lite from 2m 58s to 1m 14s, and trivial from 77 seconds to 30. By August, the median review was 14% slower than what we reported in April and the 99th percentile 48% slower, so a good part of this work just got us back to where we had been. Review quality A cheaper review isn't worth much if it also finds fewer problems, and the first chart here looks like that's what happened. With code quality on Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, it posts 40% fewer critical and warning findings than it did in late August. Security and performance, which stay at medium effort, post 56% and 71% fewer. A fall in severe findings doesn't tell you on its own whether real problems are being missed or noise is being cut, so we looked at it from two directions. First, we checked whether authors act on what the reviewer flags. For samples of critical and warning findings, we compared the commit that was reviewed with the author's next push, and counted a finding as acted on if the lines it pointed at had changed. Lines 30 to 40 away from each finding changed about 15% of the time in every period, which gives a baseline for edits that happen by coincidence. Before the changes, authors acted on 34% of the code quality reviewer's serious findings. Now it's 59%. The reviewer flags fewer things, but those it flags are much more likely to lead to a change, so the number of findings that led to a change per 1,000 reviews is about the same. We now saw 132 against 145 before, which is within the margin of error. Across all four reviewers, serious findings that led to a change went from 229 to 321 per 1,000 reviews. Second, we had two models from different providers judge a blinded sample of 657 findings from the three Sonnet reviewers, with the diff each one referred to and without knowing which period it came from. Disagreements went to a third model. Each finding was labelled important, minor, duplicate, wrong, or unverifiable, and its severity was marked as fair, too high, or too low. Most of what disappeared was minor findings, plus some duplicates and findings the judges couldn't verify from the diff. Important findings per review went from 0.28 before to 0.30 now, and the intervals overlap. The bigger change was in severity. Before, the judges rated 0.46 critical or warning findings per review as more severe than they deserved. Now that's 0.14, a 70% drop and the clearest result in the research. Much of the drop in critical findings is the reviewer no longer calling minor things critical. So the answer depends on the reviewer. For code quality at high effort, what disappeared was mostly noise and inflated severity, and it still finds about as many real problems as before. Medium effort did lose real findings. In the randomized split, code quality at medium led to roughly a quarter as many acted-on findings as at high, which is why we're moving it to high. Performance also lost real findings: the judges found about 64% fewer important performance issues per review, which in practice is about one fewer important finding every 24 full-tier reviews. Security fell by about a quarter, though that isn't statistically significant. Both are still at medium effort, and testing them at high is next. Neither method is perfect. An author changing the flagged lines shows they did something, not that the finding was right. The judges are models too, and there are only 35 to 66 findings in each group. The "now" window is also only a day long. Even so, the two methods agree with each other, and neither suggests that code quality is finding fewer real problems. Reliability has held up as well. Reviews that end without a verdict went from 0.79% to 0.27%, and security reviewer retries from 3.5% to 0.04%. Where this leaves us An average review now costs $0.77 instead of $2.43, and the median one finishes in 1m 32s instead of 4m 9s. The biggest single saving came from checking what actually reached the provider on each session’s first request, and finding a way to order those messages in a way that was as consistent as possible across commits, merge requests and repositories. The remaining cost savings came from relentlessly experimenting with different models and effort mixes, while making sure we put any preconceived bias for particular models aside. Lower cost reviews didn’t automatically mean worse quality, but it didn’t automatically mean fine either. Code quality at high effort finds about as many real problems as before, with much less noise and far fewer inflated severities. Performance lost real findings at medium effort, and security may have, too, so testing both at high effort is next. If you run agents at any kind of volume, the two things we’d check first are whether each session’s first request actually reads from the cache, and whether your reviewers still find real problems at the effort level you’re paying for. If you’re at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco, I’m talking about how we built the reviewer instead of buying one in my session, It’s time to build, not buy , on Tuesday, October 20 at 12:30 PM PDT. I’ll also be in the Speaker Connection Lounge from 1:10 PM if you want to ask about any of the numbers in this post.

The two agreed on the approval decision in 98% of the merge requests we tested, so we moved everyone over in one go in early October and removed the v1 code. Comparing two days with the same models, full-tier reviews on v2 finish about 13% faster. We’re also currently experimenting with other ways to run our internal AI reviewer, including solely on Durable Objects using pi-durable. We’re hopefully going to have more on this coming soon, so keep an eye out!

So, where were the tokens going?

Right before we started focusing on cost optimization, our AI review spend was split by: output tokens making up about 23%,  cache writes cost 43%, and cache reads cost 34%. This means that  most of the money was going on context the model had already seen or was about to see again.

That makes complete sense when you look into a single session. The code quality reviewer made 16.6 large language model (LLM) calls per review on average and over those calls it wrote 72k tokens to the cache and read back 1.08m, because each call sends the whole conversation as context. A session's cost grows with both the number of calls and the size of the context, and over the last few months we had slowly increased both.

It’s worth taking a few minutes to read about how Anthropic's prompt cache works. It works by caching parts of the prompt that have already been computed by the large language model (LLM). These are known as prefixes, because they only work on the messages at the start of the conversation, not mid way through or the end. This means that a future request can reuse an earlier prefix, up to the part of the conversation that changes from what’s been cached. In our case, the harness tools, system prompt and messages at the start of our AI reviewer sessions rarely change, so they’re a great candidate for prefix caching. A prefix is only stored where a cache breakpoint ends it. Writing to the cache costs 1.25 times the normal input price and reading costs 0.1 times, and an entry expires after five minutes unless something reads it.

That means we had two things to work on: make the first request of each session read from the cache instead of writing to it, and make each session use fewer calls.

Sharing a cached prefix between every repository

Beginning September 14, the reviewer recorded the token usage of each reviewer's first LLM call, plus a hash of the first system block exactly as it was sent to the provider.

The data showed that the first request of a session found a cached prefix only 14% to 26% of the time. Every session starts with the same tool definitions and the same agent prompt, between 11k and 21k tokens that are identical in every repository we review, so almost all of them should have been cache hits.

The problem ended up being in how OpenCode v1 constructed the system prompt: It built one block containing our agent prompt, followed by an environment section with the working directory and the date, and placed the only cache breakpoint at the end of that block. The shared part was never stored on its own, so a review in one repository could never reuse what a reviewer ran in another repository had written.

On September 16, we added a marker to the end of every agent prompt and a plugin hook that split the block in two at that marker. The first half now ended on bytes that every job shares, and got its own breakpoint. To keep it that way we had to remove anything repository-specific from in front of it, so the list of available skills is disabled and tool descriptions can't change between jobs.

The same day we also moved our internal standards (Codex) reviewer's reference index (a table of internal standards, a skill file and a list of reference files) into its prompt. Until then every session had spent its first three turns reading those files with tool calls. Its LLM calls per run decreased from 15.9 to 9.6, and its cost per run dropped from $1.12 to $0.72.

Together these took the cost per review from $2.47 down to $2.02, and the drop was noticeable as soon as we kicked off the release.

Fewer calls, fewer dollars

The next set of changes went out on September 21 and 23. None of them were particularly impressive by themselves, but together they took about $0.20 off every review.

Change

What was happening

Effect of change

Removing tools that reviewers couldn't use

Sub-reviewers could see the tool that posts the final review comment. In 57% to 76% of sessions they tried to call it, were rejected by a check on the server, and spent another call recovering.

One wasted call gone, and about 2.9k fewer tokens of tool definitions in every sub-reviewer request

Reading files in parallel

In 64% of the code quality reviewer's turns, the model made exactly one tool call, usually to read a single file.

Reviewers read the shared context and all of their patches in their first response, up to 150 KB

Skipping reviewers on re-reviews

About two-thirds of our jobs are a second or later review of the same merge request, and often three of the reviewers have nothing new to look at.

On full-tier re-reviews, AGENTS.md reviews are skipped 56% of the time, performance reviews skipped 23% and documentation reviews skipped 13%.

Stopping after the review is posted

OpenCode passed the result back to the model for one more turn, which read the entire conversation again to write a summary nobody saw.

About $0.07 saved per job

Treating a slow reviewer differently from a broken provider

A reviewer that hit its time limit was treated like a provider failure and started again with the same time limit.

Together with longer time limits and lower effort, security reviewer timeouts went from 1.8% of runs to almost none

Canceling canceled jobs

GitLab's Kubernetes executor doesn't send a signal to a job's script when the job is cancelled. In a sample of 446 cancelled jobs, 358 kept running until the review was finished.

Jobs check their own status every 15 seconds and stop if cancelled

The most involved change was sharing one prefix between three reviewers. The code quality, security, and performance reviewers now send identical first requests with the same tools, a shared rules file, then the merge request with every patch included. Each reviewer's own instructions follow after that, and we make sure that one of them writes the cache and the other two read from it.

A cache entry can't be read until the response that wrote it has started streaming, and the three reviewers start at the same time. So the second and third wait for the first one's response to begin, for up to 20 seconds, before sending their own first request. It slows them down slightly and saves about nine cents per reviewer.

Changing models and effort

The next chart shows the same line from the start of September, with each change marked.

When we split the period at every release and every configuration change, the code changes turn out to be the smaller part of the saving.

Code changes account for $0.65 of the $1.67, and model and effort changes for $1.06. Each step compares the weekday hours before a change with the hours after it, so this isn't a statistically sound controlled experiment.

The coordinator had been running three model and effort combinations since August. On the same model, full-tier jobs on medium effort finished 20% sooner, so we dropped the other two. In a later randomized split, Opus 5.5 at medium showed no measurable change in review outcomes or critical findings compared with Opus 5, so we switched. Opus 5.5 at high effort cost more than Opus 5.5 at medium while not producing a meaningful increase in findings.

Opus 5.5 is cheaper per token than Opus 5, but price is only responsible for about $0.20 of the drop. The rest comes from sending and generating fewer tokens. Since the start of September cache reads per review are down 82%, cache writes down 54%, and output down 67%.

The most recent change was a new model. On October 3, we split every Sonnet reviewer 50/50 between Sonnet 5 and Sonnet 5.5. After two and a half days, Sonnet 5.5 was 62% cheaper per run for code quality, 58% for performance and 47% for security. The two models cost the same per token, so all of that comes from using fewer tokens. On full-tier reviews, the 5.5 reviewers posted about as many critical and warning findings as the Sonnet 5 ones, so on October 5 we moved all of them to 5.5.

On Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort, the code quality reviewer makes 1.7 LLM calls per run instead of 6.2, and more than half of its runs finish in a single call, which means they don't open any other file in the repository. At high effort it makes 3.4 calls per run. We were concerned that this made reviews shallower, which we cover in the quality section below.

To see whether more effort brings findings back on the larger tiers, the code quality reviewer has been split 50/50 between medium and high effort on 5.5 since October 5. After one day, high effort costs 61% more per run and posts 58% more critical and warning findings. That's about two cents per review, and the quality section below shows those extra findings are worth having, so we're moving code quality to high effort. The cost figures in this post assume that.

Latency

We weren't aiming to make reviews faster, but fewer calls also means less waiting, which means faster reviews and happier engineers.

The slowest reviews improved the most. In the four weeks before September 14, 37.9% of reviews took longer than five minutes and now just 0.7% do. The 99th percentile today is faster than three quarters of reviews were in April. Every tier got faster along the way with the median full-tier review going from 5m 16s to 1m 54s, lite from 2m 58s to 1m 14s, and trivial from 77 seconds to 30.

By August, the median review was 14% slower than what we reported in April and the 99th percentile 48% slower, so a good part of this work just got us back to where we had been.

Review quality

A cheaper review isn't worth much if it also finds fewer problems, and the first chart here looks like that's what happened.

With code quality on Sonnet 5.5 at high effort, it posts 40% fewer critical and warning findings than it did in late August. Security and performance, which stay at medium effort, post 56% and 71% fewer. A fall in severe findings doesn't tell you on its own whether real problems are being missed or noise is being cut, so we looked at it from two directions.

First, we checked whether authors act on what the reviewer flags. For samples of critical and warning findings, we compared the commit that was reviewed with the author's next push, and counted a finding as acted on if the lines it pointed at had changed. Lines 30 to 40 away from each finding changed about 15% of the time in every period, which gives a baseline for edits that happen by coincidence.

Before the changes, authors acted on 34% of the code quality reviewer's serious findings. Now it's 59%. The reviewer flags fewer things, but those it flags are much more likely to lead to a change, so the number of findings that led to a change per 1,000 reviews is about the same. We now saw 132 against 145 before, which is within the margin of error. Across all four reviewers, serious findings that led to a change went from 229 to 321 per 1,000 reviews.

Second, we had two models from different providers judge a blinded sample of 657 findings from the three Sonnet reviewers, with the diff each one referred to and without knowing which period it came from. Disagreements went to a third model. Each finding was labelled important, minor, duplicate, wrong, or unverifiable, and its severity was marked as fair, too high, or too low.

Most of what disappeared was minor findings, plus some duplicates and findings the judges couldn't verify from the diff. Important findings per review went from 0.28 before to 0.30 now, and the intervals overlap. The bigger change was in severity. Before, the judges rated 0.46 critical or warning findings per review as more severe than they deserved. Now that's 0.14, a 70% drop and the clearest result in the research. Much of the drop in critical findings is the reviewer no longer calling minor things critical.

So the answer depends on the reviewer. For code quality at high effort, what disappeared was mostly noise and inflated severity, and it still finds about as many real problems as before. Medium effort did lose real findings. In the randomized split, code quality at medium led to roughly a quarter as many acted-on findings as at high, which is why we're moving it to high. Performance also lost real findings: the judges found about 64% fewer important performance issues per review, which in practice is about one fewer important finding every 24 full-tier reviews. Security fell by about a quarter, though that isn't statistically significant. Both are still at medium effort, and testing them at high is next.

Neither method is perfect. An author changing the flagged lines shows they did something, not that the finding was right. The judges are models too, and there are only 35 to 66 findings in each group. The "now" window is also only a day long. Even so, the two methods agree with each other, and neither suggests that code quality is finding fewer real problems.

Reliability has held up as well. Reviews that end without a verdict went from 0.79% to 0.27%, and security reviewer retries from 3.5% to 0.04%.

Where this leaves us

An average review now costs $0.77 instead of $2.43, and the median one finishes in 1m 32s instead of 4m 9s. The biggest single saving came from checking what actually reached the provider on each session’s first request, and finding a way to order those messages in a way that was as consistent as possible across commits, merge requests and repositories. The remaining cost savings came from relentlessly experimenting with different models and effort mixes, while making sure we put any preconceived bias for particular models aside.

Lower cost reviews didn’t automatically mean worse quality, but it didn’t automatically mean fine either. Code quality at high effort finds about as many real problems as before, with much less noise and far fewer inflated severities. Performance lost real findings at medium effort, and security may have, too, so testing both at high effort is next. If you run agents at any kind of volume, the two things we’d check first are whether each session’s first request actually reads from the cache, and whether your reviewers still find real problems at the effort level you’re paying for.

If you’re at Cloudflare Connect in San Francisco, I’m talking about how we built the reviewer instead of buying one in my session, It’s time to build, not buy, on Tuesday, October 20 at 12:30 PM PDT. I’ll also be in the Speaker Connection Lounge from 1:10 PM if you want to ask about any of the numbers in this post.

items.title: Where Does My Microsoft Entra ID Data Reside? Understanding Azure Regions and Data Residency
items.summary: Hello everyone! Zoheb Shaikh here again. I’m a Senior Cloud Solution Architect with Microsoft, based in Doha, Qatar. It’s been almost three years since my last blog, and I’m happy to be back sharing another interesting customer conversation. This time, we’ll explore what the new Saudi Azure region really means for Microsoft Entra ID and data residency. I was recently having a conversation with a customer about Microsoft’s announcement of the Saudi Arabia East Azure region, which is expected to become available in November 2026. Naturally, there was a lot of excitement around it. We started discussing what this means for workloads, applications, data, resiliency and, of course, data residency. And then came a very simple question. “Great. So once the Saudi Azure region is available, our Microsoft Entra ID will also be in Saudi, right?” It is actually a very good question. And I think this is something we are going to hear more often as local Azure regions become available across different countries. My answer was: “Not exactly. Azure region availability and Microsoft Entra ID data residency are two different things.” And that started an interesting conversation. “But Entra runs on Azure, right?” Yes , But this is where we need to understand the difference between a workload that we deploy into Azure and a cloud service that Microsoft operates for us. Think about a normal Azure workload, y ou want to deploy a VM > Azure asks you: Where do you want to deploy it? Saudi Arabia East , UAE North , UK South , West Europe. You select the region based on your requirements. The same concept applies to many other supported Azure services. With the new Saudi Arabia East region, customers will be able to access supported Microsoft cloud and AI services and host eligible workloads and data locally in the Kingdom. Microsoft has announced that the region will also include three Availability Zones. That is the Azure region conversation But Microsoft Entra ID is different. You don’t create your Microsoft Entra tenant and then say: “Deploy my Entra tenant into Saudi Arabia East.” That is not how the service is designed. So how does Microsoft Entra actually work? This is where the architecture becomes interesting. Microsoft Entra ID is designed as a geographically distributed identity service. When an Entra tenant is created in the public cloud, the country or region selected during tenant creation is mapped by Microsoft Entra to a geo-location and a scale unit. Microsoft’s documentation currently lists geo-locations such as EMEA, North America, Asia/Pacific, Japan, Australia and Worldwide. The tenant location isn’t simply determined by where you later deploy your Azure VMs or applications. I explained it to the customer like this. If you deploy an application into Azure, you are largely deciding : “Where should my workload run?” For Microsoft Entra, Microsoft is managing a global identity platform and deciding: “How do we keep identity available, resilient and responsive while respecting the service’s data-residency architecture?” They are two very different design problems. Then the customer asked the next obvious question “Why does Entra need to work this way?” And this is probably my favourite part of the discussion. Imagine your company’s entire authentication service was dependent on one datacenter. Your users are signing in , Your applications are authenticating , Microsoft 365 depends on identity , Azure depends on identity. Thousands of applications may depend on the same identity platform and n ow imagine that datacenter has a problem. Identity is one of those services where availability really matters, t his is one of reasons Microsoft Entra uses a distributed architecture. Microsoft’s published architecture describes a directory partition as having a primary replica and multiple secondary replicas. The primary replica handles writes , Before a write is acknowledged as successful, Microsoft Entra replicates that write to a secondary replica in another datacenter. Reads work differently , Directory reads, including authentication requests, can be serviced by secondary replicas that are geographically distributed. Microsoft routes these requests so that they can be serviced from datacenters close to customers. Now the architecture starts making more sense. It isn’t distributed randomly, It is distributed because the identity platform needs to provide things such as: availability , resiliency, performance and data durability. “So when I authenticate, am I always talking to where my directory data is stored?” Not necessarily in the way we traditionally think about it. This was another useful part of our conversation. Microsoft documents the Microsoft Entra authentication service itself as stateless. The directory data required for authentication resides in the Microsoft Entra Core Store. When users authenticate, Microsoft can route them to an authentication service instance in the geographically nearest datacenter that forms part of the applicable Microsoft Entra logical region. This is an important concept. The place from which a service responds to you and the place where the underlying authoritative data is managed do not always have to be the same thing. That is quite normal in large cloud services. And then came the real question: “Where is my data?” This is where I normally slow the conversation down a little. Because there are actually a few different questions hiding inside that one question. The customer might be asking: Where does my application data reside ? Or Where does my Microsoft Entra directory data reside ? Or Where is my authentication request being processed? Or perhaps the actual concern is Do I meet a specific regulatory requirement? These questions sound similar. But technically, they are not the same. For Microsoft Entra ID, Microsoft’s public documentation says the country/region selected during tenant creation is mapped to a Microsoft Entra geo-location and a scale unit. Microsoft Entra Core Store data is then managed according to that geo-location, considering areas such as performance, usability, residency and other requirements. That is why simply saying: “I have an Azure datacenter in my country, therefore every Microsoft cloud service must now store its data there” would be an oversimplification. There is actually an interesting Saudi-specific detail here At this point the conversation usually gets a little more interesting. Microsoft’s public documentation explains that Microsoft Entra directory location is determined when the tenant is originally created. Changing the country code later doesn’t move the directory data location. There is also some historical behaviour worth understanding. Microsoft documents that several country codes — including Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman — were mapped to the Asia region until 2013 and later mapped to Europe. As a result, tenants from those countries created before July 2013 can be provisioned differently from tenants created afterward. Why do I like this example? Because it makes one thing very clear : You shouldn’t determine your Microsoft Entra data location simply by looking at where your Azure workloads are deployed today but t enant provisioning history matters as well. “Okay, but is distributed data less secure?” This is another place where two conversations sometimes get mixed together. Data residency and security are related, but they are not the same thing. Data residency generally talks about where data is geographically stored. Security talks about how that data and the service around it are protected. Microsoft documents several protections around the Entra service. For example, Microsoft Entra directory data is signed and encrypted while it is being transferred between datacenters within a scale unit, and customer-facing web services use TLS. Microsoft also documents tenant-isolation controls around the Entra Core Store. Microsoft Entra also uses geographically distributed replicas, automated routing, monitoring and failover as part of its service architecture. So I wouldn’t look at a distributed architecture and conclude: “The data isn’t sitting in my local Azure region, therefore it is less secure.” That isn’t the right comparison. But I also wouldn’t say: “The service is secure, therefore data residency doesn’t matter.” That isn’t correct either. Security and regulatory residency are two different conversations This is probably the most important takeaway from the whole discussion. Imagine a customer tells me: “Our concern is security.” Then we should discuss the security architecture, tenant isolation, encryption, authentication controls, privileged access, service resilience and the controls Microsoft has put around the service. But imagine the customer says: “Our regulator specifically requires this category of data to be stored within Saudi Arabia.” That becomes a data-residency and compliance conversation. The right thing to do in that situation is not to make an assumption based on the availability of a local Azure region. Instead, check the official Microsoft documentation for the specific service and the specific data type involved. Microsoft’s Trust Center provides service-specific information for Microsoft Azure, Microsoft 365, Microsoft Entra ID, Intune, Defender and other cloud services. This is important because not every Microsoft cloud service follows exactly the same data-storage architecture. Back to the Saudi Azure region, So after all of this, we came back to where our conversation started. What does Saudi Arabia East actually change ? A lot. Microsoft has announced that Saudi Arabia East will allow government and private-sector organizations to access supported Microsoft cloud and AI services and host eligible workloads and data locally in the Kingdom. The region will contain three Availability Zones, providing another important building block for organizations designing resilient local architectures . For customers running Azure applications, data platforms, infrastructure and AI workloads, this is a very significant development. But does that automatically mean an existing Microsoft Entra tenant moves into the Saudi Arabia East Azure region? No , And that shouldn’t really be surprising once we understand how Microsoft Entra is designed. The easiest way I explain it By the end of the conversation, I normally reduce everything into two simple questions. Azure Region is “Where do I want to deploy my workload?” For eligible Azure services, Saudi Arabia East gives customers another local option . Microsoft Entra ID “How does Microsoft’s identity service manage and protect my directory data?” That involves Microsoft Entra geo-locations, scale units, replicas and a geographically distributed service architecture. And then there is a third question which is equally important: Data residency “What does Microsoft commit to regarding the storage of my specific data for this specific cloud service?” That answer should always come from the relevant service documentation rather than from assumptions about where the nearest Azure datacenter happens to be. One last thought I actually think conversations like this are healthy. When customers ask “Where is my data? ”, we shouldn’t try to answer the question with one sentence. Because modern cloud architecture doesn’t always work like the datacenter architecture we grew up with. An Azure region. A Microsoft Entra geography. A scale unit. A service endpoint. A replica. A data-residency commitment. They can all be part of the same cloud architecture, but they don’t necessarily mean the same thing. The Saudi Arabia East region is a major step forward for customers wanting to run Azure workloads locally in the Kingdom. And at the same time, it gives us a great opportunity to have a deeper conversation about how global cloud services such as Microsoft Entra ID are actually built . My conversation with the customer started with: “So Entra will now also be in Saudi, right?” By the end, the question had changed to something much better: “What is our actual data-residency requirement, and how does Microsoft Entra meet it?” And I think that is the right conversation to have. References Microsoft announces Saudi Arabia East datacenter region https://news.microsoft.com/source/emea/2026/08/microsoft-announces-saudi-arabia-east-datacenter-region-will-be-available-in-november-2026/ Microsoft Entra ID and data residency https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/data-residency Microsoft Entra architecture https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/architecture/architecture Customer data storage and processing for European customers in Microsoft Entra ID https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/data-storage-eu Microsoft Entra data protection considerations https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/data-protection-considerations Microsoft Trust Center – Data location https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/trust-center/privacy/data-location I hope this blog helped clarify the difference between Azure regions and Microsoft Entra ID data residency. These are the kinds of interesting customer conversations that I enjoy sharing, and I hope to continue writing more regularly. As always, feel free to share your thoughts, questions or experiences in the comments. I'd love to hear your views! Thanks for reading, and until next time! Zoheb Shaikh Senior Cloud Solution Architect | Microsoft Doha, Qatar

That isn’t correct either. 

Security and regulatory residency are two different conversations 

This is probably the most important takeaway from the whole discussion. Imagine a customer tells me: “Our concern is security.” 

Then we should discuss the security architecture, tenant isolation, encryption, authentication controls, privileged access, service resilience and the controls Microsoft has put around the service. 

But imagine the customer says: “Our regulator specifically requires this category of data to be stored within Saudi Arabia.” 

That becomes a data-residency and compliance conversation. The right thing to do in that situation is not to make an assumption based on the availability of a local Azure region. 

Instead, check the official Microsoft documentation for the specific service and the specific data type involved. 

Microsoft’s Trust Center provides service-specific information for Microsoft Azure, Microsoft 365, Microsoft Entra ID, Intune, Defender and other cloud services. 

This is important because not every Microsoft cloud service follows exactly the same data-storage architecture. 

Back to the Saudi Azure region,
So after all of this, we came back to where our conversation started. What does Saudi Arabia East actually change? 

A lot. 

Microsoft has announced that Saudi Arabia East will allow government and private-sector organizations to access supported Microsoft cloud and AI services and host eligible workloads and data locally in the Kingdom. 

The region will contain three Availability Zones, providing another important building block for organizations designing resilient local architectures. 

For customers running Azure applications, data platforms, infrastructure and AI workloads, this is a very significant development. 

But does that automatically mean an existing Microsoft Entra tenant moves into the Saudi Arabia East Azure region? 

No, And that shouldn’t really be surprising once we understand how Microsoft Entra is designed. 

The easiest way I explain it 

By the end of the conversation, I normally reduce everything into two simple questions. 

Azure Region is “Where do I want to deploy my workload?” 

For eligible Azure services, Saudi Arabia East gives customers another local option. 

Microsoft Entra ID  

“How does Microsoft’s identity service manage and protect my directory data?” 

That involves Microsoft Entra geo-locations, scale units, replicas and a geographically distributed service architecture. 

And then there is a third question which is equally important: 

Data residency 

“What does Microsoft commit to regarding the storage of my specific data for this specific cloud service?” 

That answer should always come from the relevant service documentation rather than from assumptions about where the nearest Azure datacenter happens to be. 

One last thought 

I actually think conversations like this are healthy.  When customers ask “Where is my data?”, we shouldn’t try to answer the question with one sentence. 

Because modern cloud architecture doesn’t always work like the datacenter architecture we grew up with. 

  • An Azure region. 
  • A Microsoft Entra geography. 
  • A scale unit. 
  • A service endpoint. 
  • A replica. 
  • A data-residency commitment. 

They can all be part of the same cloud architecture, but they don’t necessarily mean the same thing. 

The Saudi Arabia East region is a major step forward for customers wanting to run Azure workloads locally in the Kingdom. 

And at the same time, it gives us a great opportunity to have a deeper conversation about how global cloud services such as Microsoft Entra ID are actually built. 

My conversation with the customer started with: “So Entra will now also be in Saudi, right?” 

By the end, the question had changed to something much better: “What is our actual data-residency requirement, and how does Microsoft Entra meet it?” And I think that is the right conversation to have. 

 

References 

Microsoft announces Saudi Arabia East datacenter region 
https://news.microsoft.com/source/emea/2026/08/microsoft-announces-saudi-arabia-east-datacenter-region-will-be-available-in-november-2026/ 

Microsoft Entra ID and data residency 
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/data-residency 

Microsoft Entra architecture 
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/architecture/architecture 

Customer data storage and processing for European customers in Microsoft Entra ID 
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/data-storage-eu 

Microsoft Entra data protection considerations 
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/fundamentals/data-protection-considerations 

Microsoft Trust Center – Data location 
https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/trust-center/privacy/data-location 

 

I hope this blog helped clarify the difference between Azure regions and Microsoft Entra ID data residency. These are the kinds of interesting customer conversations that I enjoy sharing, and I hope to continue writing more regularly.

As always, feel free to share your thoughts, questions or experiences in the comments. I'd love to hear your views!

Thanks for reading, and until next time!

Zoheb Shaikh
Senior Cloud Solution Architect | Microsoft
Doha, Qatar

items.title: Critical Drupal RCE Vulnerability Could Let Attackers Take Over Websites Without Authentication
items.summary: Drupal has released security updates for a critical remote code execution vulnerability that could let attackers take over affected websites without logging in. Tracked as CVE-2026-108097, the flaw affects the Field UI module in Drupal core. The Drupal Security Team published its warning on October 14, 2026. The official security advisory, SA-CORE-2026-014, assigns the issue a risk score of 19 out of 25 under Drupal’s rating system. Successful exploitation could expose all private website data and allow attackers to change or delete information. The score is not a CVSS rating. The most important detail is that Drupal core alone does not provide a direct path to exploit the flaw. However, the security team confirmed that several serious attack paths exist when contributed modules are present. These are additional modules used to extend a website’s features beyond its core functions. At least one known attack path requires no authentication, meaning an attacker would not need a valid account. Custom website code may also expose the vulnerable functionality. Site owners should consider installed extensions and custom development, rather than judging exposure by Drupal version alone. Critical Drupal RCE Vulnerability The public advisory does not name the contributed modules involved or provide a working exploit. Its rating describes exploitation as theoretical, with no public exploit code or development documentation. That wording should not be mistaken for proof of safety, given the confirmed attack paths described by the security team. The issue follows earlier concerns about Drupal security, including coverage of a Drupal core SQL injection vulnerability . That report concerns a separate flaw. Its exploitation status should not be applied to this Field UI vulnerability, for which the current advisory does not report attacks in the wild. The affected ranges cover Drupal versions from 8.9.0 before 10.6.19, 11.0.0 before 11.3.19, and 11.4.0 before 11.4.10. Drupal 12 development releases from 12.0.0-alpha1 before 12.0.0-beta2 are also affected. The broad version coverage makes it important to check every deployed site, especially where organizations maintain several Drupal installations. Administrators running Drupal 11.4.x should install Drupal 11.4.10. Those using Drupal 11.3.x should move to 11.3.19, while Drupal 10.6.x users should install 10.6.19. Drupal 11.2.x and earlier, Drupal 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 8 and 9 no longer receive security coverage. Drupal says uninstalling the core Field UI module (field_ui) protects while sites are updated. Drupal Steward also blocks some known attack paths, but it doesn’t cover every possible exploit. Organizations using that service still need to upgrade rather than treat filtering as a permanent fix. For teams reviewing possible compromise, guidance on detecting and investigating webshells offers useful background on malicious scripts that enable remote commands. The immediate priority for this vulnerability remains clear. Apply the supported security release, or uninstall Field UI while preparing the update, without relying solely on partial network protection measures. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Microsoft Says AI Agents Cannot Be Trusted and Could Become Insider Security Threats
items.summary: Microsoft warns organizations to treat AI agents as potential insider risks not because they are automatically malicious, but because they can access company data, apps, and tools and act on that access at high speed. The warning, published on October 19, 2026, comes as businesses use agents to handle tasks such as writing code, reviewing documents, and processing expenses. An agent’s actions can change as its instructions, data, or working context change. It may make a mistake, follow harmful directions hidden in a document, or be compromised. Because agents can act across connected systems, an unsafe action could expose sensitive information or change business records before a person notices. Microsoft’s point is not that every agent is dangerous. It is that organizations should not assume an agent will always behave as intended. The risk grows when an agent receives more access than its task requires. An agent used to review expense claims, for example, may need to read submissions and check company rules. It should not automatically inherit all the permissions of the employee who set it up. If it encounters hidden instructions in a file or tries to take an unrelated action, security controls should be able to limit what it can do. items.summary_html:
Microsoft warns organizations to treat AI agents as potential insider risks not because they are automatically malicious, but because they can access company data, apps, and tools and act on that access at high speed.

The warning, published on October 19, 2026, comes as businesses use agents to handle tasks such as writing code, reviewing documents, and processing expenses.

An agent’s actions can change as its instructions, data, or working context change. It may make a mistake, follow harmful directions hidden in a document, or be compromised.

Because agents can act across connected systems, an unsafe action could expose sensitive information or change business records before a person notices. Microsoft’s point is not that every agent is dangerous. It is that organizations should not assume an agent will always behave as intended.

The risk grows when an agent receives more access than its task requires. An agent used to review expense claims, for example, may need to read submissions and check company rules. It should not automatically inherit all the permissions of the employee who set it up. If it encounters hidden instructions in a file or tries to take an unrelated action, security controls should be able to limit what it can do.

AI Models as Insider Threats

Microsoft says those controls should operate outside the AI model. The model can provide answers or plans, but separate security systems should decide what data it can access and which actions it can take.

This matters because a model should not be able to change or bypass the safeguards that govern it. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has described this approach as separating the supply of intelligence from the authority to act.

I recently wrote about why we need to treat models as insider risks, with security controls sitting outside the model itself.

Today, we're putting that principle into practice by expanding Project Perception with new capabilities to help continuously assess agent risk, adapt…

— Satya Nadella (@satyanadella) October 19, 2026

To support this approach, Microsoft announced plans to expand agent discovery and controls through Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365. The company says it is adding support for 35 more types of local agents, bringing its total to 60, and expanding Microsoft Entra Agent ID so agents can have identities separate from their human sponsors. That separation can help security teams track who owns an agent and distinguish its actions from a person’s.

Microsoft also described Dynamic Permissions, Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents. The proposed controls would give agents only the access needed for a task and adjust that access as risk changes.

For example, an organization might let an agent continue reading information while blocking it from making changes, restrict the systems it can reach, or require human approval before a sensitive action. At higher risk, the agent could be isolated or stopped.

The company also introduced Guardian Agents, intended to help security teams monitor agent activity and respond to changes at machine speed. Microsoft says people would still set the rules and retain control of important decisions, while Guardian Agents could investigate alerts and apply permitted safeguards. The announcements describe Microsoft’s planned security approach, not a guarantee that every agent-related threat can be prevented.

For security teams, the message is to build agent oversight into deployment from the start. That means tracking which agents exist, assigning clear identities, limiting permissions, monitoring activity, and keeping an independent way to stop unsafe actions.

Related coverage from Cybersecurity News examines Microsoft’s prompt-injection protection for Office 365 and execution containers for securing AI workflows. When agents can act across company systems, visibility and limits are essential to using them safely.
