items.title: Introducing Clairic, a new System One class of extraction models
items.summary: Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic. We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs. Context When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow , a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows. We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours? None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models. Introducing System One extraction models Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and Clef take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. Clairic is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with values directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it. Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds. An extraction model can return: Extracted values: Text copied from the input, such as a name, an order ID or a description. Each one comes back as a span with its character offsets and a confidence score. Including, computed values: Numbers, dates, times, datetimes, durations and lists, read from the input or worked out from it. They follow the rules of their type (for example, two decimals for cents) and come with a confidence score. Estimated values: Values the input doesn't state but gives evidence for. Each one comes back as a distribution inside the bounds you declare, on the grid you specify, with a median and an 80% interval. Forecasted values: Future values of a series, one estimate per step ahead, each with its own 80% interval. And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look. Here’s how extraction models fit into the landscape of System One and System Two models: System One: Extract System One: Decide System Two Example models Clairic Jev, Clef GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek Sampling One parallel pass One parallel pass One token at a time Purpose Predict values Make decisions Write and reason ML framing Regression and extraction Classification Generation Thinking mode System 1: fast, one pass System 1: fast, one pass System 2: slow, deliberate Output Typed values: spans, numbers, dates, times, lists, distributions, with calibrated probabilities Typed decisions: options with calibrated probabilities Free-form strings Output space Continuous, but typed and bounded by your schema A finite set of options you list Anything What it answers What's the amount? When does it happen? How much will it be? Which category is it? Is it legitimate? Which action should we take? Why did it happen? How should we approach it? Can you fix it? Output always a valid response? Yes: every answer is a value of its declared type (or null), inside your bounds Yes: answers are always one of your options No: strings must be parsed and checked Together, these models can work together in unison to help you get closer to parsing through real-world data, making decisions on inputs, and then taking actions. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words. How a request works Clairic is designed differently than an LLM. Similar to a decision model, it only processes input tokens with a single forward pass, and thus has no charge for output tokens. It is much faster, cheaper, and more accurate than an LLM for certain use cases. A request is a state (the text to read, plus up to four optional images) and a map of typed fields . You name each field, give it a type and optional plain-language instructions , and get back one typed answer per field, all from one parallel pass. There is no reasoning and no output tokens – everything computes in a single forward pass, which means it is both fast and cheap. Type Returns text A specific span of the input, with its offsets number A number read or computed, honoring integer and decimals date , time , datetime Calendar dates and valid times, in ISO form duration A length of time in the unit you choose list Matching text, number or date, in input order estimate A distribution inside your [min, max] , on your step grid, linear or log scale. forecast One estimate per future step of a series Every scalar answer comes with p_null (the probability that the value isn’t in the inputs) and confidence . Every estimate answer comes with a median and an 80% interval ( p10 to p90 ), plus all 99 percentiles on request. There's no limit on the number of fields: if they don't fit beside the input in one pass, the server splits them into parallel passes that each see the whole input, then merges the answers. Here are some examples to illustrate the model’s features. Of course, using these features in a workflow would require appropriate inputs. An example: Extracting values Extraction is probably the most common job handed to LLMs today: "return the invoice number, vendor and due date as JSON." It works most of the time, but the failure modes are hard to catch. The output may not be valid JSON, a digit can be misread as it's generated, and once a text excerpt comes back, there's no way to trace it to where it appeared in the source. Most people build extraction pipelines to combat this, with multiple layers of parsing, schema validation, retries and spot checks. On top of that, you pay for reasoning and output tokens on every field of every document. Clairic operates differently; it doesn’t generate text answers. Instead, you get: Values extracted from your input, so an answer is grounded. Computed values , so it can parse through unstructured data without pre-sanitizing it. Character offset spans , so you can reference where in the input the data was. Confidence labels , so you can determine which values need a second look. A strongly typed output , so numbers and dates are formed under the rules of their type (e.g., a cents field has two decimals). Handling for null values , where a missing field returns with null as an answer (along with an estimated probability of null and a guess). Cheaper and faster answers , because every field is answered in the same parallel pass. So asking for thirty fields costs about the same as asking for three. Let’s walk through an example to illustrate the ways Clairic can extract values from unstructured data and make estimates. Take a customer support email: Hi, order A-88412 arrived on Sept 28, 2026 with a cracked screen and a dented corner. I paid $649.00 plus $52.10 tax. It's now Oct 9, 2026 and I'd like this fixed or refunded. Thanks, Dana From a Worker, you would make a request to Clairic to process this data: const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", { state: email, fields: { order_id: { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" }, delivered_on: { type: "date", instructions: "Delivery date" }, amount_paid: { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" }, days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true, instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" }, damage: { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" }, tracking_number: { type: "text" }, }, }); Clairic returns the extracted values, spans in the input, probability that it is null (p_null) and confidence score: { "order_id": { "type": "text", "p_null": 3.4e-6, "span": [10, 17], "guess": "A-88412", "confidence": 0.999957, "value": "A-88412" }, "delivered_on": { "type": "date", "p_null": 6.5e-8, "guess": "2026-09-28", "confidence": 0.999999, "value": "2026-09-28" }, "amount_paid": { "type": "number", "p_null": 1.6e-5, "guess": 701.1, "confidence": 0.999944, "value": 701.1 }, "days_since_delivery": { "type": "duration", "p_null": 6.1e-9, "unit": "days", "guess": 11, "confidence": 0.999999, "value": 11 }, "damage": { "type": "list", "value": ["cracked screen", "dented corner"], "spans": [[50, 64], [71, 84]] }, "tracking_number": { "type": "text", "p_null": 1, "span": [106, 112], "guess": "$52.10", "confidence": 0.416016, "value": null } } A few things to notice: amount_paid isn't written anywhere in the email. In this example, Clairic added the price and the tax in the same pass and returns the sum. days_since_delivery is also worked out from two dates in the text, not directly in the input. damage lists both kinds of damage as exact spans, so you can highlight them in the source. tracking_number isn't in the email, so it comes back null instead of a plausible-looking guess. guess shows what the model would otherwise have picked. Clairic also works with images Here’s a real-life photo of a receipt — the text is not perfect and the angle of the image doesn’t help its legibility. We passed this image to Clairic to see what it could extract: { "model": "clairic", "answers": { "order_number": { "type": "number", "p_null": 0.0040206750854849815, "guess": 77245, "confidence": 0.776249383996532, "value": 77245 }, "purchased_at": { "type": "datetime", "p_null": 4.136094133855295e-08, "guess": "2026-07-01T13:34:00", "confidence": 0.831464227002992, "value": "2026-07-01T13:34:00" }, "quantity": { "type": "number", "p_null": 5.2313655629632194e-08, "guess": 2, "confidence": 0.9997007500403496, "value": 2 }, "unit_price": { "type": "number", "p_null": 0.001599092734977603, "guess": 7.99, "confidence": 0.9991279019989127, "value": 7.99 }, "subtotal": { "type": "number", "p_null": 9.69956488461321e-08, "guess": 15.98, "confidence": 0.9999881983893096, "value": 15.98 }, "sales_tax": { "type": "number", "p_null": 2.5511653802823275e-06, "guess": 0, "confidence": 0.9999800924450729, "value": 0 }, "tip": { "type": "number", "p_null": 5.953857908025384e-05, "guess": 2.39, "confidence": 0.9335768781214697, "value": 2.39 }, "discount": { "type": "number", "p_null": 0.9994148015975952, "guess": 0, "confidence": 0.91852733929319, "value": null } } } As you can see, it was able to extract all the values from the images, alongside a confidence score. It also correctly stated that there was no discount shown in the receipt, giving the value as null. An example: Estimating values Some values aren't in the input at all, but the input carries evidence for them. For example, values might not be in plain text but can be discerned from values around it. If you ask an LLM for an estimation, you usually get a single number with no sense of how sure the model is. It will make safe guesses or hallucinate, or reason its way around the answer. If you land on an estimate, any downstream processing can't tell a confident $180 from an unconfident $180, so it can't help you decide what is appropriate to automate in the circumstances. It is also a lot slower and more expensive to do reasoning through LLMs. A decision model can approximate an estimate by choosing among buckets ("under $100", "$100–500", …), but buckets are coarse, every bucket adds input tokens, and each new category adds more sources of confusion for the model during its decision making process. Clairic returns a distribution over the range you declare: a point value, a median, an 80% interval, and every percentile on request. The estimate is designed to fall inside your bounds, so there's nothing to clamp or round afterward. The width of the interval reflects data confidence: a narrow range signals high certainty, while a wide range indicates low certainty, information you can use to route another check. Here’s another example, where Clairic looks at historical home prices and comparable sales, to determine an estimate : const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", { state: `Comparable sales: sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood,sale_price 1450,3,1998,Elm Park,412000 2100,4,2006,Elm Park,585000 980,2,1975,Riverside,265000 1600,3,2003,Elm Park,449000 1300,3,1990,Riverside,318000 Subject property: sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood 1620,3,2001,Elm Park`, fields: { sale_price: { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 50000, max: 5000000, scale: "log", step: 1000 } }); Clairic will return an estimated value: { "sale_price": { "type": "estimate", "value": 418000, "median": 415000, "p10": 370000, "p90": 470000, "p_below": 0.0, "p_above": 0.0 } } Values always fall inside your bounds, and the width of the interval shows how much the input informs the prediction: price is narrow ($370,000-$470,000), days on market is wide (24-148). Because fields are unlimited and answered in parallel, you can score many items in one call (one estimate per candidate, lead, or listing) and sort them in code. An example: Forecasting values Forecasting values in a time series is quite hard for generalized models — it usually means you have to either build a specific pipeline per metric (parse the data, fit a model, tune it, deploy it), or you paste 36 months of numbers into an LLM and ask for the next three. The first is accurate but really expensive and time-consuming to set up for every new series. The second is easy, but you get point forecasts with no intervals, forecasts that shift depending on how the prompt is worded, and answers with limited confidence. Clairic sits between the two — it is not claiming to replace a dedicated time-series model, but it is a little faster and cheaper than your regular LLM. A forecast field takes the history as plain text in state and returns, for every step ahead, a value and an 80% interval, inside the bounds you declare. It reads the history the way you already have it, whether that's a CSV export, a pasted dashboard, or rows mixed with notes, and may often work with no need to clean up your data beforehand. To see how that holds up on real data, we used a public series: the number of people the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screens at U.S. airport checkpoints each day. Each morning we asked Clairic for the next day's count, given the real counts so far, for 21 days in a row: const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", { state: `Daily number of people screened at TSA checkpoints at US airports. date,weekday,travelers 2026-07-16,Thu,2850229 ... 2026-10-13,Tue,2353356 Forecast date: 2026-10-14 (Wed)`, fields: { travelers: { type: "forecast", horizon: 1, interval: "day", min: 500000, max: 4000000, scale: "log", instructions: "Number of people screened tomorrow" }, }, }); Which returns: { "travelers": { "type": "forecast", "value": [2416117], "median": [2419283], "p10": [2270774], "p90": [2556769] } } In actuality, TSA screened 2,419,474 people that day, which is right around the median 2,419,283 that Clairic predicted. Data: TSA checkpoint travel numbers , accessed Oct. 15, 2026. Across the 21 days, Clairic's forecasts were off by 3.3% on average, and 17 of the 21 actual counts landed inside its 80% interval, which follows what an 80% interval should do. It picked up the weekly rhythm from the numbers alone: quieter Tuesdays and Saturdays, busier Thursdays, Fridays, and Sundays. The misses are also interesting: three of the four days outside the interval fall on the Columbus Day weekend, when more people flew than the previous weeks suggested. Clairic forecasts from the patterns in the series but doesn't account for events the series doesn't show, like holidays. Thinking fast and slow These models are designed to fit alongside your existing agentic workflows. An extraction model predicts values, a decision model decides what to do with these values, and an LLM takes action with them. It is a perfect marriage between System One and System Two models. It bridges the existing gap, where you either have to manually extract data for LLMs, or have an LLM parse through messy data (which is costly, time-consuming, and can lead to hallucinations). With System One extraction models, you can work with real-world data with more speed, efficiency, and precision. Here's an example of the damaged-product claim from earlier, illustrating how all the models can work together. We built this into a live demo you can try here . // 1. Clairic turns the email into values const facts = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", { state: email, fields: { customer_name: { type: "text", instructions: "Customer's first name" }, order_id: { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" }, amount_paid: { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" }, days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true, instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" }, damage: { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" }, repair_cost: { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 10, max: 5000, scale: "log", step: 1, instructions: "Cost to repair the damage described" }, }, })).answers; const { customer_name, order_id, amount_paid, days_since_delivery, damage, repair_cost } = facts; // 2. Clef decides from Clairic's values and the policy, not from the raw email const options = { refund: "Full refund of the amount paid", repair: "Free repair, with a prepaid shipping label", }; const { choice } = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clef", { state: `Damage claim for order ${order_id.value}. Paid: $${amount_paid.value.toFixed(2)}. Delivered ${days_since_delivery.value} days ago. Damage reported: ${damage.value.join(", ")}. Estimated repair cost: $${repair_cost.median} (80% range $${repair_cost.p10}-$${repair_cost.p90}). Policy: refunds within 30 days of delivery. Prefer repair when it costs less than 60% of the price and the damage doesn't stop the product from working.`, questions: { resolution: { type: "choice", instructions: "What should we offer?", criteria: options }, }, })).answers.resolution; // 3. An LLM writes the reply, from the decision and the facts it needs const { response } = await env.AI.run("@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3", { messages: [{ role: "user", content: `Write a short, warm reply to ${customer_name.value}. Use only these facts: order ${order_id.value}; ` + `damage: ${damage.value.join(", ")}; what happens next: ${options[choice]}. Under 60 words.`, }], }); Each step gets cleaner input than the one before. Clef decides from a five-line summary of typed values instead of a free-form email, which can also be susceptible to prompt injection. The LLM never sees the email, only the decision and the predictions it needs, so there are fewer numbers for it to misuse. Every step is typed and auditable, and only one step generates text. In the all-LLM version of this pipeline, all three steps are generative calls, and every value in the reply has to be checked by hand. We ran this pipeline against an all-LLM version with GLM-5.3 writing the reply in both. In the all-LLM version, GLM-5.3 also does the extraction and the decision, from the same email, policy and prompts: Clairic → Clef → GLM-5.3 GLM-5.3 for every step Latency, end to end 19.3 s 61.7 s 1. Extract Clairic: 0.46 s GLM-5.3: 16.1 s 2. Decide Clef: 0.22 s GLM-5.3: 21.9 s 3. Reply GLM-5.3: 18.6 s GLM-5.3: 16.4 s Input tokens 701 ($184 per million claims) 390 ($546 per million claims) Output tokens 1,329 ($5,848 per million claims) 2,544 ($11,194 per million claims) Cost per million claims $6,032 $11,740 The cascade finished in 19.3 seconds against 61.7 seconds: 69% less time, or about 3.2 times faster . Clairic and Clef handled extraction and the decision in under a second combined, where GLM-5.3 took 38 seconds for the same two steps. It also costs 49% less to use the cascaded pipeline vs the all-LLM pipeline. With GLM, both pipelines got the facts and the decision right in every run, but Clairic's repair estimate was identical each time, while GLM-5.3's changed on every run ($250, $250 and $220, with different ranges each time). Notably, under the all-LLM pipeline both Gemma 4 and Qwen failed at this task, as they were unable to deduce values like repair_cost from the inputs, showing how LLMs are not great at data extraction tasks. Preview release Today, we're releasing a hosted endpoint for Clairic on Workers AI. We intend to release the model with open weights soon. We wanted to take the time first to introduce the concept of a System One extraction model, so you can start thinking about how this class of model would fit into appropriate workflows. The current endpoint is an early checkpoint and we expect it to get better. Here are our early impressions: Reading is strong, but multi-step arithmetic isn't yet. One- and two-step calculations (totals, differences, conversions, date arithmetic) seem reliable. Longer chains of dependent steps are hard for any one-pass model without a scratchpad. The same goes for aggregating across many rows of a table. At least for now, have Clairic predict the value and let code do the math. Estimates need evidence. Clairic estimates best from comparables, history, or descriptive text in the input. Asking it for a value it has no evidence for may be limited in specificity. Calibration is measured, not guaranteed. Intervals are trained to be calibrated and are on most held-out sets, but they can run narrow on unfamiliar data. Forecasting is basic . The model is not designed to accurately replace or predict time-series models that are trained on specific data. You should use it where appropriate, such as non-critical, general pattern matching, not detailed long-horizon forecasting. Use confidence. The architecture makes every answer well formed, not necessarily correct. Use confidence , p_null and the intervals to decide what to automate (in an appropriate workflow context) and what to send off for additional review. We'll keep working on the arithmetic, estimation and forecasting sides of the model with each checkpoint. After some more work, we plan to release the model open-weights for everyone to play around with as well. Try it out Clairic is available as a preview on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic . Call it from a Worker with env.AI.run() , or from anywhere with the REST API. We have full model docs here , as well as a new docs explainer on how the extraction model API looks. P.S. Since you liked the etymology of the name Clef , here’s how we landed on the name Clairic. We started with a desire to keep the name of the model thematically and sonically similar to Clef. Clair came to mind, sharing the same “cl” sound, as well as roots in music (“Clair de Lune”). More importantly, we wanted the name to be descriptive to the nature of the model. The Clairic model should be able to help you with clerical tasks like extracting data clearly from a corpus of inputs and upholding accuracy in tasks like bookkeeping. The prediction aspect of the model leans into the “ Clair ” root — allowing you to estimate and predict future values, similar to clairvoyance . Lastly, we like the idea of having this be [Cl]oudflare’s [AI R]egression model. Thus, Clairic was born into the world. We hope you enjoy it.
items.summary_html:
Today, we're announcing a preview of a new class of System One-style models: extraction models. Our first one, Clairic, is available hosted on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic.We intend to release the model open-weights soon. Clairic is an extraction model that is able to extract, compute, estimate, and forecast values from unstructured inputs — all at a significantly higher accuracy, faster latency, and cheaper cost than traditional LLMs.

Context

When System One models were announced by TypeSafe a month ago, it took the industry by storm. As referenced by TypeSafe in their blog and defined by Daniel Kahneman’s book Thinking, Fast and Slow, a System One model should be fast and precise, which contrasts a System Two model that is capable of deliberate reasoning (like LLMs). With this, TypeSafe introduced Jev — a model that is purpose-fit for a specific use case, and priced accessibly given its niche domain. It excelled where LLMs failed, helping users make decisions based on probabilities and well-typed outputs. The introduction of Jev prompted people to start thinking about a new class of models that were not LLMs and how to integrate them into their workflows.

We were inspired by the concept of System One models and started thinking about other tasks where LLMs are inefficient. There are many structured-output calls going to frontier LLMs today with the same shapes again and again: What's the invoice total? When was this delivered? How many days late is it? What will this repair cost? What will traffic look like over the next 24 hours? None of these have answers you can list out in advance, which is needed for a decision model to give probabilities against. That led us to the class of models we're introducing today: System One extraction models.

Introducing System One extraction models

Until now, every System One model has been a decision model: Jev and Clef take an input state and a list of questions and give probabilities against the inputs and your listed questions. Clairic is the first model in a new class: System One extraction models. It is still fast, typed, and cheap, but it answers with values directly extracted from the input, computed from it, or predicted beyond it.

Most model tasks ask for one of three kinds of output: a number, a choice from a fixed set, or open-ended text. Clairic handles the first, returning numbers with an 80% range, and also pulls typed values like names, dates and lists out of the input. Clef handles the second: it picks among options and returns a probability for each. LLMs handle the third. We call Clairic and Clef System One models because they answer in a single pass, without reasoning or generating tokens. They charge only for input and typically respond in under a second, while an LLM that reasons through the same step takes several seconds.

An extraction model can return:

  • Extracted values: Text copied from the input, such as a name, an order ID or a description. Each one comes back as a span with its character offsets and a confidence score.
  • Including, computed values: Numbers, dates, times, datetimes, durations and lists, read from the input or worked out from it. They follow the rules of their type (for example, two decimals for cents) and come with a confidence score.
  • Estimated values: Values the input doesn't state but gives evidence for. Each one comes back as a distribution inside the bounds you declare, on the grid you specify, with a median and an 80% interval.
  • Forecasted values: Future values of a series, one estimate per step ahead, each with its own 80% interval.

And because it generates no tokens, it can't produce a mistyped answer or “hallucinate” in the same way as an LLM (though it can, of course, make mistakes). Outputs are a value of the type you asked for, or null when the model fails to find an answer in the input. It also comes with confidence scores against the outputs to help you evaluate if it is appropriate to trust the model or to take a second look.

Here’s how extraction models fit into the landscape of System One and System Two models:

System One: Extract

System One: Decide

System Two

Example models

Clairic

Jev, Clef

GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek

Sampling

One parallel pass

One parallel pass

One token at a time

Purpose

Predict values

Make decisions

Write and reason

ML framing

Regression and extraction

Classification

Generation

Thinking mode

System 1: fast, one pass

System 1: fast, one pass

System 2: slow, deliberate

Output

Typed values: spans, numbers, dates, times, lists, distributions, with calibrated probabilities

Typed decisions: options with calibrated probabilities

Free-form strings

Output space

Continuous, but typed and bounded by your schema

A finite set of options you list

Anything

What it answers

What's the amount? When does it happen? How much will it be?

Which category is it? Is it legitimate? Which action should we take?

Why did it happen? How should we approach it? Can you fix it?

Output always a valid response?

Yes: every answer is a value of its declared type (or null), inside your bounds

Yes: answers are always one of your options

No: strings must be parsed and checked

Together, these models can work together in unison to help you get closer to parsing through real-world data, making decisions on inputs, and then taking actions. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values, decision models turn values into decisions, and LLMs turn decisions into words.

How a request works

Clairic is designed differently than an LLM. Similar to a decision model, it only processes input tokens with a single forward pass, and thus has no charge for output tokens. It is much faster, cheaper, and more accurate than an LLM for certain use cases.

A request is a state (the text to read, plus up to four optional images) and a map of typed fields. You name each field, give it a type and optional plain-language instructions, and get back one typed answer per field, all from one parallel pass. There is no reasoning and no output tokens – everything computes in a single forward pass, which means it is both fast and cheap.

Type

Returns

text

A specific span of the input, with its offsets

number

A number read or computed, honoring integer and decimals

date, time, datetime

Calendar dates and valid times, in ISO form

duration

A length of time in the unit you choose

list

Matching text, number or date, in input order

estimate

A distribution inside your [min, max], on your step grid, linear or log scale.

forecast

One estimate per future step of a series

Every scalar answer comes with p_null (the probability that the value isn’t in the inputs) and confidence. Every estimate answer comes with a median and an 80% interval (p10 to p90), plus all 99 percentiles on request. There's no limit on the number of fields: if they don't fit beside the input in one pass, the server splits them into parallel passes that each see the whole input, then merges the answers.

Here are some examples to illustrate the model’s features. Of course, using these features in a workflow would require appropriate inputs.

An example: Extracting values

Extraction is probably the most common job handed to LLMs today: "return the invoice number, vendor and due date as JSON." It works most of the time, but the failure modes are hard to catch. The output may not be valid JSON, a digit can be misread as it's generated, and once a text excerpt comes back, there's no way to trace it to where it appeared in the source. Most people build extraction pipelines to combat this, with multiple layers of parsing, schema validation, retries and spot checks. On top of that, you pay for reasoning and output tokens on every field of every document.

Clairic operates differently; it doesn’t generate text answers. Instead, you get:

  • Values extracted from your input, so an answer is grounded.
  • Computed values, so it can parse through unstructured data without pre-sanitizing it.
  • Character offset spans, so you can reference where in the input the data was.
  • Confidence labels, so you can determine which values need a second look.
  • A strongly typed output, so numbers and dates are formed under the rules of their type (e.g., a cents field has two decimals).
  • Handling for null values, where a missing field returns with null as an answer (along with an estimated probability of null and a guess).
  • Cheaper and faster answers, because every field is answered in the same parallel pass. So asking for thirty fields costs about the same as asking for three.

Let’s walk through an example to illustrate the ways Clairic can extract values from unstructured data and make estimates. Take a customer support email:

Hi, order A-88412 arrived on Sept 28, 2026 with a cracked screen and a dented corner. I paid $649.00 plus $52.10 tax. It's now Oct 9, 2026 and I'd like this fixed or refunded. Thanks, Dana

From a Worker, you would make a request to Clairic to process this data:

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: email,
  fields: {
    order_id:            { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" },
    delivered_on:        { type: "date", instructions: "Delivery date" },
    amount_paid:         { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" },
    days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true,
                           instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" },
    damage:              { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" },
    tracking_number:     { type: "text" },
  },
});

Clairic returns the extracted values, spans in the input, probability that it is null (p_null) and confidence score:

{
  "order_id": {
    "type": "text",
    "p_null": 3.4e-6,
    "span": [10, 17],
    "guess": "A-88412",
    "confidence": 0.999957,
    "value": "A-88412"
  },
  "delivered_on": {
    "type": "date",
    "p_null": 6.5e-8,
    "guess": "2026-09-28",
    "confidence": 0.999999,
    "value": "2026-09-28"
  },
  "amount_paid": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 1.6e-5,
    "guess": 701.1,
    "confidence": 0.999944,
    "value": 701.1
  },
  "days_since_delivery": {
    "type": "duration",
    "p_null": 6.1e-9,
    "unit": "days",
    "guess": 11,
    "confidence": 0.999999,
    "value": 11
  },
  "damage": {
    "type": "list",
    "value": ["cracked screen", "dented corner"],
    "spans": [[50, 64], [71, 84]]
  },
  "tracking_number": {
    "type": "text",
    "p_null": 1,
    "span": [106, 112],
    "guess": "$52.10",
    "confidence": 0.416016,
    "value": null
  }
}

A few things to notice:

  • amount_paid isn't written anywhere in the email. In this example, Clairic added the price and the tax in the same pass and returns the sum.
  • days_since_delivery is also worked out from two dates in the text, not directly in the input.
  • damage lists both kinds of damage as exact spans, so you can highlight them in the source.
  • tracking_number isn't in the email, so it comes back null instead of a plausible-looking guess. guess shows what the model would otherwise have picked.
Clairic also works with images

Here’s a real-life photo of a receipt — the text is not perfect and the angle of the image doesn’t help its legibility. We passed this image to Clairic to see what it could extract:

{
  "model": "clairic",
  "answers": {
   "order_number": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 0.0040206750854849815,
    "guess": 77245,
    "confidence": 0.776249383996532,
    "value": 77245
   },
   "purchased_at": {
    "type": "datetime",
    "p_null": 4.136094133855295e-08,
    "guess": "2026-07-01T13:34:00",
    "confidence": 0.831464227002992,
    "value": "2026-07-01T13:34:00"
   },
   "quantity": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 5.2313655629632194e-08,
    "guess": 2,
    "confidence": 0.9997007500403496,
    "value": 2
   },
   "unit_price": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 0.001599092734977603,
    "guess": 7.99,
    "confidence": 0.9991279019989127,
    "value": 7.99
   },
   "subtotal": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 9.69956488461321e-08,
    "guess": 15.98,
    "confidence": 0.9999881983893096,
    "value": 15.98
   },
   "sales_tax": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 2.5511653802823275e-06,
    "guess": 0,
    "confidence": 0.9999800924450729,
    "value": 0
   },
   "tip": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 5.953857908025384e-05,
    "guess": 2.39,
    "confidence": 0.9335768781214697,
    "value": 2.39
   },
   "discount": {
    "type": "number",
    "p_null": 0.9994148015975952,
    "guess": 0,
    "confidence": 0.91852733929319,
    "value": null
   }
  }
}

As you can see, it was able to extract all the values from the images, alongside a confidence score. It also correctly stated that there was no discount shown in the receipt, giving the value as null.

An example: Estimating values

Some values aren't in the input at all, but the input carries evidence for them. For example, values might not be in plain text but can be discerned from values around it. If you ask an LLM for an estimation, you usually get a single number with no sense of how sure the model is. It will make safe guesses or hallucinate, or reason its way around the answer. If you land on an estimate, any downstream processing can't tell a confident $180 from an unconfident $180, so it can't help you decide what is appropriate to automate in the circumstances. It is also a lot slower and more expensive to do reasoning through LLMs.

A decision model can approximate an estimate by choosing among buckets ("under $100", "$100–500", …), but buckets are coarse, every bucket adds input tokens, and each new category adds more sources of confusion for the model during its decision making process.

Clairic returns a distribution over the range you declare: a point value, a median, an 80% interval, and every percentile on request. The estimate is designed to fall inside your bounds, so there's nothing to clamp or round afterward. The width of the interval reflects data confidence: a narrow range signals high certainty, while a wide range indicates low certainty, information you can use to route another check.

Here’s another example, where Clairic looks at historical home prices and comparable sales, to determine an estimate :

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: `Comparable sales:
sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood,sale_price
1450,3,1998,Elm Park,412000
2100,4,2006,Elm Park,585000
980,2,1975,Riverside,265000
1600,3,2003,Elm Park,449000
1300,3,1990,Riverside,318000

Subject property:
sqft,beds,year_built,neighborhood
1620,3,2001,Elm Park`,
  fields: {
    sale_price:     { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 50000, max: 5000000, scale: "log", step: 1000 }
});

Clairic will return an estimated value:

{
  "sale_price":     { "type": "estimate", "value": 418000, "median": 415000, "p10": 370000, "p90": 470000, "p_below": 0.0, "p_above": 0.0 }
}

Values always fall inside your bounds, and the width of the interval shows how much the input informs the prediction: price is narrow ($370,000-$470,000), days on market is wide (24-148). Because fields are unlimited and answered in parallel, you can score many items in one call (one estimate per candidate, lead, or listing) and sort them in code.

An example: Forecasting values

Forecasting values in a time series is quite hard for generalized models — it usually means you have to either build a specific pipeline per metric (parse the data, fit a model, tune it, deploy it), or you paste 36 months of numbers into an LLM and ask for the next three. The first is accurate but really expensive and time-consuming to set up for every new series. The second is easy, but you get point forecasts with no intervals, forecasts that shift depending on how the prompt is worded, and answers with limited confidence.

Clairic sits between the two — it is not claiming to replace a dedicated time-series model, but it is a little faster and cheaper than your regular LLM. A forecast field takes the history as plain text in state and returns, for every step ahead, a value and an 80% interval, inside the bounds you declare. It reads the history the way you already have it, whether that's a CSV export, a pasted dashboard, or rows mixed with notes, and may often work with no need to clean up your data beforehand.

To see how that holds up on real data, we used a public series: the number of people the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screens at U.S. airport checkpoints each day. Each morning we asked Clairic for the next day's count, given the real counts so far, for 21 days in a row:

const { answers } = await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: `Daily number of people screened at TSA checkpoints at US airports.
date,weekday,travelers
2026-07-16,Thu,2850229
...
2026-10-13,Tue,2353356
Forecast date: 2026-10-14 (Wed)`,
  fields: {
    travelers: { type: "forecast", horizon: 1, interval: "day",
                 min: 500000, max: 4000000, scale: "log",
                 instructions: "Number of people screened tomorrow" },
  },
});

Which returns:

{
  "travelers": { "type": "forecast", "value": [2416117], "median": [2419283], "p10": [2270774], "p90": [2556769] }
}

In actuality, TSA screened 2,419,474 people that day, which is right around the median 2,419,283 that Clairic predicted.

Data: TSA checkpoint travel numbers, accessed Oct. 15, 2026.

Across the 21 days, Clairic's forecasts were off by 3.3% on average, and 17 of the 21 actual counts landed inside its 80% interval, which follows what an 80% interval should do. It picked up the weekly rhythm from the numbers alone: quieter Tuesdays and Saturdays, busier Thursdays, Fridays, and Sundays.

The misses are also interesting: three of the four days outside the interval fall on the Columbus Day weekend, when more people flew than the previous weeks suggested. Clairic forecasts from the patterns in the series but doesn't account for events the series doesn't show, like holidays.

Thinking fast and slow

These models are designed to fit alongside your existing agentic workflows. An extraction model predicts values, a decision model decides what to do with these values, and an LLM takes action with them. It is a perfect marriage between System One and System Two models. It bridges the existing gap, where you either have to manually extract data for LLMs, or have an LLM parse through messy data (which is costly, time-consuming, and can lead to hallucinations). With System One extraction models, you can work with real-world data with more speed, efficiency, and precision.

Here's an example of the damaged-product claim from earlier, illustrating how all the models can work together.  We built this into a live demo you can try here.

// 1. Clairic turns the email into values
const facts = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clairic", {
  state: email,
  fields: {
    customer_name:       { type: "text", instructions: "Customer's first name" },
    order_id:            { type: "text", instructions: "Order number" },
    amount_paid:         { type: "number", decimals: 2, unit: "USD", instructions: "Total paid including tax" },
    days_since_delivery: { type: "duration", unit: "days", integer: true,
                           instructions: "Days from delivery to the date the customer wrote" },
    damage:              { type: "list", items: "text", instructions: "Each kind of damage described" },
    repair_cost:         { type: "estimate", unit: "USD", min: 10, max: 5000, scale: "log", step: 1,
                           instructions: "Cost to repair the damage described" },
  },
})).answers;
const { customer_name, order_id, amount_paid, days_since_delivery, damage, repair_cost } = facts;

// 2. Clef decides from Clairic's values and the policy, not from the raw email
const options = {
  refund:  "Full refund of the amount paid",
  repair:  "Free repair, with a prepaid shipping label",
};
const { choice } = (await env.AI.run("@cf/cloudflare/clef", {
  state: `Damage claim for order ${order_id.value}.
Paid: $${amount_paid.value.toFixed(2)}. Delivered ${days_since_delivery.value} days ago.
Damage reported: ${damage.value.join(", ")}.
Estimated repair cost: $${repair_cost.median} (80% range $${repair_cost.p10}-$${repair_cost.p90}).
Policy: refunds within 30 days of delivery. Prefer repair when it costs less than 60% of the price and the damage doesn't stop the product from working.`,
  questions: {
    resolution: { type: "choice", instructions: "What should we offer?", criteria: options },
  },
})).answers.resolution;

// 3. An LLM writes the reply, from the decision and the facts it needs
const { response } = await env.AI.run("@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3", {
  messages: [{
    role: "user",
    content: `Write a short, warm reply to ${customer_name.value}. Use only these facts: order ${order_id.value}; ` +
             `damage: ${damage.value.join(", ")}; what happens next: ${options[choice]}. Under 60 words.`,
  }],
});

Each step gets cleaner input than the one before. Clef decides from a five-line summary of typed values instead of a free-form email, which can also be susceptible to prompt injection. The LLM never sees the email, only the decision and the predictions it needs, so there are fewer numbers for it to misuse. Every step is typed and auditable, and only one step generates text. In the all-LLM version of this pipeline, all three steps are generative calls, and every value in the reply has to be checked by hand.

We ran this pipeline against an all-LLM version with GLM-5.3 writing the reply in both. In the all-LLM version, GLM-5.3 also does the extraction and the decision, from the same email, policy and prompts:

Clairic → Clef → GLM-5.3

GLM-5.3 for every step

Latency, end to end

19.3 s

61.7 s

1. Extract

Clairic: 0.46 s

GLM-5.3: 16.1 s

2. Decide

Clef: 0.22 s

GLM-5.3: 21.9 s

3. Reply

GLM-5.3: 18.6 s

GLM-5.3: 16.4 s

Input tokens

701 ($184 per million claims)

390 ($546 per million claims)

Output tokens

1,329 ($5,848 per million claims)

2,544 ($11,194 per million claims)

Cost per million claims

$6,032

$11,740

The cascade finished in 19.3 seconds against 61.7 seconds: 69% less time, or about 3.2 times faster. Clairic and Clef handled extraction and the decision in under a second combined, where GLM-5.3 took 38 seconds for the same two steps. It also costs 49% less to use the cascaded pipeline vs the all-LLM pipeline. With GLM, both pipelines got the facts and the decision right in every run, but Clairic's repair estimate was identical each time, while GLM-5.3's changed on every run ($250, $250 and $220, with different ranges each time).

Notably, under the all-LLM pipeline both Gemma 4 and Qwen failed at this task, as they were unable to deduce values like repair_cost from the inputs, showing how LLMs are not great at data extraction tasks.

Preview release

Today, we're releasing a hosted endpoint for Clairic on Workers AI. We intend to release the model with open weights soon. We wanted to take the time first to introduce the concept of a System One extraction model, so you can start thinking about how this class of model would fit into appropriate workflows.

The current endpoint is an early checkpoint and we expect it to get better. Here are our early impressions:

  • Reading is strong, but multi-step arithmetic isn't yet. One- and two-step calculations (totals, differences, conversions, date arithmetic) seem reliable. Longer chains of dependent steps are hard for any one-pass model without a scratchpad. The same goes for aggregating across many rows of a table. At least for now, have Clairic predict the value and let code do the math.
  • Estimates need evidence. Clairic estimates best from comparables, history, or descriptive text in the input. Asking it for a value it has no evidence for may be limited in specificity.
  • Calibration is measured, not guaranteed. Intervals are trained to be calibrated and are on most held-out sets, but they can run narrow on unfamiliar data.
  • Forecasting is basic. The model is not designed to accurately replace or predict time-series models that are trained on specific data. You should use it where appropriate, such as non-critical, general pattern matching, not detailed long-horizon forecasting.
  • Use confidence. The architecture makes every answer well formed, not necessarily correct. Use confidence, p_null and the intervals to decide what to automate (in an appropriate workflow context) and what to send off for additional review.

We'll keep working on the arithmetic, estimation and forecasting sides of the model with each checkpoint. After some more work, we plan to release the model open-weights for everyone to play around with as well.

Try it out

Clairic is available as a preview on Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clairic. Call it from a Worker with env.AI.run(), or from anywhere with the REST API. We have full model docs here, as well as a new docs explainer on how the extraction model API looks.

P.S. Since you liked the etymology of the name Clef, here’s how we landed on the name Clairic. We started with a desire to keep the name of the model thematically and sonically similar to Clef. Clair came to mind, sharing the same “cl” sound, as well as roots in music (“Clair de Lune”). More importantly, we wanted the name to be descriptive to the nature of the model. The Clairic model should be able to help you with clerical tasks like extracting data clearly from a corpus of inputs and upholding accuracy in tasks like bookkeeping. The prediction aspect of the model leans into the “Clair” root — allowing you to estimate and predict future values, similar to clairvoyance. Lastly, we like the idea of having this be [Cl]oudflare’s [AI R]egression model. Thus, Clairic was born into the world. We hope you enjoy it.

items.title: Bright Security Introduces STAR Fuzzer, Agentic Fuzzing That Writes Its Own Harnesses and Proves Every Finding
items.summary: San Rafael, United States, October 19th, 2026, CyberNewswire Built on an evolutionary engine first released in 2018, STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security finds crashes, memory exhaustion and memory-safety bugs in security-critical code without a running application. In its first open source research run, it found High or Critical issues in 45% of the projects tested, and in its first month of availability it produced ten published findings in eight projects, including the Crystal standard library, htop and RIOT OS. Bright Security , the Agentic Offensive Application Security company, today announced the official launch of STAR Fuzzer, an agentic application fuzzer that automatically identifies security-critical functions, generates a fuzzing harness for each one, searches for faults with an evolutionary algorithm, and delivers every confirmed finding with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it. STAR Fuzzer is a self-contained mode of the Bright STAR platform and is available now at brightsec.com/fuzzer . Agentic fuzzing applies AI agents to the parts of fuzzing that have traditionally required a specialist: choosing what to test, writing the harness, and deciding which crashes matter. STAR Fuzzer uses AI for those steps and an evolutionary search engine for the fuzzing itself, so the parts that need judgment are automated and the search stays fast, repeatable and evidence based. Why Fuzzing Needed a New Approach Coverage-guided fuzzers such as AFL++ and libFuzzer are proven and widely used, and programs like Google’s OSS-Fuzz have shown how much they can find. But they depend on people to write and maintain a harness for every target and to triage the crashes that come back. That cost has kept fuzzing concentrated in specialist teams and a subset of critical projects. Other testing approaches don’t fill the gap. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) tests what an attacker can reach over HTTP, so it rarely exercises the parsing and processing code behind input validation. LLM-based pentesting is effective at known vulnerability patterns but tends to look where a model expects bugs to be. The result is a class of outage-level and memory-safety defects, often triggered by tiny malformed inputs, that most AppSec programs never test for. How STAR Fuzzer compares with traditional coverage-guided fuzzers (such as AFL++ and libFuzzer) and DAST: What it Tests: Traditional fuzzers test functions exposed through a hand-written harness. DAST tests running applications over HTTP. STAR Fuzzer tests security-critical functions on untrusted-input paths, chosen automatically. Harness: Traditional fuzzers need harnesses written and maintained by engineers. DAST doesn’t use one. STAR Fuzzer generates a harness per function with AI, then verifies it reaches its target. Search: Traditional fuzzers use coverage-guided mutation. DAST sends request-level attack payloads. STAR Fuzzer uses a structure-aware evolutionary search guided by coverage and multiple fitness signals. Running App Needed: Traditional fuzzers, no. DAST, yes. STAR Fuzzer, no. Triage: Manual for traditional fuzzers and built into the scanner for DAST. STAR Fuzzer triages automatically for reachability and impact. Output: Traditional fuzzers return crash inputs and logs. DAST returns a vulnerability report. STAR Fuzzer delivers the file, function and byte-exact payload in a pull request. Fix Validation: Traditional fuzzers need a manual re-run and DAST needs a rescan. With STAR Fuzzer, teams replay the payload. Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss Ask an LLM to audit a parser and it will find the bug classes it already knows from training. The zero-days that survive for years in mature, widely deployed code are the ones that match no known pattern. STAR Fuzzer uses AI to choose targets and build harnesses, but the search that finds the bugs is not an LLM. It doesn’t read the code or guess where a bug might be. It runs the program millions of times, observes what actually happens, and keeps whatever pushes the target into code it hasn’t reached yet. In Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss , Bright Security CTO Bar Hofesh gives four reasons LLM code review does not replace fuzzing for zero-day discovery: Scale: A single fuzzing campaign runs 1 million to 10 million concrete inputs against the compiled target. At about 2,000 tokens per reasoned test case, matching one million executions with an LLM would take about two billion tokens for one target, and each of those test cases would still be a prediction. Speed and Ground Truth: A persistent harness runs hundreds to a few thousand inputs per second per worker, across several parallel workers, so one million executions take minutes to tens of minutes. One LLM reasoning pass over one hypothesis takes several seconds, so one million would take months. The fuzzer also observes real behavior, such as a sanitizer reporting a heap read one byte out of bounds. An LLM has to predict how compiled code behaves, including struct layouts, integer widths, allocator behavior and build flags that aren’t visible in the source. Coverage: STAR Fuzzer’s libxml2 harness reaches about 13,600 code regions in a 5-million-execution run. Coverage feedback shows which regions each input reached, and inputs that reach new code become starting points for deeper search. Code review has no equivalent signal for how much of a large parser it has actually covered. The Unexpected: LLMs, code reviewers and static analyzers look for the same known patterns, so in mature code most of those bugs are already fixed. The fuzzer has no expectations about where a bug should be. The target’s own behavior decides what is interesting. Reproducibility is the other difference. Many plausible-looking LLM findings don’t reproduce, and maintainers need a reproducer before they can act. A fuzzer finding is a reproducer by construction, and Bright Security replays every one in a fresh container before filing it. How STAR Fuzzer Works STAR Fuzzer’s search engine drives any target through a small harness over IPC, so the code under test can be written in C, C++, Rust, Go, Java, Kotlin, Crystal, Node or any language that can read an input and report back. Structure-aware parsing with no per-target grammar: Every seed is parsed into a typed tree of fields by a format-agnostic parsing layer, and the tree serializes back to the original bytes exactly. No grammar or dictionary file is written per target, and each format added to the parsing layer improves every target that uses it. Mutations that get past the first check: Byte-level mutation mostly produces inputs a parser rejects at its first sanity check. Mutating the fields of a valid structured input keeps most executions past framing and validation, so the testing budget is spent on the deeper logic behind them. Evolution with exact replay: Each organism in the population carries a genome, an ordered list of mutations. Each epoch, organisms mutate, run and are scored. Improvements are kept, unproductive changes are reverted, and organisms breed. Replaying a genome reproduces its payload exactly, so every result can be regenerated from a logged random seed. Results from Open-Source Testing Before release, Bright Security ran STAR Fuzzer for two days in an automated pipeline against multiple open source projects, from libraries and applications to low-level binary parsers. 45% of the projects tested had High or Critical issues, and 37% of the vulnerable projects are part of Google’s OSS-Fuzz program. In its first month of availability, STAR Fuzzer produced ten published findings in eight projects written in C, Go, JVM languages and Crystal. Each was replayed in a fresh container before filing: TwelveMonkeys: In the DDS reader, the mipMapCount header field sizes an uncapped array, so a 38-byte file forces a multi-gigabyte allocation (CWE-789). GHSA-fwp7-38wp-mmxw, fixed in 3.15.0. Fider: Upload validation checks an image’s compressed size, then fully decodes it, so a 436 KB PNG expands to about 562 MB. Any authenticated user can trigger it (CWE-409). STAR Fuzzer found it in about 12 minutes, in a release already benchmarked by multiple AI pentesting vendors. GHSA-7cw3-7xh9-529r, fixed in 0.38.0. Crystal standard library (XML): XML::Node#namespace type confusion. ENTITY_DECL is missing from an allowlist, so a field of libxml2’s xmlEntity struct is read as an xmlNs* (CWE-843). GHSA-c267-9cqj-hv9f, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1. Crystal standard library (YAML): YAML::Any#hash overflows the stack on a self-referencing anchor and alias cycle. An 88-byte input causes an uncatchable SIGSEGV (CWE-674). GHSA-fj8w-2r88-5v7w, fixed in Crystal 1.21.1. libsolv: Two vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-104621 and CVE-2026-104622. Details are under embargo. htop: An out-of-bounds read in the /proc/PID/stat parser, caused by a missing bounds check on field 22 (CWE-125). Fixed (#2101). universal-ctags: A null-pointer member access in foreachEntriesInScope (CWE-476). Fixed in commit 780bd7a (#4497). scrimage: An uncapped width-times-height pixel count lets a 35-byte GIF trigger allocation attempts of about 2 GB, and over 8 GB in a second variant (CWE-789). Fixed in 4.6.8 (#893). RIOT OS: An off-by-one in _dirlist_cb (link_format.c). The bounds check runs after the write, so a NUL byte lands one past the buffer (CWE-193). Fix submitted in PR #22879. Several of these bugs sit in code that looks correct on review. The Fider upload has a size limit, but it measures compressed size. The TwelveMonkeys field reads as image metadata, not as a length. The Crystal allowlist looks complete. The YAML hash function is correct for trees, and the bug is a cycle in the input. The full methodology and results are published in two parts: Part I on brightsec.com, and Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss by Bar Hofesh. Where STAR Fuzzer Fits Best STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security is designed for teams whose code handles untrusted input below the HTTP layer, including: Applications that process uploaded files, images, documents or archives Parsers, serialization code and raw binary protocols Non-web software such as embedded and IoT firmware, desktop applications and backend services Codebases with a growing share of AI-generated code that needs testing beyond pattern matching Security teams that want to confirm static analysis (SAST) findings by exercising the flagged functions live It supports C/C++, Rust, Go, Java/Kotlin, .NET, Node, Python and Crystal, and runs inside the customer’s environment with no running application, cloud scanner or authentication required. In persistent mode, harness execution is about 51 times faster than running a new process per input. Executive Perspectives “Fuzzing has always found the bugs that matter most, the ones that take a service down or corrupt memory, but it has been too expensive for most teams to run,” said Bar Hofesh, Co-founder and CTO of Bright Security . “The search was never the bottleneck. The harnesses and the triage were. STAR Fuzzer automates both, so the evolutionary engine we built in 2018 can finally run across a whole codebase.” “When Nevada opened the Boulder City Bypass in 2018, it took navigation apps months to start sending drivers down it,” Hofesh added. “LLMs auditing code work the same way. They find the bugs they’ve already seen. The zero-days that have lived for years in mature code are the ones nobody has seen before, and that’s exactly where a fuzzer shines.” “Security teams are being asked to keep up with code written faster than ever, much of it by AI,” said Gadi Bashvitz, Co-founder and CEO of Bright Security. “Testing that only looks where bugs are expected won’t keep pace. STAR Fuzzer looks everywhere else, and it hands developers the proof they need to fix what it finds.” “AppSec teams keep asking us the same thing: if AI is writing more of our code, what’s testing the parts AI can’t, see?” said Eyal Dror, CMO of Bright Security. “STAR Fuzzer is our answer. In its first month it found ten real bugs in mature open-source projects, and everyone came with the exact input that triggers it. That’s proof a developer can act on the same day, not another alert to argue about.” Availability STAR Fuzzer is available now as a mode of Bright STAR. Learn more and book a demo at brightsec.com/fuzzer . Frequently Asked Questions: What is Agentic Fuzzing? Agentic fuzzing uses AI agents to automate the judgment-heavy steps of fuzzing: selecting which functions to test, writing and verifying harnesses, and triaging results. The fuzzing itself is performed by a search engine that mutates inputs to trigger faults. How is STAR Fuzzer Different from AFL++ or libFuzzer? AFL++ and libFuzzer are fuzzing engines that need engineers to write a harness for each target and to triage crashes by hand. STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security selects targets, generates and verifies harnesses, triages faults for reachability and impact, and delivers findings in a pull request with a reproducing payload. Can LLMs Find Zero-Day Vulnerabilities in Parsers? LLMs are effective at known bug classes, such as an unchecked memcpy length or string-built SQL, but they look where their training says bugs should be. In mature code, the bugs that survive are the ones that match no known pattern, which is where evolutionary, coverage-guided fuzzing is strongest. Why Use a Fuzzer Instead of LLM Code Review? A fuzzing campaign runs millions of real executions against compiled code and observes what happens, while an LLM predicts behavior from the source. Matching one million executions with LLM reasoning would take about two billion tokens per target. Every fuzzer finding also comes with an input that reproduces it. How are STAR Fuzzer Findings Verified? Every finding comes with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it, and Bright Security replays each one in a fresh container before filing it. Any result can also be regenerated from a logged random seed. Does STAR Fuzzer Need Grammars or Dictionary Files? No. A format-agnostic parsing layer turns each seed into a typed tree of fields, so no per-target grammar or dictionary is required. Does STAR Fuzzer Replace DAST? No. DAST tests a running application from the outside in, over HTTP. STAR Fuzzer tests security-critical functions from the inside out, without a running application. Bright STAR runs both, with the same agent and the same pull-request output. What Kinds of Bugs Does STAR Fuzzer Find? Crashes, hangs, out-of-memory conditions and unbounded allocations, memory-safety bugs such as out-of-bounds reads and off-by-one writes, type confusion, stack overflows from recursive input structures, and algorithmic-complexity blow-ups, including decompression bombs triggered by inputs of a few dozen bytes. Which languages does STAR Fuzzer Support? C/C++, Rust, Go, Java/Kotlin, .NET, Node, Python and Crystal. About Bright Security Bright Security is the Agentic Offensive Application Security company, helping organizations secure software at the speed of AI-driven development. Its AI-powered Bright STAR platform integrates security directly into the development lifecycle, automating detection, remediation and validation across web applications, APIs and code, and fitting into both developer and AppSec workflows. Formerly known as NeuraLegion, Bright Security is headquartered in California. Learn more at brightsec.com . Contact CMO Eyal Dror Bright Security Inc eyal.dror@brightsec.com

Several of these bugs sit in code that looks correct on review. The Fider upload has a size limit, but it measures compressed size. The TwelveMonkeys field reads as image metadata, not as a length.

The Crystal allowlist looks complete. The YAML hash function is correct for trees, and the bug is a cycle in the input.

The full methodology and results are published in two parts: Part I on brightsec.com, and Back to the Fuzzer II: Finding the Bugs LLMs Miss by Bar Hofesh.

Where STAR Fuzzer Fits Best

STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security is designed for teams whose code handles untrusted input below the HTTP layer, including:

  • Applications that process uploaded files, images, documents or archives
  • Parsers, serialization code and raw binary protocols
  • Non-web software such as embedded and IoT firmware, desktop applications and backend services
  • Codebases with a growing share of AI-generated code that needs testing beyond pattern matching
  • Security teams that want to confirm static analysis (SAST) findings by exercising the flagged functions live

It supports C/C++, Rust, Go, Java/Kotlin, .NET, Node, Python and Crystal, and runs inside the customer’s environment with no running application, cloud scanner or authentication required.

In persistent mode, harness execution is about 51 times faster than running a new process per input.

Executive Perspectives

“Fuzzing has always found the bugs that matter most, the ones that take a service down or corrupt memory, but it has been too expensive for most teams to run,” said Bar Hofesh, Co-founder and CTO of Bright Security.

“The search was never the bottleneck. The harnesses and the triage were. STAR Fuzzer automates both, so the evolutionary engine we built in 2018 can finally run across a whole codebase.”

“When Nevada opened the Boulder City Bypass in 2018, it took navigation apps months to start sending drivers down it,” Hofesh added. “LLMs auditing code work the same way.

They find the bugs they’ve already seen. The zero-days that have lived for years in mature code are the ones nobody has seen before, and that’s exactly where a fuzzer shines.”

“Security teams are being asked to keep up with code written faster than ever, much of it by AI,” said Gadi Bashvitz, Co-founder and CEO of Bright Security.

“Testing that only looks where bugs are expected won’t keep pace. STAR Fuzzer looks everywhere else, and it hands developers the proof they need to fix what it finds.”

“AppSec teams keep asking us the same thing: if AI is writing more of our code, what’s testing the parts AI can’t, see?” said Eyal Dror, CMO of Bright Security.

“STAR Fuzzer is our answer. In its first month it found ten real bugs in mature open-source projects, and everyone came with the exact input that triggers it. That’s proof a developer can act on the same day, not another alert to argue about.”

Availability

STAR Fuzzer is available now as a mode of Bright STAR. Learn more and book a demo at brightsec.com/fuzzer.

Frequently Asked Questions:

What is Agentic Fuzzing? Agentic fuzzing uses AI agents to automate the judgment-heavy steps of fuzzing: selecting which functions to test, writing and verifying harnesses, and triaging results. The fuzzing itself is performed by a search engine that mutates inputs to trigger faults.

How is STAR Fuzzer Different from AFL++ or libFuzzer? AFL++ and libFuzzer are fuzzing engines that need engineers to write a harness for each target and to triage crashes by hand. STAR Fuzzer by Bright Security selects targets, generates and verifies harnesses, triages faults for reachability and impact, and delivers findings in a pull request with a reproducing payload.

Can LLMs Find Zero-Day Vulnerabilities in Parsers? LLMs are effective at known bug classes, such as an unchecked memcpy length or string-built SQL, but they look where their training says bugs should be. In mature code, the bugs that survive are the ones that match no known pattern, which is where evolutionary, coverage-guided fuzzing is strongest.

Why Use a Fuzzer Instead of LLM Code Review? A fuzzing campaign runs millions of real executions against compiled code and observes what happens, while an LLM predicts behavior from the source. Matching one million executions with LLM reasoning would take about two billion tokens per target. Every fuzzer finding also comes with an input that reproduces it.

How are STAR Fuzzer Findings Verified? Every finding comes with a byte-exact payload that reproduces it, and Bright Security replays each one in a fresh container before filing it. Any result can also be regenerated from a logged random seed.

Does STAR Fuzzer Need Grammars or Dictionary Files? No. A format-agnostic parsing layer turns each seed into a typed tree of fields, so no per-target grammar or dictionary is required.

Does STAR Fuzzer Replace DAST? No. DAST tests a running application from the outside in, over HTTP. STAR Fuzzer tests security-critical functions from the inside out, without a running application. Bright STAR runs both, with the same agent and the same pull-request output.

What Kinds of Bugs Does STAR Fuzzer Find? Crashes, hangs, out-of-memory conditions and unbounded allocations, memory-safety bugs such as out-of-bounds reads and off-by-one writes, type confusion, stack overflows from recursive input structures, and algorithmic-complexity blow-ups, including decompression bombs triggered by inputs of a few dozen bytes.

Which languages does STAR Fuzzer Support? C/C++, Rust, Go, Java/Kotlin, .NET, Node, Python and Crystal.

About Bright Security

Bright Security is the Agentic Offensive Application Security company, helping organizations secure software at the speed of AI-driven development.

Its AI-powered Bright STAR platform integrates security directly into the development lifecycle, automating detection, remediation and validation across web applications, APIs and code, and fitting into both developer and AppSec workflows.

Formerly known as NeuraLegion, Bright Security is headquartered in California. Learn more at brightsec.com.
