items.summary: An enterprise environment emits events by the million every hour. During an incident, the responder rarely needs all of them. They need the few hundred that tell the story: the burst of 4625 failures followed by a single 4624 success, the encoded PowerShell spawned by winword.exe, the new service installed at 03:12 on a domain controller. Logs analysis is the discipline of getting from the first number to the second fast enough to matter. That job has become harder in two directions at once. Attackers using AI tooling generate evidence at machine speed and pad real actions with benign-looking activity. Meanwhile, the obvious shortcut of pushing logs into an LLM runs into guardrails, context-window limits and data-protection obligations. Hugging Face’s responders hit exactly that wall in July 2026, when roughly 17,000 events were refused by frontier models and had to be processed on a local model instead. Below, we cover log analysis end to end, then look at LogTotal, SOC Prime’s free answer to the incident-time version of the problem. What Are the Fundamentals of Log Analysis? Every log analysis workflow, whether it runs in a SIEM, a data lake or a responder’s laptop, rests on the same five stages. Skipping one usually shows up later as a missed detection or a false positive nobody can explain. Collection. Agents, syslog forwarders, API pollers and cloud-native exporters move events off the source. Gaps here are silent: a Sysmon config that drops Event ID 10 (process access) means credential-dumping via LSASS never appears downstream. Parsing and normalization. Raw lines become fields. A source IP should be the same field whether it came from a firewall, an IdP or an EDR, which is why schemas like ECS and OCSF exist. Enrichment. Asset criticality, user role, GeoIP and threat intelligence turn an IP address into context an analyst can act on. Correlation. Single events rarely prove anything. Linking them by host, user, process GUID or session ID is what produces an attack narrative. Retention and integrity. Hot storage for search, cold storage for forensics, and tamper evidence so the record holds up later. What Is Log Analysis? Log analysis is the process of examining machine-generated records to reconstruct what happened on a system, decide whether it matters, and determine what to do next. In security operations, it answers five questions about any suspicious activity: who acted, on what asset, when, from where, and by which mechanism. It is distinct from log management. Management is plumbing: ingestion, storage, retention, access control. Analysis is interpretation. A team can have a well-run log pipeline and still miss an intrusion because nobody, human or machine, is asking the right questions of the data. In practice, log analysis runs in three modes: Detection. Rules and models evaluate events continuously and raise alerts when known malicious behavior appears. Investigation. After an alert or a tip-off, analysts pivot through related events to scope the incident and find root cause. Threat hunting. Analysts start from a hypothesis, such as abuse of a specific LOLBin, and search proactively for evidence the detection layer missed. Of all the teams that use logs, security has the least room for gaps. Why Is Log Analysis So Important? Because time drives breach cost, and logs are where time is won or lost. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report puts the mean time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days, the first increase in five years. Breaches with a lifecycle over 200 days averaged $5.65 million, against $4.32 million for those contained faster. Beyond cost, log analysis underpins four obligations every security program carries: Detection. EDR and NDR see slices of activity. Logs from identity providers, SaaS audit trails and cloud control planes fill the gaps between them. Scoping and root cause. Without event-level evidence, responders cannot say which accounts were touched or how the attacker got in, so remediation becomes guesswork. Regulatory reporting. PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 10 mandates audit-log review and 12 months of retention. The SEC’s Form 8-K Item 1.05 gives listed companies four business days after a materiality determination, which is impossible without fast scoping. Detection engineering. Real telemetry is how rules get tested and tuned. There is a catch. The same logs that make all of this possible carry usernames, IP addresses, session cookies and bearer tokens. Analyzing them well increasingly means analyzing them safely. What Are the Types of Log Data? Security-relevant logs fall into six families. Each answers a different question, and an investigation that relies on only one or two of them will have blind spots an attacker can live in. Log family Typical sources What it tells the analyst Endpoint and OS Windows Security (4624, 4688, 7045), Sysmon, Linux auditd, journald Which process ran, under which account, with what parent and command line Identity Active Directory (4768, 4769), Entra ID sign-ins, Okta System Log Who authenticated, from where, with which protocol and MFA result Network Firewall, DNS, web proxy, Zeek, NetFlow Who talked to whom, how much data moved, which domains resolved Cloud control plane AWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, GCP Audit Logs, Kubernetes audit Which API calls changed infrastructure, roles or policies Application and SaaS Web server access logs, Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Log, Google Workspace What users did inside business applications and data stores Security controls EDR, IDS/IPS (Suricata), WAF, email gateway What other tools already flagged, and why The highest-value findings usually sit at the seams. A Kerberoasting attempt shows up as a cluster of 4769 requests with RC4 encryption in identity logs. Proving what the attacker did with the cracked service account then takes endpoint and cloud data. What Are Common Log File Formats and Structures? Logs range from fully structured to free text, and the parsing burden scales accordingly. Four formats cover most of what a SOC handles day to day. Syslog. Still the lingua franca for network devices and Unix hosts. RFC 3164 (BSD syslog) is loosely defined and timestamp-poor. RFC 5424 adds a version field, ISO 8601 timestamps, MSGID and a STRUCTURED-DATA block, but the message body itself is often vendor-specific free text. CEF. ArcSight’s Common Event Format wraps events in a pipe-delimited header followed by key=value extensions: CEF:0|Acme|FW|7.2|4625|Logon failure|5|src=10.1.4.22 suser=jdoe dst=10.1.0.5 It is easy to parse but shallow, and vendors map fields inconsistently. LEEF, used by QRadar, follows the same idea. JSON and NDJSON. The default for cloud and SaaS audit logs. One object per line makes NDJSON streamable, while deep nesting and arrays complicate flattening into a fixed schema. Windows EVTX. A binary format of chunked records holding XML event data. You cannot grep it; it needs a dedicated parser, and the useful fields live in EventData. A practical test for any analysis tool is whether it ingests all four natively, without an analyst writing conversion scripts in the middle of an incident. Real-Time Log Monitoring Real-time monitoring means evaluating events as they arrive rather than on a search schedule. A scheduled SIEM query running every 15 minutes over a 20-minute lookback window, behind several minutes of ingestion and indexing lag, can easily put half an hour between an attacker’s action and the first alert. Streaming architectures close that gap by moving detection logic upstream. Events flow through a bus such as Kafka or a pipeline such as Cribl Stream, and rules are evaluated in flight with stateful windows for counts and sequences. Only enriched, tagged events and alerts continue to the SIEM, which also cuts ingestion cost. Three engineering problems come with it: Late and out-of-order events. Windows need watermarks or grace periods, or a sequence split across a delayed batch never completes. State management. Tracking 10,000 hosts across a 30-minute window is a memory problem, not a query problem. Alert volume. Faster detection of noisy rules only produces noise faster. Real-time pipelines also have a blind spot by design. They only see what is wired into them. Logs pulled from an isolated server, a contractor laptop or a newly acquired subsidiary still need fast, standalone analysis. What Are the Main Pattern Recognition Techniques in Logs? Pattern recognition in logs works in layers, from single events up to whole attack chains. Atomic matching. One event, one condition: a known-bad hash, rundll32.exe loading from a user-writable path, a Sigma rule on a suspicious command line. Fast and precise, but blind to anything that is only malicious in context. Aggregation and thresholds. Counting over a window. Twenty failed logons against one account suggests brute force; one failure each against twenty accounts from the same source suggests password spraying. Same event ID, different pattern. Sequence correlation. Ordered events within a time window, such as a new local admin created and then used for an RDP logon within ten minutes. Baselining and anomaly detection. First-seen parent-child process pairs, rare user-agent strings, logons outside a user’s normal hours. Higher-order correlation. Rules that run over detections rather than raw events, stitching individual hits into a chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics. This is the layer that turns 400 alerts into one incident. What Are the Essential Logs Analysis Tools? No single product covers the whole job. Mature teams combine logs analysis tools from four categories. SIEMs assume the data is already onboarded. DFIR utilities are fast but run a limited rule set and leave correlation to the analyst. General-purpose LLMs hit context limits and refuse security content. A tool built for the first hour of an incident needs a short list of properties: native ingestion of EVTX, syslog, CEF and JSON a large, maintained detection library, not a few hundred rules correlation into attack chains, not a flat list of hits results in minutes on commodity infrastructure a privacy model that survives a DPO’s review Why Is LogTotal One of the Best? LogTotal checks every item on that list, and it does so for free. SOC Prime opened it as a public preview on August 26, 2026 and announced general release on October 15 . The workflow is simple: upload, sanitize, get an investigation back. The reasoning about what each attack looks like was done in advance and compiled into detection content, so the engine matches and correlates instead of generating tokens. The privacy model is what gets LogTotal past legal review. The open-source @socprime/logtotal-sanitizer (Apache-2.0) swaps credentials, IPs, hostnames and usernames for stable HMAC tokens, so one user across three hosts stays one entity after redaction. You keep the key. Each analysis runs on a disposable, immutable instance that is deleted afterward. An enterprise environment emits events by the million every hour. During an incident, the responder rarely needs all of them. They need the few hundred that tell the story: the burst of 4625 failures followed by a single 4624 success, the encoded PowerShell spawned by winword.exe, the new service installed at 03:12 on a domain controller. Logs analysis is the discipline of getting from the first number to the second fast enough to matter.

That job has become harder in two directions at once. Attackers using AI tooling generate evidence at machine speed and pad real actions with benign-looking activity. Meanwhile, the obvious shortcut of pushing logs into an LLM runs into guardrails, context-window limits and data-protection obligations. Hugging Face’s responders hit exactly that wall in July 2026, when roughly 17,000 events were refused by frontier models and had to be processed on a local model instead.

Below, we cover log analysis end to end, then look at LogTotal, SOC Prime’s free answer to the incident-time version of the problem.

What Are the Fundamentals of Log Analysis?

Every log analysis workflow, whether it runs in a SIEM, a data lake or a responder’s laptop, rests on the same five stages. Skipping one usually shows up later as a missed detection or a false positive nobody can explain.

  1. Collection. Agents, syslog forwarders, API pollers and cloud-native exporters move events off the source. Gaps here are silent: a Sysmon config that drops Event ID 10 (process access) means credential-dumping via LSASS never appears downstream.
  2. Parsing and normalization. Raw lines become fields. A source IP should be the same field whether it came from a firewall, an IdP or an EDR, which is why schemas like ECS and OCSF exist.
  3. Enrichment. Asset criticality, user role, GeoIP and threat intelligence turn an IP address into context an analyst can act on.
  4. Correlation. Single events rarely prove anything. Linking them by host, user, process GUID or session ID is what produces an attack narrative.
  5. Retention and integrity. Hot storage for search, cold storage for forensics, and tamper evidence so the record holds up later.
What Is Log Analysis?

Log analysis is the process of examining machine-generated records to reconstruct what happened on a system, decide whether it matters, and determine what to do next. In security operations, it answers five questions about any suspicious activity: who acted, on what asset, when, from where, and by which mechanism.

It is distinct from log management. Management is plumbing: ingestion, storage, retention, access control. Analysis is interpretation. A team can have a well-run log pipeline and still miss an intrusion because nobody, human or machine, is asking the right questions of the data.

In practice, log analysis runs in three modes:

  • Detection. Rules and models evaluate events continuously and raise alerts when known malicious behavior appears.
  • Investigation. After an alert or a tip-off, analysts pivot through related events to scope the incident and find root cause.
  • Threat hunting. Analysts start from a hypothesis, such as abuse of a specific LOLBin, and search proactively for evidence the detection layer missed.

Of all the teams that use logs, security has the least room for gaps.

Why Is Log Analysis So Important?

Because time drives breach cost, and logs are where time is won or lost. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report puts the mean time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days, the first increase in five years. Breaches with a lifecycle over 200 days averaged $5.65 million, against $4.32 million for those contained faster.

Beyond cost, log analysis underpins four obligations every security program carries:

  • Detection. EDR and NDR see slices of activity. Logs from identity providers, SaaS audit trails and cloud control planes fill the gaps between them.
  • Scoping and root cause. Without event-level evidence, responders cannot say which accounts were touched or how the attacker got in, so remediation becomes guesswork.
  • Regulatory reporting. PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 10 mandates audit-log review and 12 months of retention. The SEC’s Form 8-K Item 1.05 gives listed companies four business days after a materiality determination, which is impossible without fast scoping.
  • Detection engineering. Real telemetry is how rules get tested and tuned.

There is a catch. The same logs that make all of this possible carry usernames, IP addresses, session cookies and bearer tokens. Analyzing them well increasingly means analyzing them safely.

What Are the Types of Log Data?

Security-relevant logs fall into six families. Each answers a different question, and an investigation that relies on only one or two of them will have blind spots an attacker can live in.

Log familyTypical sourcesWhat it tells the analystEndpoint and OSWindows Security (4624, 4688, 7045), Sysmon, Linux auditd, journaldWhich process ran, under which account, with what parent and command lineIdentityActive Directory (4768, 4769), Entra ID sign-ins, Okta System LogWho authenticated, from where, with which protocol and MFA resultNetworkFirewall, DNS, web proxy, Zeek, NetFlowWho talked to whom, how much data moved, which domains resolvedCloud control planeAWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, GCP Audit Logs, Kubernetes auditWhich API calls changed infrastructure, roles or policiesApplication and SaaSWeb server access logs, Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Log, Google WorkspaceWhat users did inside business applications and data storesSecurity controlsEDR, IDS/IPS (Suricata), WAF, email gatewayWhat other tools already flagged, and why

The highest-value findings usually sit at the seams. A Kerberoasting attempt shows up as a cluster of 4769 requests with RC4 encryption in identity logs. Proving what the attacker did with the cracked service account then takes endpoint and cloud data.

What Are Common Log File Formats and Structures?

Logs range from fully structured to free text, and the parsing burden scales accordingly. Four formats cover most of what a SOC handles day to day.

Syslog. Still the lingua franca for network devices and Unix hosts. RFC 3164 (BSD syslog) is loosely defined and timestamp-poor. RFC 5424 adds a version field, ISO 8601 timestamps, MSGID and a STRUCTURED-DATA block, but the message body itself is often vendor-specific free text.

CEF. ArcSight’s Common Event Format wraps events in a pipe-delimited header followed by key=value extensions:

CEF:0|Acme|FW|7.2|4625|Logon failure|5|src=10.1.4.22 suser=jdoe dst=10.1.0.5

It is easy to parse but shallow, and vendors map fields inconsistently. LEEF, used by QRadar, follows the same idea.

JSON and NDJSON. The default for cloud and SaaS audit logs. One object per line makes NDJSON streamable, while deep nesting and arrays complicate flattening into a fixed schema.

Windows EVTX. A binary format of chunked records holding XML event data. You cannot grep it; it needs a dedicated parser, and the useful fields live in EventData.

A practical test for any analysis tool is whether it ingests all four natively, without an analyst writing conversion scripts in the middle of an incident.

Real-Time Log Monitoring

Real-time monitoring means evaluating events as they arrive rather than on a search schedule. A scheduled SIEM query running every 15 minutes over a 20-minute lookback window, behind several minutes of ingestion and indexing lag, can easily put half an hour between an attacker’s action and the first alert.

Streaming architectures close that gap by moving detection logic upstream. Events flow through a bus such as Kafka or a pipeline such as Cribl Stream, and rules are evaluated in flight with stateful windows for counts and sequences. Only enriched, tagged events and alerts continue to the SIEM, which also cuts ingestion cost.

Three engineering problems come with it:

  • Late and out-of-order events. Windows need watermarks or grace periods, or a sequence split across a delayed batch never completes.
  • State management. Tracking 10,000 hosts across a 30-minute window is a memory problem, not a query problem.
  • Alert volume. Faster detection of noisy rules only produces noise faster.

Real-time pipelines also have a blind spot by design. They only see what is wired into them. Logs pulled from an isolated server, a contractor laptop or a newly acquired subsidiary still need fast, standalone analysis.

What Are the Main Pattern Recognition Techniques in Logs?

Pattern recognition in logs works in layers, from single events up to whole attack chains.

  • Atomic matching. One event, one condition: a known-bad hash, rundll32.exe loading from a user-writable path, a Sigma rule on a suspicious command line. Fast and precise, but blind to anything that is only malicious in context.
  • Aggregation and thresholds. Counting over a window. Twenty failed logons against one account suggests brute force; one failure each against twenty accounts from the same source suggests password spraying. Same event ID, different pattern.
  • Sequence correlation. Ordered events within a time window, such as a new local admin created and then used for an RDP logon within ten minutes.
  • Baselining and anomaly detection. First-seen parent-child process pairs, rare user-agent strings, logons outside a user’s normal hours.
  • Higher-order correlation. Rules that run over detections rather than raw events, stitching individual hits into a chain mapped to MITRE ATT&CK tactics. This is the layer that turns 400 alerts into one incident.
What Are the Essential Logs Analysis Tools?

No single product covers the whole job. Mature teams combine logs analysis tools from four categories.

The gap shows up during incident response. SIEMs assume the data is already onboarded. DFIR utilities are fast but run a limited rule set and leave correlation to the analyst. General-purpose LLMs hit context limits and refuse security content. A tool built for the first hour of an incident needs a short list of properties:

  • native ingestion of EVTX, syslog, CEF and JSON
  • a large, maintained detection library, not a few hundred rules
  • correlation into attack chains, not a flat list of hits
  • results in minutes on commodity infrastructure
  • a privacy model that survives a DPO’s review
Why Is LogTotal One of the Best?

The speed is not a GPU trick. The reasoning about what each attack looks like was done in advance and compiled into detection content, so the engine matches and correlates instead of generating tokens.

Main Trends for Log Analysis in 2026

Five shifts are reshaping how teams analyze logs this year.

  1. AI-speed attacks change what “suspicious” looks like. IBM reports that more than one in four organizations faced an AI-driven attack, up 56% year over year. Volume anomalies in benign event classes are becoming a detection signal in their own right.
  2. The SIEM is splitting. Gartner’s 2026 Hype Cycle for Security Operations shows the market dividing into integrated SOC platforms and security data lakes, with AI SOC agents at the peak of inflated expectations. Analysis increasingly happens where the data lives.
  3. Detection moves into the pipeline. Running rules on the stream, before indexing, cuts both mean time to detect and ingestion spend.
  4. OCSF becomes the shared schema. Normalized data is what lets the same detection, or the same AI agent, work across vendors.
  5. Privacy-preserving analysis becomes standard practice. IBM counted shadow-AI involvement in 43% of incidents, up from 20%. Pasting raw logs into a chatbot is exactly that. Keyed pseudonymization before logs leave the organization is turning from good practice into an expectation.

items.title: AOMEI Backupper update servers hijacked to push malware: Check your PC
items.summary: The Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) reports that attackers compromised AOMEI Technology’s update and notification infrastructure in a campaign investigated between April and July. AOMEI Backupper is backup software that the company says is used by more than 100 million people worldwide. It lets users back up files, copy entire drives, and recover data if something goes wrong with their PC. The attackers briefly altered AOMEI’s update and notification infrastructure to make customers’ software download and run malware . The same system also serves AnyViewer customers, but the report does not separately identify confirmed AnyViewer infections. For brief periods, the attackers changed the software’s download instructions to point to a malicious ZIP archive. They also changed the expected version number and MD5 checksum so the client would accept it. Because the same remote configuration file provided the download address and expected checksum, the attackers could change both the download and the information the software used to accept it. The researchers confirmed three tampering windows lasting ten, six, and five minutes, but more may have occurred. While these short windows provided fewer opportunities to infect machines, they also made the attack harder to spot. The attack used an initial downloader to install a persistent remote-access backdoor . The researchers did not identify the delivered malware as ransomware or an infostealer, but the backdoor lets attackers run commands and install additional malware. That means an infected PC could remain open to further attacks. How to check if you were affected If you used AOMEI Backupper during the affected period, update your security software and run a scan. You can download Malwarebytes Free to check for and remove malware. Malwarebytes’ AI detection engine identifies the initial malware downloader, upgrade-now.exe , as Malware.AI.4006642887 so ThreatDown and Malwarebytes customers were protected by the real-time detection component. Malwarebytes detects the malware dropper upgrade-now.exe If you’re comfortable checking Windows settings and files, these are additional warning signs: Open Windows Task Scheduler and check the Task Scheduler Library for a task named RadminComponentRuntime . Look in your AOMEI Backupper installation folder, particularly its version-specific html and Tmphtml folders, for an unsigned upgrade-now.exe or an unexpected upgrade-now.zip . Note that the malware downloader deletes itself after staging the next payload and creating persistence, so its absence does not mean the PC is clean. If you’re seeing outgoing traffic to promotion.storage-data.com , aomei.storage-data.com , storage-data.com , 8.210.84.56 , 47.239.60.117 , or 8.218.65.184 , whether blocked or allowed. Malwarebytes blocks 8.218.65.184 If you encounter one of these signs, get help rather than trying to clean everything manually. Disconnect the PC from the internet if you suspect it is actively compromised, and contact a trusted computer technician, Malwarebytes Support , or your organization’s IT/security team. From reporting threats to removing them. Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today .

items.title: Investigations and Analysis
items.summary: Something I've seen consistently, from the very beginning when I first brushed up against this business of "digital forensics", is the default focus on, "...this is how you analyze this artifact...", and rarely extending beyond that. I'm guilty of this, too. My first 8 books took this approach, listing data sources and artifacts, describing what they were in a general sense, and then maybe showing how to parse them. Each of those efforts basically left it up to the reading to stitch together their investigation on their own, and I justified this with the adage that each investigation is different. But then, I realized that what makes each investigation different isn't the incident itself, or the data sources. No, it's the investigator. Everyone of us approaches an incident investigation supported by our own knowledge and experience, and that's really the only thing that makes each investigation different. So, yes, while it's important to understand the value and nuances of the various data sources available on a Windows endpoint, something I can to realize is that this must be done in the context of an overall investigation. I recently ran across a blog post titled, How Do You Investigate Windows Event Logs? , with the subtitle, Windows Eventlog Analysis 101 . While I am very supportive of analysts developing a thorough understanding of various data sources, so that they can leverage and truly exploit those data sources in their investigations, I also very firmly believe that this must be part of an overall analysis process. This is why I wrote Investigating Windows Systems , to show how all of this information is, or can be, tied together by an analysis process. Once you have a process down, adding or removing data sources becomes thoughtful, intentional, and justified by data, not something that's done on a whim or because we forgot. There's a good bit of really good advice in the article, but what stood out to me most was one of the things I absolutely do NOT want to see in any discussion of investigative or analysis processes, and that's the recommendation to "search by event ID". I've said it before, and I'll say it again...event IDs are not unique. There's no requirement for that. In fact, MS itself doesn't use unique event IDs. For example, event IDs 4624 and 4625 mean something entirely different if the source is "Microsoft-Windows-Security-Auditing", or if it is "EventSystem". That's right...not even Microsoft uses unique event IDs. When you start digging into the Application Event Log, and even add other applications that either write their events to the Application Event Log, or to their own log, then things really start to take a turn. The point here is that any investigation or analysis advice that relies on a single data source, or suggests opening a single Windows Event Log in a viewer and then "search for event IDs" should be viewed as insufficient. Such advice is being shared by someone who doesn't have a defined analysis process. What we should be looking to is using several data sources (WEVTX, file system, EDR telemetry, etc.), normalizing them into a common format, enriching them with data from either our own prior investigations or from external sources (or both), and then displaying them in a timeline format, so that we can see the progression and timing of the activity. Another example of the narrow-aperture way of conducting analysis can be seen clearly in this LinkedIn post , and there are many more just like it. The shortfall of all of this is that this is what AI models are being trained on, and because they're capable of doing it at scale, today's up-and-coming analysts will not be able to keep up. They won't be able to see the gaps, and they won't know when the model is hallucinating a finding. They simply won't be able to discern valid findings.

items.title: Securing the agentic insider
items.summary: In the last few months, concerns have arisen about AI safety as a growing number of incidents were publicly disclosed. These incidents exposed how powerful models have become and how they represent a significant threat if not handled well. And with the global race on innovation, the challenge will compound as models become even more powerful. While most have been worried about threat actors using powerful models to attack, the focus has been less on agents within our own walls. Since we were the ones who deployed agents internally for our companies, we implicitly trusted our agents. Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted . This is not because models are inherently malicious. Models have been trained to attain results, which often leads to reward hacking, and models are not optimized around organizational norms or judgment. Agents are unpredictable. They will adapt as the context changes, may not behave as intended and will collaborate and collude with other agents to reach their objectives, without needing to be compromised. Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise. They are agentic insiders. Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly. To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7. An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime. In July, we announced Project Perception , an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise. The same cyber stack is also directly applicable to managing and governing the agentic insiders that run in the enterprise. Project Perception can be leveraged to contain agentic insiders, implementing deterministic controls on non-deterministic intelligence: Sensors/Signals/Actuators: bring together signals across the various sensors (identity, data, cloud, endpoint, network, runtime) to discover agents in the enterprise and bring them under management by assigning an identity, container and set of policy and permissions . Context: use those signals to compute, dynamically , the risk associated with what the agents are attempting to do. Harness/agents/models: based on dynamic agent risk , a team of Guardian Agents , with green and blue agents, actively and continually supervise every action of every agent and surgically respond as the risk profile increases, in real time. This is where agentic security changes the equation for security practitioners. Project Perception can supervise in real time while providing traceability for practitioners to examine what happened, understand why the risk emerged and apply the judgment needed to update their security system accordingly. Agentic security provides speed . Practitioners provide judgment . That is how defenders begin operating at the same speed as the systems they are protecting against. Today, security systems can reliably observe the actions of the agents. Those signals are essential and tell us what we need to contain. Our security controls should increasingly be able to ask not only “What is happening?” but also “Why is it happening?” Is this consistent with the intent of the task?” This will require greater transparency into the model itself, not only the input and output tokens, but the thinking and chain of thought tokens. Only then can we truly understand whether the model’s intent is aligned with the purpose of the agent. Model transparency will not replace containment. It will make containment smarter and stronger . And it will allow us to better inform accountability and traceability. This needs to be the next step in securing agentic insiders. With Project Perception, you can get started today on the journey to secure your agentic insiders . There should not be a choice between innovation and safety. Hayete Gallot leads Microsoft’s work to help organizations operate securely in an AI-driven world. Her scope includes identity, threat protection, compliance and data security at global scale.

Agents have been unleashed in the enterprise, at scale, and their numbers are growing rapidly. These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes. They have become active participants in the enterprise.

They are agentic insiders.

Monitoring and securing those agents must become continuous. We need to understand in real time what the agents are doing and what risks those actions create, and we need to adjust their ability to act accordingly.

To manage and control these insiders, we will need Guardian Agents — an established industry term — that watch and moderate every action of every agent, before it happens, 24/7.

An agent brings together a model, a harness that orchestrates its work, an action space of tools and resources and a runtime in which it executes. Securing agents requires protection across multiple layers: identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud and runtime.

In July, we announced Project Perception, an agentic security system that uses our new cyber stack and teams of red, blue and green agents to help defenders act with speed, while defending against AI driven attacks from outside of the enterprise.

The same cyber stack is also directly applicable to managing and governing the agentic insiders that run in the enterprise.

Project Perception can be leveraged to contain agentic insiders, implementing deterministic controls on non-deterministic intelligence:

  • Sensors/Signals/Actuators: bring together signals across the various sensors (identity, data, cloud, endpoint, network, runtime) to discover agents in the enterprise and bring them under management by assigning an identity, container and set of policy and permissions.
  • Context: use those signals to compute, dynamically, the risk associated with what the agents are attempting to do.
  • Harness/agents/models: based on dynamic agent risk, a team of Guardian Agents, with green and blue agents, actively and continually supervise every action of every agent and surgically respond as the risk profile increases, in real time.

This is where agentic security changes the equation for security practitioners.

Project Perception can supervise in real time while providing traceability for practitioners to examine what happened, understand why the risk emerged and apply the judgment needed to update their security system accordingly. Agentic security provides speed. Practitioners provide judgment. That is how defenders begin operating at the same speed as the systems they are protecting against.

Today, security systems can reliably observe the actions of the agents. Those signals are essential and tell us what we need to contain. Our security controls should increasingly be able to ask not only “What is happening?” but also “Why is it happening?” Is this consistent with the intent of the task?” This will require greater transparency into the model itself, not only the input and output tokens, but the thinking and chain of thought tokens. Only then can we truly understand whether the model’s intent is aligned with the purpose of the agent. Model transparency will not replace containment. It will make containment smarter and stronger. And it will allow us to better inform accountability and traceability. This needs to be the next step in securing agentic insiders.

With Project Perception, you can get started today on the journey to secure your agentic insiders. There should not be a choice between innovation and safety.

items.title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
items.summary: The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update. If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls. This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server? Citrix released software updates to address the flaw , and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch. Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth , to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue. Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform. The NetScaler exploit Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks. CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771 . In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the connection workflow . The entire exploit stems from the fact that the Gateway has to be publicly accessible on the Internet, otherwise users would not be able to initiate their desktop connection. Put the access decision in front of the authentication server The best thing that you can do, after patching all your instances, is move any publicly accessible login pages or applications behind single sign-on before the request ever hits the target server. Cloudflare Access can enforce an independent access policy before the request reaches the existing gateway server. The Citrix environment continues to determine which desktop the user may launch and to validate the resulting session ticket. The additional boundary ensures that an attacker could never get to the Gateway server to try running specific exploits. They would only see the Cloudflare Access login page. That decision no longer depends on recognizing an exploit signature and blocking that way, but rather on a set of Zero Trust policies that determine if someone should even be there to begin with. More attacks like this are coming, and adopting Zero Trust controls throughout your network is the single most important thing you should do next. This follows the principle described in Cloudflare's own architecture as customer zero : reduce exposure and use independent defenses so that one flaw does not become a compromise. Here, the practical starting point is the service that users reach before they enter their applications. Protecting the web authentication path adds a boundary in front of the existing Citrix controls. It does not automatically extend that boundary to other gateway services, including DTLS-enabled listeners. Those interfaces still need their own exposure review and applicable security updates, even when the desktop sessions they support already require authentication. The origin connection must enforce the same boundary Changing a DNS record and enforcing Access policies are not enough. If an attacker can connect to the original address or an alternate hostname, they can avoid the controls placed in front of it. Access enforces a specific hostname: if the authentication server can be reached via an IP address or alternative hostname, then the Access policy enforcement is worthless. It’s important to take steps to ensure that all traffic comes from a request that was validated by Access. There are a few different approaches to accomplish this, based on your internal architecture. Cloudflare Tunnel is the most commonly used approach. It establishes an outbound only tunnel from your application server and allows you to close all inbound IP traffic. This means that you won’t have a public IP for the server that can be reached by anyone. When a public origin IP Address must remain or connector software cannot be run, network restrictions and origin authentication need to constrain the connections it accepts. For example, Dedicated CDN Egress IPs give an account dedicated source addresses for traffic from Cloudflare to its origins. The application server’s firewall can allow those addresses and reject other sources. This makes the network restriction specific to the account's traffic , rather than broadly allowing traffic from Cloudflare's shared address ranges. Authenticated Origin Pulls can add further depth with mutual TLS to verify the Cloudflare-to-origin connection. An origin that supports it can also validate the Access JSON Web Token , including its signature, issuer, expiry, and intended application audience. This is the best way to guarantee that a request was authenticated by Access. If you're unsure where to start, speak with a Cloudflare expert to review your architecture and identify which controls fit your environment. Protect the web-facing authentication service Cloudflare Access determines who may reach the web application; Cloudflare's web application firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP requests to that same protected service. The WAF runs before any Access authentication checks, which gives you the ability to completely block known malicious IPs, specific countries, ASNs, or other attributes you know definitely shouldn’t be accessing your applications. The firewall runs continuously on all requests and will also identify users who managed to authenticate attempting to run exploits with known CVE signatures. Alongside managed CVE signatures, WAF Attack Score uses machine learning to identify potentially malicious requests that do not exactly match a known rule. Administrators can use the score in rules that block or challenge requests. The WAF attack score is powered by network observations from Cloudflare's global network traffic and Cloudforce One investigations feed Cloudflare's shared threat-intelligence platform . Customers with a Cloudforce One threat intelligence subscription can also use live threat indicators in WAF policies . That adds context about known malicious sources alongside inspection of the request itself. Reducing exposure does not remove an attacker who already has a foothold. Seriously: go patch your system if you haven’t, and follow Citrix's suspected-compromise guidance . They lay out how to preserve evidence, revoke credentials and certificates, investigate connected systems, and rebuild or restore from a known-good state. Extend Zero Trust to desktop access, or remove the desktop dependency Protecting web authentication can be an initial step without making it the final architecture. Cloudflare's Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktops also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone. Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads, Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop access connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel, without a local remote desktop client . If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation can replace that web-access use case without a full virtual desktop. Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration. Decide which authentication services need to be public The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone. Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default. Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment: Request the protected hostname without signing in. Confirm the request stops at Cloudflare rather than reaching the origin. Sign in with a test account outside the permitted group. Confirm it still cannot reach the protected application. Test direct-origin addresses and alternate hostnames. Confirm none bypasses the access policy. Sign in as an approved user. Confirm authentication, desktop launch, and session reconnection still work. Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed. Bring the controls together The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic. Get started Speak with a Cloudflare expert to plan the right controls for your environment. Download the solution brief and sign up for the upcoming webinar . Andrei Migia, Nathan Sackett, and Doug Shepherd contributed to this post.
