But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch.

Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth, to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue.

Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform.

The NetScaler exploit

Citrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks.

CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771.

In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. The gateway validates the ticket before proxying the desktop connection. Citrix documents these as distinct stages of the connection workflow. The entire exploit stems from the fact that the Gateway has to be publicly accessible on the Internet, otherwise users would not be able to initiate their desktop connection.

Put the access decision in front of the authentication server

The best thing that you can do, after patching all your instances, is move any publicly accessible login pages or applications behind single sign-on before the request ever hits the target server. Cloudflare Access can enforce an independent access policy before the request reaches the existing gateway server. The Citrix environment continues to determine which desktop the user may launch and to validate the resulting session ticket. The additional boundary ensures that an attacker could never get to the Gateway server to try running specific exploits. They would only see the Cloudflare Access login page.

That decision no longer depends on recognizing an exploit signature and blocking that way, but rather on a set of Zero Trust policies that determine if someone should even be there to begin with. More attacks like this are coming, and adopting Zero Trust controls throughout your network is the single most important thing you should do next.

This follows the principle described in Cloudflare's own architecture as customer zero: reduce exposure and use independent defenses so that one flaw does not become a compromise. Here, the practical starting point is the service that users reach before they enter their applications.

Protecting the web authentication path adds a boundary in front of the existing Citrix controls. It does not automatically extend that boundary to other gateway services, including DTLS-enabled listeners. Those interfaces still need their own exposure review and applicable security updates, even when the desktop sessions they support already require authentication.

The origin connection must enforce the same boundary

Changing a DNS record and enforcing Access policies are not enough. If an attacker can connect to the original address or an alternate hostname, they can avoid the controls placed in front of it. Access enforces a specific hostname: if the authentication server can be reached via an IP address or alternative hostname, then the Access policy enforcement is worthless. It’s important to take steps to ensure that all traffic comes from a request that was validated by Access. There are a few different approaches to accomplish this, based on your internal architecture.

Cloudflare Tunnel is the most commonly used approach. It establishes an outbound only tunnel from your application server and allows you to close all inbound IP traffic. This means that you won’t have a public IP for the server that can be reached by anyone.

When a public origin IP Address must remain or connector software cannot be run, network restrictions and origin authentication need to constrain the connections it accepts. For example, Dedicated CDN Egress IPs give an account dedicated source addresses for traffic from Cloudflare to its origins. The application server’s firewall can allow those addresses and reject other sources. This makes the network restriction specific to the account's traffic, rather than broadly allowing traffic from Cloudflare's shared address ranges.

Authenticated Origin Pulls can add further depth with mutual TLS to verify the Cloudflare-to-origin connection.

An origin that supports it can also validate the Access JSON Web Token, including its signature, issuer, expiry, and intended application audience. This is the best way to guarantee that a request was authenticated by Access.

If you're unsure where to start, speak with a Cloudflare expert to review your architecture and identify which controls fit your environment.

Protect the web-facing authentication service

Cloudflare Access determines who may reach the web application; Cloudflare's web application firewall (WAF) inspects HTTP requests to that same protected service. The WAF runs before any Access authentication checks, which gives you the ability to completely block known malicious IPs, specific countries, ASNs, or other attributes you know definitely shouldn’t be accessing your applications. The firewall runs continuously on all requests and will also identify users who managed to authenticate attempting to run exploits with known CVE signatures.

Alongside managed CVE signatures, WAF Attack Score uses machine learning to identify potentially malicious requests that do not exactly match a known rule. Administrators can use the score in rules that block or challenge requests. The WAF attack score is powered by network observations from Cloudflare's global network traffic and Cloudforce One investigations feed Cloudflare's shared threat-intelligence platform.

Customers with a Cloudforce One threat intelligence subscription can also use live threat indicators in WAF policies. That adds context about known malicious sources alongside inspection of the request itself.

Reducing exposure does not remove an attacker who already has a foothold. Seriously: go patch your system if you haven’t, and follow Citrix's suspected-compromise guidance. They lay out how to preserve evidence, revoke credentials and certificates, investigate connected systems, and rebuild or restore from a known-good state.

Extend Zero Trust to desktop access, or remove the desktop dependency

Protecting web authentication can be an initial step without making it the final architecture. Cloudflare's Zero Trust architecture for virtual desktops also supports controlling access to the desktop infrastructure itself. With the Cloudflare One Client and private-network connectivity, teams can restrict who and which devices may reach the endpoints carrying desktop traffic, including an existing Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) path. This requires its own routing and policy design; it is not a capability supplied by the browser authentication proxy alone.

Some workflows can remove the ICA dependency instead. For supported Windows workloads,  Cloudflare's browser-based remote desktop access connects users to a Windows host through Cloudflare Tunnel, without a local remote desktop client. If users only need a desktop to open web applications, Access and Browser Isolation can replace that web-access use case without a full virtual desktop.

Start by protecting the authentication service and existing desktop connections. Then replace virtual desktops used only for web access, and move supported Windows workflows to browser-based remote desktops. Reducing exposure does not have to wait for a full desktop migration.

Decide which authentication services need to be public

The same assessment applies beyond virtual desktops. An employee portal or management console may need to be reachable by approved users from anywhere, without needing to accept application requests from everyone.

Not every authentication page can require a prior employee identity. Consumer login pages and the identity-provider endpoints required to establish an initial session may need to remain publicly reachable. Protect those intentionally, and avoid introducing circular authentication dependencies. The point is to make reachability a design decision rather than an inherited default.

Start with one restricted service. Map the web and non-web paths into it, then put the access decision ahead of its authentication surface. Before expanding the rollout, validate the boundary in your own environment:

  1. Request the protected hostname without signing in. Confirm the request stops at Cloudflare rather than reaching the origin.
  2. Sign in with a test account outside the permitted group. Confirm it still cannot reach the protected application.
  3. Test direct-origin addresses and alternate hostnames. Confirm none bypasses the access policy.
  4. Sign in as an approved user. Confirm authentication, desktop launch, and session reconnection still work.

Check the relevant policy, firewall, and origin logs rather than relying only on what the browser displays. Repeat these checks when routing, identity, or failover settings change, so the next configuration update does not quietly reopen the path you closed.

Bring the controls together

The full architecture brings the access decision, web inspection, and availability controls in front of NetScaler, with restrictions on the connection to the origin. The public origin and Tunnel paths are alternatives. The native desktop connection remains separate, with an optional Zero Trust network access layer around that traffic.

Get started

Speak with a Cloudflare expert to plan the right controls for your environment. Download the solution brief and sign up for the upcoming webinar.

Andrei Migia, Nathan Sackett, and Doug Shepherd contributed to this post.

items.title: Agents are your newest insiders. Security must move at their speed.
items.summary: Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk. This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale. Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them. “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.” Satya Nadella Project Perception—Securing your agentic insider We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents. Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider . Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response. Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365 share signals, context, and a unified registry giving IT and security teams a consistent view of agents and risk, with the controls each needs. This builds on a simple security principle: surround non-deterministic intelligence with deterministic controls, independent evidence, and containment boundaries. Assume an agent can fail or be compromised. Observe it continuously. Minimize and tailor its authority before it acts. And continuously adjust that authority as risk changes. This requires protection across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime. The system has four continuous responsibilities: Know which agents exist, who owns them, why they exist, and what they are doing. Contain what each agent can access and do before it acts. Protect the data, tools, runtime, resources, and systems in the agent’s path. Adapt protection continuously as behavior, context, and risk change. These are not four products or sequential phases. They operate together. Evidence changes risk. Risk changes policy. Policy changes what the agent is allowed to do. Consider an expense-approval agent. It may need to read expense submissions, check policy, and approve routine reimbursements, but it should not inherit every permission of the employee who sponsors it. Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start. If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it. This is what continuous containment looks like in practice. Know every agent and give it an accountable identity You cannot secure what you cannot see. Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process. Microsoft Security uses native integrations, connectors, and sensors across the cyber stack to discover more of the agent estate. We are expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, bringing the total to 60 supported local agents , including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Organizations can bring these agents into a unified registry, regardless of how they were discovered, to understand ownership, activity, and risk. Discovery tells you that an agent exists. Identity gives security and governance systems a durable anchor for controlling it. Every agent should have a first-class identity distinct from the person using or sponsoring it. We are extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security. Agent identity anchors attribution, ownership, lifecycle, risk, permissions, authorization, and policy, so the enterprise can distinguish what a person did from what an agent did on that person’s behalf. Contain what the agent can do before it acts Being able to find and identify an agent is necessary, but it is just the start. We need to understand the potential impact the agent can have in the enterprise environment. The next step is to bound the agent across its runtime, its paths to tools and resources, and the authority it can exercise. Contain the runtime The model and harness should execute inside a controlled environment rather than inherit fully-privileged access to the device. Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task. They also create an enforcement boundary where security controls and observability can operate outside the agent’s reach. If the agent or harness is compromised, it should not be able to disable the controls watching it. Control the action space An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find. Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy. Controlling the destination alone is not enough. Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior. Start with no permissions, or least privilege We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people. Agents make those principles even more important. An agent should not automatically inherit all the standing access of its user. It should begin with no authority and receive only what it needs for the approved task, for only as long as the task requires. To enable this, we are introducing Dynamic Permissions. Organization-wide policy sets the outer boundary, including preventing an agent from obtaining authority its user does not have. Permissions can then be scoped to the task, made time-bound, and contracted or removed as the task changes or completes. Higher-impact actions can require verified human approval. The employee retains the employee’s access. The agent receives its own identity, permissions and its own authority scoped to its current task and for the duration of the task only. Adapt protection as agent risk changes Least privilege reduces exposure, but it does not eliminate risk. An expense-approval agent may begin a task with the right access and then encounter a prompt injection in an external document. Its configuration has not changed, but its behavior and risk have. For human users, a delay between detection and response may be manageable. For an agent operating at machine speed, it can be the difference between containment and impact. The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal. That is why we are introducing Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents. Dynamic Agent Risk Dynamic Agent Risk combines signals from identity, data, endpoints, cloud, network, runtime, and the agent’s own activity. It considers how securely the agent is configured, what resources it can reach, the potential impact if something goes wrong, and whether its actions are drifting from the user’s or organization’s intent. The result is not a one-time score assigned at onboarding. It is a continuously updated understanding of the agent’s current risk and whether its current authority still matches that risk. The question is not simply whether the agent should run or stop. It is what the agent should be allowed to read, change, invoke, or approve at that moment. Dynamic Conditional Access Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points. The response is graduated, not binary. Policy can reduce permissions, preserve reads while blocking writes, narrow the data and resources the agent can reach, restrict network paths, shorten or revoke time-bound access, or require provable human approval before a consequential action proceeds. At the highest levels of risk, it can isolate the runtime or stop execution entirely. Return to the expense agent. It begins with narrowly scoped permission to review and approve expenses within policy. When it encounters untrusted content and attempts an unrelated action, new evidence raises its Dynamic Agent Risk. Policy responds proportionately: it can preserve read access while removing the ability to approve or write, block access to sensitive resources, and require cryptographically provable human approval for a high-impact step. If the risk continues to rise, the system can isolate the runtime or stop execution. The employee remains productive. The agent is constrained without treating every risk change as a kill-switch event. Secure agentic systems at scale with Guardian Agents As organizations deploy thousands or hundreds of thousands of agents, manually triaging every alert and coordinating every response will not scale. Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set. That is why we are introducing new Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. People define policy, approval boundaries, and delegation rules. Playbooks define the desired security outcome and coordinate protective actions. Guardian Agents carry out the work at machine speed, adapting as agent activity, risk, security context, and organizational policy change. Guardian Agents can help teams understand why risk changed, investigate the relevant evidence, recommend or apply containment, and use what they learn to harden policy. This is not about outsourcing judgment. People retain control over objectives and consequential decisions. The system carries the continuous work that does not scale through manual operations. Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale. At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats. Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.” — Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft Extending containment to the model As model transparency increases, it creates a new source of security evidence. Chain-of-thought and other model-level signals can help identify intent drift, understand whether untrusted information is influencing reasoning, and detect when an agent’s planned actions are diverging from the task it was given. We are bringing this deeper evidence into Dynamic Agent Risk, together with signals from across the cyber stack. This builds on Satya Nadella’s principle: increase transparency into the model while keeping security decisions and enforcement independent of it. Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk. But the core security principle does not change: the model cannot be its own security boundary. Independent systems must observe every layer, including the model itself, and ultimately determine and enforce what the system is allowed to do. These are not separate pillars. They make the same containment architecture stronger: better evidence, stronger assurance, more accurate risk, and more effective protection. Confidence to move faster Organizations are adopting agents to serve customers better, solve problems faster, and give people more time for the work that matters most. The goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable before it can be useful. The goal is to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not. That requires a clear division of responsibility. Models supply intelligence. People and organizations retain authority. Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action. Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works. You should not have to choose between innovation and safety. That is what we are working toward: an agentic world where organizations can put intelligence to work with confidence because security can observe it, govern it, and contain it at the same speed. Learn more here and join us at Microsoft Ignite . To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn ( Microsoft Security ) and X ( @MSFTSecurity ) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity.
items.summary_html:
Agents are rapidly becoming part of how work gets done. They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk.

This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale.

Satya Nadella, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Microsoft, recently described the trust architecture this new era requires: we must separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. We should not ask a model to be its own security authority. The controls that determine what it can access, what actions it can take, and whether it should continue operating must sit outside the model, where the model cannot bypass or tamper with them.

“The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.”

Satya Nadella
Project Perception—Securing your agentic insider

We introduced Project Perception and the Microsoft cyber stack to help organizations defend with agents. Today, we are extending Perception to secure the agentic insider. Guardian Agents help security teams operate continuously, at machine speed and scale, while sensors, context, and actuators across the cyber stack help understand changing agent risk and continuously adapt protection in response. Project Perception and Microsoft Agent 365 share signals, context, and a unified registry giving IT and security teams a consistent view of agents and risk, with the controls each needs.

This builds on a simple security principle: surround non-deterministic intelligence with deterministic controls, independent evidence, and containment boundaries. Assume an agent can fail or be compromised. Observe it continuously. Minimize and tailor its authority before it acts. And continuously adjust that authority as risk changes.

This requires protection across identity, permissions, data, endpoints, network, cloud, and runtime. The system has four continuous responsibilities:

  • Know which agents exist, who owns them, why they exist, and what they are doing.
  • Contain what each agent can access and do before it acts.
  • Protect the data, tools, runtime, resources, and systems in the agent’s path.
  • Adapt protection continuously as behavior, context, and risk change.

These are not four products or sequential phases. They operate together. Evidence changes risk. Risk changes policy. Policy changes what the agent is allowed to do. Consider an expense-approval agent. It may need to read expense submissions, check policy, and approve routine reimbursements, but it should not inherit every permission of the employee who sponsors it. Its identity, runtime, access paths, and task-scoped authority should be explicit from the start. If it later encounters a prompt injection or attempts an action outside that task, the system should respond proportionately: preserve safe reads while blocking writes, narrow the resources it can reach, require provable human approval for a consequential step, or isolate and stop the agent when the risk warrants it. This is what continuous containment looks like in practice.

Know every agent and give it an accountable identity

You cannot secure what you cannot see. Agents can be created through Microsoft platforms, integrated through partner platforms and software development kits (SDKs), or introduced locally without a central deployment process. Microsoft Security uses native integrations, connectors, and sensors across the cyber stack to discover more of the agent estate.

We are expanding discovery to 35 additional types of local agents, bringing the total to 60 supported local agents, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. Organizations can bring these agents into a unified registry, regardless of how they were discovered, to understand ownership, activity, and risk.

Discovery tells you that an agent exists. Identity gives security and governance systems a durable anchor for controlling it.

Every agent should have a first-class identity distinct from the person using or sponsoring it. We are extending Microsoft Entra Agent ID with identity types for additional agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents discovered through security sensors. This means an agent can become a policy target even when it was not originally integrated with Microsoft Security. Agent identity anchors attribution, ownership, lifecycle, risk, permissions, authorization, and policy, so the enterprise can distinguish what a person did from what an agent did on that person’s behalf.

Contain what the agent can do before it acts

Being able to find and identify an agent is necessary, but it is just the start. We need to understand the potential impact the agent can have in the enterprise environment. The next step is to bound the agent across its runtime, its paths to tools and resources, and the authority it can exercise.

Contain the runtime

The model and harness should execute inside a controlled environment rather than inherit fully-privileged access to the device. Sandboxes such as Microsoft Execution Container (MXC) provide policy-controlled access to resources the agent needs to complete its task. They also create an enforcement boundary where security controls and observability can operate outside the agent’s reach. If the agent or harness is compromised, it should not be able to disable the controls watching it.

Control the action space

An agent should not be free to call any tool, API, Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, resource, or other agent it can find. Local and network and data controls must mediate those paths, observe the calls, and enforce enterprise policy. Controlling the destination alone is not enough. Security must also understand the content flowing into and out of the agent, including its sensitivity, provenance, and whether untrusted data may be influencing the agent’s behavior.

Start with no permissions, or least privilege

We have spent decades applying Zero Trust and least privilege to people. Agents make those principles even more important. An agent should not automatically inherit all the standing access of its user. It should begin with no authority and receive only what it needs for the approved task, for only as long as the task requires.

To enable this, we are introducing Dynamic Permissions. Organization-wide policy sets the outer boundary, including preventing an agent from obtaining authority its user does not have. Permissions can then be scoped to the task, made time-bound, and contracted or removed as the task changes or completes. Higher-impact actions can require verified human approval.

The employee retains the employee’s access. The agent receives its own identity, permissions and its own authority scoped to its current task and for the duration of the task only.

Adapt protection as agent risk changes

Least privilege reduces exposure, but it does not eliminate risk. An expense-approval agent may begin a task with the right access and then encounter a prompt injection in an external document. Its configuration has not changed, but its behavior and risk have.

For human users, a delay between detection and response may be manageable. For an agent operating at machine speed, it can be the difference between containment and impact. The security system must be able to understand what changed and act before a person can manually investigate every signal.

That is why we are introducing Dynamic Agent Risk and Dynamic Conditional Access for agents.

Dynamic Agent Risk

Dynamic Agent Risk combines signals from identity, data, endpoints, cloud, network, runtime, and the agent’s own activity. It considers how securely the agent is configured, what resources it can reach, the potential impact if something goes wrong, and whether its actions are drifting from the user’s or organization’s intent.

The result is not a one-time score assigned at onboarding. It is a continuously updated understanding of the agent’s current risk and whether its current authority still matches that risk. The question is not simply whether the agent should run or stop. It is what the agent should be allowed to read, change, invoke, or approve at that moment.

Dynamic Conditional Access

Dynamic Conditional Access extends Microsoft Entra Conditional Access for agents so a change in risk can drive coordinated action across multiple enforcement points. The response is graduated, not binary. Policy can reduce permissions, preserve reads while blocking writes, narrow the data and resources the agent can reach, restrict network paths, shorten or revoke time-bound access, or require provable human approval before a consequential action proceeds. At the highest levels of risk, it can isolate the runtime or stop execution entirely.

Return to the expense agent. It begins with narrowly scoped permission to review and approve expenses within policy. When it encounters untrusted content and attempts an unrelated action, new evidence raises its Dynamic Agent Risk. Policy responds proportionately: it can preserve read access while removing the ability to approve or write, block access to sensitive resources, and require cryptographically provable human approval for a high-impact step. If the risk continues to rise, the system can isolate the runtime or stop execution. The employee remains productive. The agent is constrained without treating every risk change as a kill-switch event.

Secure agentic systems at scale with Guardian Agents

As organizations deploy thousands or hundreds of thousands of agents, manually triaging every alert and coordinating every response will not scale. Securing agents must itself become agentic, while remaining inside boundaries people set.

That is why we are introducing new Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. People define policy, approval boundaries, and delegation rules. Playbooks define the desired security outcome and coordinate protective actions. Guardian Agents carry out the work at machine speed, adapting as agent activity, risk, security context, and organizational policy change.

Guardian Agents can help teams understand why risk changed, investigate the relevant evidence, recommend or apply containment, and use what they learn to harden policy. This is not about outsourcing judgment. People retain control over objectives and consequential decisions. The system carries the continuous work that does not scale through manual operations.

Agents will only be adopted at scale if they can be trusted at scale. At Microsoft, we are already operating in a world of hundreds of thousands of agents. As Customer Zero, we have learned that securing agents requires continuous visibility into agent activity, proactive protection of access and data, and adaptive protection that keeps pace with evolving threats. Those lessons directly inform the innovations we are delivering to help every organization adopt agents with confidence.”

—Terrell Cox, Corporate Vice President (CVP) and Deputy Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), Customer Security, Microsoft

Extending containment to the model

As model transparency increases, it creates a new source of security evidence. Chain-of-thought and other model-level signals can help identify intent drift, understand whether untrusted information is influencing reasoning, and detect when an agent’s planned actions are diverging from the task it was given.

We are bringing this deeper evidence into Dynamic Agent Risk, together with signals from across the cyber stack. This builds on Satya Nadella’s principle: increase transparency into the model while keeping security decisions and enforcement independent of it.

Greater model transparency gives security systems deeper evidence to detect suspicious behavior and inform Dynamic Agent Risk. But the core security principle does not change: the model cannot be its own security boundary. Independent systems must observe every layer, including the model itself, and ultimately determine and enforce what the system is allowed to do.

These are not separate pillars. They make the same containment architecture stronger: better evidence, stronger assurance, more accurate risk, and more effective protection.

Confidence to move faster

Organizations are adopting agents to serve customers better, solve problems faster, and give people more time for the work that matters most. The goal is not to make every model perfectly predictable before it can be useful. The goal is to build systems that remain secure even when the model is not.

That requires a clear division of responsibility. Models supply intelligence. People and organizations retain authority. Independent controls establish identity, limit privilege, protect data, preserve evidence, and contain unsafe action. Security continuously reassesses risk and adapts protection as the agent works.

You should not have to choose
between innovation and safety.

That is what we are working toward: an agentic world where organizations can put intelligence to work with confidence because security can observe it, govern it, and contain it at the same speed.

Learn more here and join us at Microsoft Ignite.

To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn (Microsoft Security) and X (@MSFTSecurity) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity.

items.title: Reinventing Endpoint Security with Cortex XDR One
items.summary: Enterprises spent the last two years racing to capture the vast potential of AI, authorizing AI agents to touch production code, internal databases, customer tickets and financial ledgers. Because these agents operate non-deterministically with broad capabilities, they can easily be manipulated into unexpected or malicious behavior. The result is agents breaking out of isolation, shifting AI risk from a hallucinating chatbot to an operational liability. items.title: A sextortion conspiracy killed his son (Lock and Code S07E21)
items.summary: This week on the Lock and Code podcast… At just 17 years old, Jordan DeMay was murdered by strangers online. That’s how Jordan’s father, John DeMay, described what happened to his son four years ago. At home in Michigan, Jordan was readying for a weekend trip when he received a friend request on Instagram. The invite was sent by a user named “dani.robertts” whose profile showed an attractive young woman. After accepting the request, Jordan and the account chatted about nothing in particular—teenage matters, getting to know one another—before “dani” became flirtatious, eventually sending Jordan what she claimed was a nude photograph of herself. Jordan responded in kind with an explicit photograph of himself. But here, a trap was revealed. “Dani Robertts” was not a young, friendly, interested woman. Dani Robertts was several men, sending messages from thousands of miles away in Lagos, Nigeria, who had followed a script to pressure young men into handing over their money. This was not the first time these men had run this scam. But with a great deal of investigative work, it hopefully has become the last. What happened to Jordan can happen to anyone—and it has happened to far too many young men and women today. It is a type of attack commonly referred to as “sextortion.” Today, on the Lock and Code podcast with host David Ruiz, we speak with John DeMay about his son Jordan, his family’s relationship with social media, and what parents should know. Tune in today to listen to the full conversation. items.title: NSA, CISA and NIST Release New Security Guidelines to Detect and Shut Down Rogue AI Agents
items.summary: NSA, CISA, and NIST have released joint security guidelines to help organizations detect, contain, and shut down AI agents that act beyond their approved tasks. Published October 16, 2026, the voluntary guidance sets out ten practices for managing incidents during superintelligence training and evaluation, with a focus on maintaining human oversight. The NIST announcement groups the practices into preparation, detection, response, recovery, and reporting. Its main audience is organizations training or testing highly capable agents on lengthy tasks with limited human supervision. The recommendations may also apply to organizations deploying these systems. The document calls these events SI control incidents. They occur when agents take significant actions without instructions and break policies or security controls that define their task boundaries. Examples include unauthorized contact with outside parties, financial transactions, or access to third-party systems. NSA, CISA and NIST Issue Rogue AI Agent Guidelines Importantly, this definition separates independent agent behavior from attacker-directed activity. Prompt injection or a deliberately backdoored model causes instructed actions, not the primary cause of an SI control incident. The guidance also covers near-misses that expose weaknesses before harm occurs. Related reporting on AI agents attempting to hack public websites shows why task boundaries matter when automated systems encounter blocked access. That reporting is separate from the new guidance, which outlines readiness measures rather than announcing a specific breach. Agencies recommend restricting agents to the data, tools, and systems they need for their tasks. Use strict allowlists for network access where possible, with permitted traffic passing through a monitored gateway. Organizations should also identify routes for hidden communication, persistence, and unauthorized copying of model weights. Detection should cover the model, its supporting software, host systems, and network activity. Agents should not be able to alter monitoring tools or logs. Where possible, teams should use monitoring models from different families to cross-check findings and reduce shared blind spots. The guidance also warns that agent outputs may contain exploits aimed at monitoring systems. This adds context to earlier coverage of NIST’s proposed AI security control overlays , which addressed access controls, monitoring and audit records across AI environments. A central recommendation is shutdown. The joint publication calls for automatically stopping affected agent runs when a control failure or ongoing incident is detected. Depending on severity, organizations should pause related training, evaluation, or deployment until protections are strengthened and verified. Response teams should preserve model weights, checkpoints, tool calls, rejected actions, and reliable logs. They should revoke exposed credentials, rebuild potentially compromised environments, and remove backdoors or hidden communication paths. Before restarting, teams should test monitoring, access limits, and shutdown controls against the incident’s actions. Organizations should notify affected parties, meet legal reporting duties, and share relevant incidents and near-misses with government experts. The guidance builds on NIST SP 800-61r3 and established incident response practices, extending them to autonomous systems. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Hackers Exploit SiteGuard WAF Vulnerability That Could Give Them Full Control of Servers
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting a command injection flaw in SiteGuard Server Edition, a web application firewall installed directly on protected servers. Tracked as CVE-2026-106931, the vulnerability could let attackers run operating system commands with root or SYSTEM privileges, potentially giving them full control of an affected server. The flaw affects the product’s statistics function, which is enabled by default. EG Secure Solutions confirmed exploitation and notified customers with direct support contracts on September 29, 2026. Japan’s vulnerability coordination service published its JVN advisory on October 14, while JPCERT/CC also issued an alert. The weakness is classified as OS command injection under CWE-78. It lets attackers run operating system commands through the affected software’s statistics-processing function. Those commands may execute with root privileges on Unix systems or SYSTEM privileges on Windows, rather than the attacker’s existing permissions. However, the published severity ratings describe a local attack requiring low privileges and no user interaction. Hackers Exploit SiteGuard WAF Vulnerability Administrators should therefore understand this as a path from limited access to higher privileges, not a confirmed login-free remote attack. The vulnerability scores 8.5 under CVSS 4.0 and 7.8 under CVSS 3.0. Neither advisory identifies the attackers, affected organizations, attack volume, or the exact exploitation method. items.title: Hackers Registered New Teams-Based Domains and Used a Login Page to Steal Your Logins
items.summary: A newly registered domain copies Microsoft Teams’ login page and interface, raising concerns about a phishing attempt targeting workplace users. Security researcher Steven Lim reported that teams-cloud[.]live was just five days old when he flagged it on October 18, 2026. He urged organizations to block the address before employees encounter the fake site. The alert highlights phishing built around a familiar business tool. A copied Teams screen could persuade employees to trust a sign-in request. However, the available report does not establish how many people visited the site, whether passwords were captured, or who operates the domain. According to Steven Lim , the site mimics both the Teams login screen and its wider user interface. He said it resembles another example he shared on October 8, 2026. That similarity warrants investigation, but it does not confirm that the same attacker controls both sites. Lim also reported that clicking an option to update Teams downloaded a TXT file. The alert does not provide the file’s contents, a hash, or evidence that it executes code. Calling it confirmed malware would therefore go beyond the available findings. The unexpected download remains a useful detail for investigators checking browser activity and downloaded files. Fake Microsoft Teams Domains Used to Steal Credentials In a pinned comment supplied with the alert, Lim identified amgen[.]teams-cloud[.]live as a healthcare-themed target. The company name appears as a subdomain beneath teams-cloud[.]live. Its presence does not establish that Amgen was breached or that an employee account was accessed. The concern is the gap between what users see and where they are browsing. A convincing Teams design does not make an unrelated domain a Microsoft service. Newly registered teams-cloud[.]live mimics the Microsoft Teams login interface (source: Steven Lim) Cyber Security News previously covered attackers posing as IT help desk staff through Teams , pushing employees toward downloads or remote access. That separate activity shows how workplace trust can support phishing without a software flaw. Another report examined fake login pages created through Teams redirects in browsers. No confirmed link exists to this domain, but both cases show why branding alone cannot validate a login prompt. Defenders should review connections to teams-cloud[.]live and the reported subdomain, then check related downloads and sign-in activity. Lim specifically recommended Tenant blocking and web filtering. Microsoft documents URL blocking through the Tenant Allow/Block List and custom domain blocking through Defender network protection. Administrators should apply controls suited to their environment and verify coverage rather than assume one setting blocks every route. Employees should avoid the reported site and verify unexpected Teams update requests through their organization’s established IT support channel before entering passwords or opening downloads. items.title: 16-Year-Old Broadcom Wi-Fi Flaw Lets Attackers Hack Routers Without Knowing Passwords
items.summary: A 16-year-old flaw in Broadcom’s Wi-Fi software can let attackers within wireless range take control of affected routers without knowing the network password. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the issue at Hexacon in Paris on October 16, 2026, warning that old code remains in widely deployed devices. According to Kaiser’s research, the flaw has existed in Broadcom’s software development kit since at least 2010. It affects its proprietary Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) implementation. It allows memory leaks and attacker-controlled code execution before normal WPS enrollment finishes. The flaw sits in code that joins fragmented Extensible Authentication Protocol messages used by WPS. Weak length checks allow crafted wireless messages to overflow a memory buffer. 16-Year-Old Broadcom Wi-Fi Flaw Attackers can then read or change memory and redirect the router’s program flow to run their own code. This is an over-the-air attack, not a password-cracking method. The attacker needs wireless reach to the target but not its network key. Kaiser demonstrated stealing the saved Wi-Fi password from an Orange Belgium ASKEY TCG3000 router and sending it back through wireless frames. He then joined the network using the stolen password. A second demonstration against a Proximus BBOX3V+ provided a remote command shell over Wi-Fi frames without a cloud command server. These tests show why a strong password alone cannot stop exploitation of the affected software. Kaiser confirmed exploitation on devices used by three Belgian internet providers. These include Proximus BBOX3V+, VOO’s Netgear CG3100 and CG3700, Technicolor TC7210 and CGA4233, and Orange’s ASKEY TCG3000. Possible exposure involving Telenet equipment remains unconfirmed. His estimates place the affected Belgian fleet at roughly 1.56 million gateways across Proximus, legacy VOO, and Orange. These are researcher estimates, not verified provider totals. He warns that the wider issue could affect millions of access points worldwide, although the full count remains unknown. The finding follows earlier Broadcom-related wireless security concerns, including the separate Kr00k Wi-Fi vulnerability . The new research concerns WPS message handling rather than that earlier flaw. Kaiser describes a 2018 patch as incomplete. In correspondence reproduced in his slides, Broadcom said it had long known about the issue and had offered replacement software based on hostapd and WPA Supplicant since 2018. That leaves device makers responsible for moving away from the old implementation. Kaiser reported the eCos issue on July 18 and the Linux issue on July 27. He says Broadcom declined to assign a CVE, and the tested Belgian devices remained unpatched as of October 15. His detection toolkit includes a wireless fingerprinting script and YARA rules for firmware checks. These are screening tools, not final proof of exploitability. Findings need further review. The risk also draws renewed attention to Nearest-Neighbor attacks , where compromised nearby systems provide wireless reach. That case used different methods, but shows why nearby Wi-Fi exposure matters. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Millions of California students’ sensitive data stolen in breach
items.summary: Personal information belonging to millions of current and former California public school students has been stolen from a system operated by Educational Testing Service (ETS). ETS is a nonprofit organization that helps run the state’s standardized tests under contract with the California Department of Education (CDE). It has begun notifying students and families after an unauthorized party accessed and copied student information from an ETS-operated secure file transfer protocol (SFTP) site. CDE is distributing the ETS breach notice to help affected individuals receive information about the incident and available resources. An investigation determined that an unauthorized party used compromised login details to ​access the site and copy files containing California student information at various ​times between May 22 and September 18. The CDE says the breach includes all students enrolled during the previous three school years, although the affected population is not limited to that group. The information involved varies by individual but may include: Student names Statewide Student Identifiers (SSIDs) Dates of birth Home addresses Demographic information Disability and program participation information Statewide assessment information, including test scores According to the CDE, over 5.7 million students were enrolled in California ​public schools during the 2025–2026 school year alone. Not every affected student had every category of information exposed. However, this is clearly more than a list of names and email addresses: The stolen files can reveal highly personal information about a student’s education and disabilities. CDE says Social Security numbers , financial account information, passwords, and parent or guardian information were not involved. ETS says it has found no evidence so far that the stolen information has been made public. How to stay safe ETS, at CDE’s direction, is notifying affected students and families. If your information or your child’s information was involved, follow the instructions in the notification and: Verify any communication about the incident through official channels. Consider enrolling in the two years of free identity-protection services. Parents or legal guardians can enroll affected minors, while affected adults can enroll themselves. Check the instructions for the appropriate age group. Watch for messages that use details about your child or their school to sound convincing. Don’t share passwords, security codes, or payment details in response to an unsolicited message or call. For more advice, read our blog “ Involved in a data breach? Here’s what you need to know. ” Pro tip: Students, faculty, and staff at participating US universities can get free security software through the Malwarebytes Student Protection Program . Visit malwarebytes.com/student to check your eligibility and sign up. Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

items.title: Training AIs to Solve CAPTCHAs
items.summary: Interesting research : Abstract : Vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHAs without task-specific training, but the agents built on them approach every challenge from scratch. For such an agent, the hundredth instance of a familiar puzzle costs as much time and compute as the first. Specialized detectors invert the trade-off, answering in milliseconds but only for categories they were trained on. Neither improves with exposure. We study what changes when a solver improves with use. Our system pairs a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector with an open-weight VLM behind a confidence-based router, and runs entirely from screenshots and operating-system input events, with no browser automation or DOM access. It reaches 85.4% overall and 84.2% macro accuracy across 16 classes, exceeding either component alone. Every answer VLM produces also serves as a training label, so the detector absorbs categories it was never trained for, typically after one or two encounters and without human annotation. The same loop also repairs it. A CAPTCHA operator can perturb images against the publicly released detector and drive its accuracy to 0%, but the perturbations leave VLM untouched, and its labels let the detector recover. Under a year-long simulated arms race in which the CAPTCHA operator re-crafts its perturbations each month, the solver recovers every round, and a cheap ~70%-accurate open-weight teacher hardens it as effectively as a perfect oracle. Visual CAPTCHA defenses that assume a failing bot stays failing therefore understate how quickly an adaptive solver returns.
