items.title: How AI workloads are reshaping Kubernetes autoscaling
items.summary: Kubernetes has quietly run much of the world’s containerized software on a division of labor between two control loops that rarely had to talk to each other. The scheduler places each pod on a node that already exists; the autoscaler adds nodes when pods have nowhere to fit. For a decade that separation was a sound design, because compute was largely interchangeable and either loop could work without knowing much about the other’s decisions. AI workloads, and the accelerators they run on, changed the terms; the clean split still serves most work well, and the pace of AI is what makes its edges worth revisiting. It surfaces in a situation anyone running GPUs will recognize. A pod that should schedule simply will not, even though the cluster is not truly out of capacity, and the delay can leave costly accelerator capacity unused. The instinct is to assume the region has run dry, and sometimes it has. In other cases, the capacity is available and the pod still stays pending, because the node the autoscaler is willing to add is not one the scheduler is willing to use. The autoscaler answers the question it was built for, whether to add a node, when the real question is whether that node is even the right shape for the work. The rest of this piece examines how the community has closed part of it, how it plans to close the rest, and how the autoscaler is likely to grow into a more scheduler-aware partner. The hard problems, and how the community is answering them Several of the challenges accelerators bring share a thread. Each is something both loops now have to understand the same way. Not all are new or unique to AI; some were long familiar to high-performance and batch computing, and accelerators made them everyone’s problem. Three show how far the shared answers have come. Reservations, capacity committed before the work arrives This one is the most familiar. Because supply is tight and idle accelerators are expensive, teams may reserve capacity ahead of demand. When a scale-up draws from a reservation, the autoscaler must consider not only whether to grow but also whether the resulting node uses capacity the team has already committed to and is paying for. Reservations are not an autoscaling invention. They are a long-standing capacity practice that an autoscaler may need to account for, because a node can be launched against committed capacity rather than relying on unreserved supply. Topology, the interconnect between devices, not just their count Topology is about how devices are wired to one another, not simply how far apart they sit. An accelerator leans on the parts that feed it, including the CPU and memory in its local NUMA domain, the network interface that shares its PCIe path, and the high-bandwidth links to its peer accelerators; it runs best when those pieces share a locality so traffic does not cross a slower hop. That locality is a hierarchy, from devices on the same bus inside a server, to servers in a rack joined by a fast accelerator fabric, to racks linked across a data-center network, each tier a step slower than the one beneath it. The largest models span many servers at once, so “keep these close” reaches well beyond a single node. Historically, Kubernetes commonly represented accelerator resources as counts and lacked a portable, structured way to express many device relationships; a node advertised a number, a pod asked for some, and the scheduler matched the two integers. Dynamic Resource Allocation supplies what was missing. Instead of a bare count, a workload files a structured claim describing what it needs, including a relationship like an accelerator together with the network interface that feeds it. The scheduler reads those claims directly, and DRA-aware autoscalers are starting to use the same information when they simulate capacity, though support still varies by implementation. The cost of a blind boundary. A DRA-aware autoscaler can account for a topology claim when selecting capacity; without that support it may provision an incompatible node. Sharing, putting a whole device to work, not part of it A modern accelerator is powerful enough that handing an entire one to a small job wastes most of it, so a single device can be partitioned into isolated instances that run concurrently. Some runtimes also time-slice devices, but that is a separate execution mechanism and not what consumable capacity models. Partitionable devices let one device be offered as smaller slices on demand, and consumable capacity goes finer, letting several workloads each draw a measured portion, so a request can be satisfied by a fraction of a device rather than requiring an entire device. The scheduler tracks those allocations directly, and DRA-aware autoscalers are starting to use the same model when they weigh a prospective node, though support still varies. Finer slicing can leave leftover fragments, but sensible minimum and step sizes help keep that smaller than the all-or-nothing waste it replaced. Efficiency moved inside the device. Partitioning splits one device into isolated fixed instances; consumable capacity lets several claims draw measured shares at once. Topology and sharing matter most for what they share. Together, DRA and its extensions give the scheduler and the autoscaler the same language for hardware, so the two are far less likely to disagree about what a viable node even looks like. That shared vocabulary is real progress, and it is also where the next problem begins. Why a shared vocabulary is not enough A common language lets the two loops agree on what a node is; it does not make them act as one, and some problems need exactly that. The clearest is gang scheduling, an all-or-nothing case that is not new but has grown far more acute under AI and tight capacity. A large job needs every pod to be scheduled together or none at all, and this is where shared facts alone fall short. This part is being addressed, but only on one side. Through workload-aware scheduling , whose Workload and PodGroup APIs are beta upstream and remain disabled by default, the scheduler is learning to treat a group as one all-or-nothing unit, holding its pods until enough can be placed together so a half-placed job no longer strands hardware. The autoscaler was not part of that change. It still reasons pod by pod, so it can add a node or two for a few pending members of a gang and waste that capacity while the job never starts. A companion mechanism, the provisioning request , is the current bridge. It lets a workload ask the autoscaler for a whole group’s capacity at once rather than pod by pod. With a configured admission check, Kueue reserves quota, creates the request, waits for capacity to be reported ready, and then admits the workload. Atomic scale-up is best effort and depends on provider support. It remains a bolt-on across a seam rather than a shared understanding, and it points at the deeper pattern. A capable autoscaler already reasons a little like a scheduler, predicting where the scheduler would place pods to decide whether a new node would help. The clearest sign is duplicated effort already baked in. The autoscaler simulates the scheduler’s placement to decide what to launch, and once the node exists the scheduler makes its own placement decision, repeating much of the same reasoning. What the community is building next This is why the two loops, which still do different jobs, increasingly have to be designed together, and that convergence is becoming an active design discussion. The workload-aware scheduling effort has signaled that its scope is meant to reach beyond the scheduler toward autoscaling over time, and a public proposal in the SIG-Autoscaling community now sketches integration APIs that let the two speak directly. One would let the scheduler see capacity that could be provisioned rather than only the nodes already present, one would express placement preferences across it, and one would request it explicitly. The deeper motivation is process. If autoscaling is a first-class concern while a feature is designed, provisioning gets considered while a new placement primitive is taking shape rather than only after it ships, so the seam becomes something the community weighs up front rather than something autoscalers scramble to close after each release. What to take away The mental model worth keeping is one hardware model, two consumers. A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it, and every place only one of them understands a capability is a place they can disagree and may leave costly hardware idle. So when a pod stays pending, do not assume the capacity is gone; check whether the scheduler and the autoscaler agree on what a usable node looks like. Inference is what makes this pressing rather than academic, since bursty serving and agentic workloads have no patience for a cold node. These interfaces are being drawn in the open right now, in SIG-Autoscaling and SIG-Scheduling rather than in any one vendor’s product, so anyone running accelerators has both a stake in the outcome and a chance to shape it before the design sets.
items.summary_html:
Kubernetes has quietly run much of the world’s containerized software on a division of labor between two control loops that rarely had to talk to each other. The scheduler places each pod on a node that already exists; the autoscaler adds nodes when pods have nowhere to fit. For a decade that separation was a sound design, because compute was largely interchangeable and either loop could work without knowing much about the other’s decisions. AI workloads, and the accelerators they run on, changed the terms; the clean split still serves most work well, and the pace of AI is what makes its edges worth revisiting.

It surfaces in a situation anyone running GPUs will recognize. A pod that should schedule simply will not, even though the cluster is not truly out of capacity, and the delay can leave costly accelerator capacity unused. The instinct is to assume the region has run dry, and sometimes it has. In other cases, the capacity is available and the pod still stays pending, because the node the autoscaler is willing to add is not one the scheduler is willing to use. The autoscaler answers the question it was built for, whether to add a node, when the real question is whether that node is even the right shape for the work. The rest of this piece examines how the community has closed part of it, how it plans to close the rest, and how the autoscaler is likely to grow into a more scheduler-aware partner.

The hard problems, and how the community is answering them

Several of the challenges accelerators bring share a thread. Each is something both loops now have to understand the same way. Not all are new or unique to AI; some were long familiar to high-performance and batch computing, and accelerators made them everyone’s problem. Three show how far the shared answers have come.

Reservations, capacity committed before the work arrives

This one is the most familiar. Because supply is tight and idle accelerators are expensive, teams may reserve capacity ahead of demand. When a scale-up draws from a reservation, the autoscaler must consider not only whether to grow but also whether the resulting node uses capacity the team has already committed to and is paying for. Reservations are not an autoscaling invention. They are a long-standing capacity practice that an autoscaler may need to account for, because a node can be launched against committed capacity rather than relying on unreserved supply.

Topology, the interconnect between devices, not just their count

Topology is about how devices are wired to one another, not simply how far apart they sit. An accelerator leans on the parts that feed it, including the CPU and memory in its local NUMA domain, the network interface that shares its PCIe path, and the high-bandwidth links to its peer accelerators; it runs best when those pieces share a locality so traffic does not cross a slower hop. That locality is a hierarchy, from devices on the same bus inside a server, to servers in a rack joined by a fast accelerator fabric, to racks linked across a data-center network, each tier a step slower than the one beneath it. The largest models span many servers at once, so “keep these close” reaches well beyond a single node. Historically, Kubernetes commonly represented accelerator resources as counts and lacked a portable, structured way to express many device relationships; a node advertised a number, a pod asked for some, and the scheduler matched the two integers. Dynamic Resource Allocation supplies what was missing. Instead of a bare count, a workload files a structured claim describing what it needs, including a relationship like an accelerator together with the network interface that feeds it. The scheduler reads those claims directly, and DRA-aware autoscalers are starting to use the same information when they simulate capacity, though support still varies by implementation.

The cost of a blind boundary. A DRA-aware autoscaler can account for a topology claim when selecting capacity; without that support it may provision an incompatible node.

Sharing, putting a whole device to work, not part of it

A modern accelerator is powerful enough that handing an entire one to a small job wastes most of it, so a single device can be partitioned into isolated instances that run concurrently. Some runtimes also time-slice devices, but that is a separate execution mechanism and not what consumable capacity models. Partitionable devices let one device be offered as smaller slices on demand, and consumable capacity goes finer, letting several workloads each draw a measured portion, so a request can be satisfied by a fraction of a device rather than requiring an entire device. The scheduler tracks those allocations directly, and DRA-aware autoscalers are starting to use the same model when they weigh a prospective node, though support still varies. Finer slicing can leave leftover fragments, but sensible minimum and step sizes help keep that smaller than the all-or-nothing waste it replaced.

Efficiency moved inside the device. Partitioning splits one device into isolated fixed instances; consumable capacity lets several claims draw measured shares at once.

Topology and sharing matter most for what they share. Together, DRA and its extensions give the scheduler and the autoscaler the same language for hardware, so the two are far less likely to disagree about what a viable node even looks like. That shared vocabulary is real progress, and it is also where the next problem begins.

Why a shared vocabulary is not enough

A common language lets the two loops agree on what a node is; it does not make them act as one, and some problems need exactly that. The clearest is gang scheduling, an all-or-nothing case that is not new but has grown far more acute under AI and tight capacity. A large job needs every pod to be scheduled together or none at all, and this is where shared facts alone fall short.

This part is being addressed, but only on one side. Through workload-aware scheduling, whose Workload and PodGroup APIs are beta upstream and remain disabled by default, the scheduler is learning to treat a group as one all-or-nothing unit, holding its pods until enough can be placed together so a half-placed job no longer strands hardware. The autoscaler was not part of that change. It still reasons pod by pod, so it can add a node or two for a few pending members of a gang and waste that capacity while the job never starts.

A companion mechanism, the provisioning request, is the current bridge. It lets a workload ask the autoscaler for a whole group’s capacity at once rather than pod by pod. With a configured admission check, Kueue reserves quota, creates the request, waits for capacity to be reported ready, and then admits the workload. Atomic scale-up is best effort and depends on provider support. It remains a bolt-on across a seam rather than a shared understanding, and it points at the deeper pattern. A capable autoscaler already reasons a little like a scheduler, predicting where the scheduler would place pods to decide whether a new node would help. The clearest sign is duplicated effort already baked in. The autoscaler simulates the scheduler’s placement to decide what to launch, and once the node exists the scheduler makes its own placement decision, repeating much of the same reasoning.

What the community is building next

This is why the two loops, which still do different jobs, increasingly have to be designed together, and that convergence is becoming an active design discussion. The workload-aware scheduling effort has signaled that its scope is meant to reach beyond the scheduler toward autoscaling over time, and a public proposal in the SIG-Autoscaling community now sketches integration APIs that let the two speak directly. One would let the scheduler see capacity that could be provisioned rather than only the nodes already present, one would express placement preferences across it, and one would request it explicitly. The deeper motivation is process. If autoscaling is a first-class concern while a feature is designed, provisioning gets considered while a new placement primitive is taking shape rather than only after it ships, so the seam becomes something the community weighs up front rather than something autoscalers scramble to close after each release.

What to take away

The mental model worth keeping is one hardware model, two consumers. A scarce accelerator is only as useful as the agreement between the loop that schedules it and the loop that provisions it, and every place only one of them understands a capability is a place they can disagree and may leave costly hardware idle. So when a pod stays pending, do not assume the capacity is gone; check whether the scheduler and the autoscaler agree on what a usable node looks like. Inference is what makes this pressing rather than academic, since bursty serving and agentic workloads have no patience for a cold node. These interfaces are being drawn in the open right now, in SIG-Autoscaling and SIG-Scheduling rather than in any one vendor’s product, so anyone running accelerators has both a stake in the outcome and a chance to shape it before the design sets.

items.title: Beyond IoCs: Start Hunting Their Patterns
items.summary: As many of you already know from my previous articles, I have always been a strong supporter of Indicators of Attack (IoAs) over Indicators of Compromise (IoCs). IoCs are useful, and I use them almost every day for investigations, Threat Hunting, and building my own Threat Intelligence feeds. But I believe we can get much more value from them than simply collecting indicators such as IP addresses, domains, or hashes. Every week, we see cybersecurity articles describing new campaigns, malware, or variations of attacks we already know. Sometimes the only difference is a new payload, a different domain, or a small change in the execution chain. Interesting research, of course, but what additional value can we extract if our detections already cover the attack behaviour? Let’s take this recent CyberSecurityNews article about ClickFix as an example. It describes malicious activity involving ClickFix and provides several IP addresses, domains, and other indicators. Great! We can import them into MISP, OpenCTI, Defender XDR, or Sentinel, investigate historical connections, and potentially block the malicious destinations. https://cybersecuritynews.com/hackers-use-clickfix/ But what happens tomorrow when the attacker creates another domain? Will the researchers update the article? Publish another one? Will someone add the new IoCs to a public feed? Everything is possible, but personally, I don’t think I will have the time or even remember to revisit the article. I will probably be busy with another incident or some other security investigation. So why don’t we try to find something more interesting behind those IoCs? Hunting IOC patterns Instead of investigating every indicator individually, let’s look at what they have in common. What happens if we enrich those IPs using WHOIS, BGP, and ASN information? See content credentials We have now a pattern (one among others) and we have a clear picture of an abused ASN infrastructure. Of course, sharing an ASN doesn’t automatically make an IP malicious. Large hosting providers can have thousands of legitimate customers but the reputation of the ASN + more than 1 month average to take a malicious domain down…is quite a big signal. In addition, what if we combine that information with other data? Imagine a user receiving an email containing a URL, clicking it, and connecting to a previously unseen domain hosted on that ASN and to an unexpected country ( such as Estonia in the image above), suddenly we have a much more interesting hunting scenario. We are no longer looking exclusively for a known malicious IP. We are investigating a combination of infrastructure and behaviour. And here comes my favourite part. Tomorrow, the attacker creates a new domain that nobody has reported yet. However, they reuse infrastructure belonging to the same ASN we have been investigating. If we have already developed hunting logic around that infrastructure and its associated behaviour, we may identify suspicious activity without waiting for someone to publish the new IoC. Imagine a new Rule such as [DR] — New Email with an URL Linked to known abused ASN (62005). From IoCs to hunting opportunities I already explored this approach in my previous article, Threat Hunting via Autonomous System Numbers (ASN) , where I discussed using network infrastructure information to identify suspicious activities beyond individual IP addresses. The same concept can be applied to published Threat Intelligence where we can use known tools such as MISP and/or OpenCTI. We can enrich indicators, identify shared infrastructure, compare it against our own telemetry, and investigate whether those relationships provide opportunities for new detections. And this is where I see the real value of Threat Hunting. Not every new article requires another detection rule, especially when we already monitor the technique. Sometimes the opportunity is somewhere else, hidden in the relationships between the published indicators. I’m not suggesting that we stop collecting IoCs. I will continue using them in my investigations and automation workflows. But rather than stopping at an exact match, I prefer to ask what else we can learn from them. IoCs tell us what has already been observed. Investigating their patterns may help us identify what comes next. And for me, that’s exactly what Threat Hunting is about. Beyond IoCs: Start Hunting Their Patterns was originally published in Detect FYI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

items.title: Frida 17.24.3 Released
items.summary: Fallout from the QuickJS rebase, found by @ShenKecyes , a V8 fix for pointer authentication by @hsorbo , and better iOS device discovery on Linux. QuickJS ShenKecyes read our allocator hooks and noticed that they never updated the heap statistics QuickJS keeps. QuickJS decides when to collect cycles based on the amount of memory allocated, so with that counter stuck at zero, cyclic garbage lived until an explicit gc() . The hooks now track usage, and collection kicks in on its own again. They also spotted that current QuickJS keeps the source along with the bytecode by default, which the old version never did. Our precompiled runtime is now stripped of its source, while the debug info stays so that stack frames in it still resolve. The runtime bytecode went from 71 to 28 KB. Thanks for the thorough report! Along the way I found that QuickJS finalizers are per class, and only the base Sampler had one, so every sampler created from JS leaked. A CallCountSampler thus stayed attached after unload, and a later Stalker test following a thread through the stale hook deadlocked on the allocator lock. V8 on arm64e Håvard tracked down a fault in the first garbage collection that scanned the stack, in processes using pointer authentication. V8’s register-pushing stack walker calls its callback through a plain BLR , but the callback arrives as a C function pointer signed with the IA key, so the branch landed on the signed value. It now branches through BLRAAZ when the host authenticates pointers. Thanks! iOS devices on Linux Discovering an iOS device over the network on Linux relied on systemd-resolved for mDNS browsing. Where it isn’t running, or has multicast DNS turned off, we now fall back to Avahi over D-Bus, resolving the pairing service the same way. And if the mDNS reply never arrives, the timeout error now suggests that a netfilter rule may be dropping it, as that is what it usually turns out to be. Two XPC fixes came out of the same session. Replies larger than the HTTP/2 window stalled, as only the connection-level window was replenished and never the stream’s. And double and date objects are now decoded instead of being rejected. macOS Our OpenSSL-backed glib-networking crashed on every macOS trust store lookup. Mistakes were made when porting our existing patch to the new glib-networking: two of the Security framework constants it looked up are CFSTR() macros rather than exported symbols, so dlsym() returned NULL . They are now created as strings. Enjoy! Changelog gumjs: Track QuickJS heap usage in the allocator hooks, so cycles are collected without an explicit gc() . Thanks @ShenKecyes ! gumjs: Strip the source from the QuickJS runtime bytecode, keeping debug info, shrinking it from 71 to 28 KB. Thanks @ShenKecyes ! gumjs: Finalize QuickJS sampler subclasses, fixing a leak that kept samplers attached after unload. v8: Authenticate the stack scan callback on arm64e. Thanks @hsorbo ! fruity: Fall back to Avahi for mDNS browsing when systemd-resolved isn’t available or has multicast DNS disabled. fruity: Suggest a firewall rule as the cause when an mDNS reply times out. fruity: Fix XPC flow control for replies larger than the HTTP/2 window. fruity: Decode double and date XPC objects. glib-networking: Fix the macOS trust store lookup, which crashed since the last SDK bump.
items.summary_html:
Fallout from the QuickJS rebase, found by @ShenKecyes, a V8 fix for pointer authentication by @hsorbo, and better iOS device discovery on Linux.

QuickJS

ShenKecyes read our allocator hooks and noticed that they never updated the heap statistics QuickJS keeps. QuickJS decides when to collect cycles based on the amount of memory allocated, so with that counter stuck at zero, cyclic garbage lived until an explicit gc(). The hooks now track usage, and collection kicks in on its own again.

They also spotted that current QuickJS keeps the source along with the bytecode by default, which the old version never did. Our precompiled runtime is now stripped of its source, while the debug info stays so that stack frames in it still resolve. The runtime bytecode went from 71 to 28 KB. Thanks for the thorough report!

Along the way I found that QuickJS finalizers are per class, and only the base Sampler had one, so every sampler created from JS leaked. A CallCountSampler thus stayed attached after unload, and a later Stalker test following a thread through the stale hook deadlocked on the allocator lock.

V8 on arm64e

Håvard tracked down a fault in the first garbage collection that scanned the stack, in processes using pointer authentication. V8’s register-pushing stack walker calls its callback through a plain BLR, but the callback arrives as a C function pointer signed with the IA key, so the branch landed on the signed value. It now branches through BLRAAZ when the host authenticates pointers. Thanks!

iOS devices on Linux

Discovering an iOS device over the network on Linux relied on systemd-resolved for mDNS browsing. Where it isn’t running, or has multicast DNS turned off, we now fall back to Avahi over D-Bus, resolving the pairing service the same way. And if the mDNS reply never arrives, the timeout error now suggests that a netfilter rule may be dropping it, as that is what it usually turns out to be.

Two XPC fixes came out of the same session. Replies larger than the HTTP/2 window stalled, as only the connection-level window was replenished and never the stream’s. And double and date objects are now decoded instead of being rejected.

macOS

Our OpenSSL-backed glib-networking crashed on every macOS trust store lookup. Mistakes were made when porting our existing patch to the new glib-networking: two of the Security framework constants it looked up are CFSTR() macros rather than exported symbols, so dlsym() returned NULL. They are now created as strings.

Enjoy!

Changelog
  • gumjs: Track QuickJS heap usage in the allocator hooks, so cycles are collected without an explicit gc(). Thanks @ShenKecyes!
  • gumjs: Strip the source from the QuickJS runtime bytecode, keeping debug info, shrinking it from 71 to 28 KB. Thanks @ShenKecyes!
  • gumjs: Finalize QuickJS sampler subclasses, fixing a leak that kept samplers attached after unload.
  • v8: Authenticate the stack scan callback on arm64e. Thanks @hsorbo!
  • fruity: Fall back to Avahi for mDNS browsing when systemd-resolved isn’t available or has multicast DNS disabled.
  • fruity: Suggest a firewall rule as the cause when an mDNS reply times out.
  • fruity: Fix XPC flow control for replies larger than the HTTP/2 window.
  • fruity: Decode double and date XPC objects.
  • glib-networking: Fix the macOS trust store lookup, which crashed since the last SDK bump.

items.title: ShinyHunters Exploits Oracle PeopleSoft to Steal Sensitive Data
items.summary: Imagine finding out that someone has been accessing your organization’s systems, stealing data, and moving between servers without anyone noticing. That’s the kind of situation organizations faced when ShinyHunters exploited a critical vulnerability in Oracle PeopleSoft. The attacks took place from May 27 to June 9, 2026, before Oracle issued its security alert. Universities were among the hardest hit, with some organizations suffering data breaches. How did the attackers get in, what should Oracle PeopleSoft users check, and what are the signs of compromise to look for? Who Are ShinyHunters? ShinyHunters is a cybercrime group that steals sensitive data and threatens to leak it unless victims pay. Instead of locking files with ransomware, it uses stolen data to pressure victims. ShinyHunters exploited a flaw to access PeopleSoft systems without logging in. Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant linked the activity to UNC6240 [1] , which they track as ShinyHunters. According to Mandiant, the attacks began in late May 2026 and continued into June. The timing matters here. Oracle published its security alert on June 10 [2] , after the reported exploitation period. That means organizations could have been exposed before they had an official alert to act on. How Did the Attack on Oracle PeopleSoft Happen? CVE-2026-35273 affects Oracle PeopleTools 8.61 and 8.62 and has a critical CVSS score of 9.8. The problem lies in the Updates Environment Management component, which is associated with the Environment Management Hub and the PSEMHUB application. To put it simply, the vulnerable component fails to appropriately verify that an individual is authorized to access it. Without logging in, an attacker may be able to execute commands on the compromised system if they can connect to the endpoint via HTTP. Attackers can exploit the exposed endpoint remotely without stolen passwords or user interaction. On June 10, 2026, Oracle issued an alert, and on June 12, CISA added the vulnerability to its KEV Catalog [3] . Getting In Was Only the Beginning What happened after the initial access is just as important as the vulnerability itself. Mandiant’s investigation uncovered tools and scripts that showed how the attackers tried to maintain access, reach other systems, and steal information. Here’s what they found. 1. Remote access tools disguised as legitimate software The attackers deployed customized MeshCentral agents disguised as Microsoft Azure-related software. This gave them a way to access compromised systems remotely without relying on the original vulnerability every time. 2. Attempts to move across internal systems Investigators found a script designed to connect to other hosts over SSH using a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords. This is called lateral movement. Once attackers get into one system, they look for ways to reach other systems connected to it. 3. Data collection and theft Attackers sent stolen data to servers connected to ShinyHunters after compressing it. 4. Extortion using stolen information Data associated with the campaign later appeared on the group’s leak site. For affected organizations, that meant the incident wasn’t just about fixing a vulnerable server. Their sensitive information could also be exposed. Universities were hit particularly hard. Mandiant reported [4] notifying more than 100 organizations whose IP addresses matched potentially vulnerable endpoints. Around 68% were in higher education, most of them in the United States. Some organizations blocked the activity, while others were compromised. The University of Nottingham confirmed a cyberattack [5] . The exposed data could affect current and former students, with consequences beyond the university’s IT systems. How Can You Tell If ShinyHunters Have Been in Your Environment? Patching the vulnerability is important, but there’s another thing organizations need to check: did attackers get in before the fix was applied? That’s why security teams should look for signs of compromise rather than assuming the problem is solved once the vulnerable component is secured. Here are some things worth investigating: Suspicious requests: Check PeopleSoft and WebLogic logs for unexpected POST requests to /PSEMHUB/hub and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector. Unfamiliar JSP files: Look for unexpected files such as x.jsp, u.jsp, tunnel.jsp, and tunnel.jspx in the PSEMHUB.war directory. Unknown remote access tools: Investigate unfamiliar MeshCentral agents and executables disguised as legitimate software. Unusual SSH activity: Check for unexpected connections from PeopleSoft servers to other internal systems. Suspicious outbound traffic: Look for unusual data transfers and connections that could indicate data staging or exfiltration . There’s another detail to keep in mind. Attackers may use different URLs to bypass security tools. In September 2026, attackers used encoded paths like /%50SEMHUB/hub to bypass some WAF rules and reach the vulnerable endpoint. So, blocking the standard URL alone may not be enough. Security teams should also review how their WAF rules handle encoded paths. What Should You Do If You Use Oracle PeopleSoft? If you use PeopleSoft, check your PeopleTools version and whether the Environment Management Hub is exposed. Oracle recommends applying the appropriate security fixes. Its guidance also includes disabling the Environment Management Hub in multi-server configurations or removing the PSEMHUB application in single-server configurations, as applicable. If you can’t disable or remove the component immediately, restrict external access to /PSEMHUB/* and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector. You can find the official instructions in Oracle's security alert for CVE-2026-35273 . And don’t forget to check for signs of an earlier compromise. Check logs, suspicious files, and unusual connections. If you find anything, investigate whether attackers accessed other systems or stole data. The important thing is to address both problems: the vulnerability itself and any attacker who may already have used it. Why Visibility Matters After an Attack The ShinyHunters attack shows how attackers can gain access, spread to other systems, and steal data. That’s why security teams need to see more than the initial alert. They need to connect activity across networks, endpoints, and cloud environments to understand what happened and where an attacker may have gone next. Fidelis Elevate ® helps security teams correlate suspicious activity and investigate potential post-breach attacks. It brings together network security, deception, and Active Directory protection to support proactive cyber defense. Download the Fidelis Elevate ® data sheet to learn more about its threat detection and investigation capabilities. Final Thoughts One exposed vulnerability can result in a much larger incident, as seen in the ShinyHunters attack on Oracle PeopleSoft. The reported activity included lateral movement , data theft, and remote access tools after the group took advantage of a vulnerability that permitted remote access without authentication. Apply Oracle’s suggested fixes and look for indications of compromise if you are using an impacted version of PeopleSoft. Because getting the vulnerability fixed is important. But making sure nobody is still inside your systems is just as important. The attackers deployed customized MeshCentral agents disguised as Microsoft Azure-related software. This gave them a way to access compromised systems remotely without relying on the original vulnerability every time.

2. Attempts to move across internal systems

Investigators found a script designed to connect to other hosts over SSH using a hardcoded list of usernames and passwords. This is called lateral movement. Once attackers get into one system, they look for ways to reach other systems connected to it.

3. Data collection and theft

Attackers sent stolen data to servers connected to ShinyHunters after compressing it.

4. Extortion using stolen information

Data associated with the campaign later appeared on the group’s leak site. For affected organizations, that meant the incident wasn’t just about fixing a vulnerable server. Their sensitive information could also be exposed.

Universities were hit particularly hard. Mandiant reported[4] notifying more than 100 organizations whose IP addresses matched potentially vulnerable endpoints. Around 68% were in higher education, most of them in the United States. Some organizations blocked the activity, while others were compromised.

The University of Nottingham confirmed a cyberattack[5]. The exposed data could affect current and former students, with consequences beyond the university’s IT systems.

How Can You Tell If ShinyHunters Have Been in Your Environment?

Patching the vulnerability is important, but there’s another thing organizations need to check: did attackers get in before the fix was applied?

That’s why security teams should look for signs of compromise rather than assuming the problem is solved once the vulnerable component is secured.

Here are some things worth investigating:

  • Suspicious requests:
    Check PeopleSoft and WebLogic logs for unexpected POST requests to /PSEMHUB/hub and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector.
  • Unfamiliar JSP files:
    Look for unexpected files such as x.jsp, u.jsp, tunnel.jsp, and tunnel.jspx in the PSEMHUB.war directory.
  • Unknown remote access tools:
    Investigate unfamiliar MeshCentral agents and executables disguised as legitimate software.
  • Unusual SSH activity:
    Check for unexpected connections from PeopleSoft servers to other internal systems.
  • Suspicious outbound traffic:
    Look for unusual data transfers and connections that could indicate data staging or exfiltration.

There’s another detail to keep in mind. Attackers may use different URLs to bypass security tools.

In September 2026, attackers used encoded paths like /%50SEMHUB/hub to bypass some WAF rules and reach the vulnerable endpoint.

So, blocking the standard URL alone may not be enough. Security teams should also review how their WAF rules handle encoded paths.

What Should You Do If You Use Oracle PeopleSoft?

If you use PeopleSoft, check your PeopleTools version and whether the Environment Management Hub is exposed.

Oracle recommends applying the appropriate security fixes. Its guidance also includes disabling the Environment Management Hub in multi-server configurations or removing the PSEMHUB application in single-server configurations, as applicable.

If you can’t disable or remove the component immediately, restrict external access to /PSEMHUB/* and /PSIGW/HttpListeningConnector.

  • You can find the official instructions in Oracle's security alert for CVE-2026-35273.

And don’t forget to check for signs of an earlier compromise. Check logs, suspicious files, and unusual connections. If you find anything, investigate whether attackers accessed other systems or stole data.

The important thing is to address both problems: the vulnerability itself and any attacker who may already have used it.

Why Visibility Matters After an Attack

The ShinyHunters attack shows how attackers can gain access, spread to other systems, and steal data.

That’s why security teams need to see more than the initial alert. They need to connect activity across networks, endpoints, and cloud environments to understand what happened and where an attacker may have gone next.

Fidelis Elevate® helps security teams correlate suspicious activity and investigate potential post-breach attacks. It brings together network security, deception, and Active Directory protection to support proactive cyber defense.

Download the Fidelis Elevate® data sheet to learn more about its threat detection and investigation capabilities.

Final Thoughts

One exposed vulnerability can result in a much larger incident, as seen in the ShinyHunters attack on Oracle PeopleSoft. The reported activity included lateral movement, data theft, and remote access tools after the group took advantage of a vulnerability that permitted remote access without authentication.

Because getting the vulnerability fixed is important. But making sure nobody is still inside your systems is just as important.

The technopolitics of ad-tech ( permalink ) "Technopolitics" are the politics embedded in technology. The Ur-text of technopolitics is "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" by the rock critic turned scholar Langdon Winner: https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~beki/cs4001/Winner.pdf With "Do Artifacts," Winner demands that we move beyond the idea of technologies having "intended consequences" and "unintended consequences" and towards a political economy of tech. In service to this, he divides the politics of artifacts into three categories: I. Artifacts that have politics embedded in them by their creators, like Robert Moses's infamous bridges over the Long Island parkways. According to Moses biographer Robert Caro, Moses deliberately specified that these bridges must be too low for a city bus to pass under, in a bid to block Black people from traveling from New York City to the beaches he'd developed on Long Island. Today those bridges are more than a century old, and they are still too low for city buses to pass under them, and this continues to mean that people who don't own private vehicles find it more difficult to get to the beach, and as it's still the case that race is a predictor of low incomes, those are still racist bridges. II. Artifacts whose politics are accidental but unavoidable. Winner cites a kind of tomato harvester that vastly improved the efficiency of tomato pickers. These harvesters became very popular, which allowed tomato farmers to lay off large numbers of agricultural workers, and also allowed them to price the mechanically harvested tomatoes so cheaply that they crowded out other kinds of tomatoes. Because these machines created a large pool of unemployed workers, they shifted power from labor to capital, and because these picking machines were too rough for all but the hardest varietals of tomato, they changed the flavor profile of tomatoes in America for the worse, towards a bland, tough tomato. These picking machines were not designed to make workers poorer, nor were they designed to make tomatoes taste worse, but because of their technical characteristics, this was the unavoidable outcome, the inextricable politics of these machines. III. Artifacts whose politics are intrinsic to their design. Here, Winner contrasts solar panels with nuclear reactors. Solar panels may require highly centralized industrial systems to produce , but once they are in the field, solar panels are compatible with looser, less coordinated political arrangements. A world of small anarchist communes is fully compatible with solar energy. Contrast this with nuclear reactors: the prudent ongoing operation of a reactor requires a highly centralized state that is capable of fielding reliable, trustworthy independent inspectors. This state must also be capable of exercising the coercive power to shut down badly maintained or incompetently operated reactors. The politics of nukes are the politics of a centralized, powerful state; the politics of solar are less determined. Solar is compatible with a wide variety of political systems, including (but not limited to) weak, decentralized states. (For a further exploration of "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" I highly recommend Ginger Coons' reading guide:) https://www.not-so-obvious.net/reading-do-artifacts-have-politics/ I really like Winner's framework for exploring technopolitics, but I have my own gloss on it. Winner's framework doesn't explicitly contemplate the idea of technological countermeasures . For example, what if someone were to design a city bus that was low enough to fit under Robert Moses's bridges? At that point, they'd cease to be "racist bridges," and merely become "bridges built by a racist": https://locusmag.com/feature/commentary-cory-doctorow-technopolitics/ Which brings me to the technopolitics of ad-tech. Lots of people think that advertising is "the original sin of the internet," setting in motion the surveillance dystopia that is closing in on us from all sides today: https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/17/mercenary-spyware/#discover-tech I think this is wrong. I think that finding ways to communicate ideas and pitches to the general public is fine. Without some channel for reaching people with ideas and propositions they may not be familiar with, it would be infinitely harder to reach people for political causes. It would also be harder for new books, movies and music to find new audiences. It would be much harder to get people out to your independent craft fair, your zine show, or your No Kings march. For me, the internet's original sin isn't advertising , it's surveillance . Contrary to what you have been told – and pax Winner's framework – the internet is fully compatible with privacy: https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/31/losing-the-crypto-wars/#surveillance-monopolism It wasn't the internet's technopolitics that made it a surveillance nightmare. It was just plain politics . Specifically, our politicians decided to stop enacting and enforcing privacy laws. The last consumer privacy law we got in America was a bill that made it illegal for video store clerks to disclose your VHS rentals: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Privacy_Protection_Act (As I type these words, the Supreme Court is poised to eliminate even that dried-up old crumb of privacy protection:) https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2026/10/supreme-court-privacy-rights-case-bork-kavanaugh.html The widespread phenomenon of ad-tech companies spying on us is the result of the decision to allow them to do so . That decision has had innumerable negative downstream effects, such as skyrocketing "surveillance prices": https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/11/nothing-personal/#instacartography And collapsing "surveillance wages": https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/18/loose-flapping-ends/#luigi-has-a-point It's created vast surveillance databases that are critical to Trump's racist pogroms, providing dossiers and precise location data on the people ICE kidnaps to Salvadoran slave-labor camps: https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/10/ice-tech/#foreseeable-outcomes Surveillance also promotes oligarchy. Without surveillance, oligarchs must give up more of their fortunes to keep the public happy, because the alternative is spending even more money on guards to keep the public from building guillotines on their lawns. Surveillance lets oligarchs make targeted strikes on restive radicals, which is much cheaper than broad-spectrum policies that make us all better off and neutralize the case for guillotines: https://pluralistic.net/2025/06/26/autostabilizer/#slicey-bois These are the technopolitics of surveillance , not advertising. There is nothing about advertising that demands surveillance. For centuries, advertising was not meaningfully linked to surveillance. The decision to fuse surveillance with advertising was just that – a decision , not an inevitability. Any time we forget this, we let spying tech bosses off the hook. After all, if advertising demands surveillance, then tech bosses are just the avatars of the great forces of history, prisoners of the imperative to spy in order to advertise. By remembering that surveillance advertising is a choice , we put the blame squarely where it belongs: on the guillotineable oligarchs who made that choice, and amassed spectacular fortunes thereby. Surveillance is political, but surveillance advertising has its own distinct technopolitics, and to understand those technopolitics, we must contrast them with the technopolitics of contextual advertising . Up until a decade or two ago, contextual advertising was simply called "advertising." Contextual advertising is the practice of running refrigerator ads next to articles on cooking and kitchen remodeling; ads for roadside restaurants on highway billboards; ads for Disney vacations in parenting magazines. Your intuition probably insists that context advertising is less effective than surveillance advertising. After all, surveillance advertising allows a running shoe company to target users who are training for a marathon no matter where they are and no matter what they're doing. Surely this translates into increased "conversions" (clicks and/or purchases, depending on who you're talking to)? It does, but not by much. Advertisers get about 5% more value from surveillance ads than they do from context ads: https://weis2019.econinfosec.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2019/05/WEIS_2019_paper_38.pdf Partly, that's because surveillance ad companies grossly overrate the efficacy of surveillance advertising: https://peoples-things.ghost.io/youre-doing-it-wrong-notes-on-criticism-and-technology-hype/ But surveillance advertising's anemic returns to advertisers are down to another aspect of the system: its tendency towards monopolization: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Google_LLC_(2023) Surveillance is a capital-intensive activity: spying on billions of people as they move through the digital and physical world is incredibly expensive. That is a good part of the reason that online advertising has collapsed into the Meta/Google duopoly, who control about 80% of display advertising. The harms of surveillance monopolies have a severely distorting effect on policy debates. For example, it's led some anti-monopolists to call for government-issued surveillance identifiers that follow us from birth to death in order to facilitate commercial spying to foster more competition in surveillance: https://www.thesling.org/what-to-do-about-googles-dominance-of-online-advertising/ Here's the thing about monopolists: they cheat. Google and Meta have an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the advertising market, overcharging advertisers and underpaying publishers: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue The ad-tech giants have taken in hundreds of billions that they simply can't account for. It's disappeared down a fraud-hole: https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/25/lying-spies/#spying-liars All of this has driven the majority of web users to install a privacy-blocker (like EFF's Privacybadger.org), meaning that surveillance ads are disproportionately likely to not even show up in a reader's browser: https://doc.searls.com/2023/11/11/how-is-the-worlds-biggest-boycott-doing/ So while it's possible that, in a state of nature, a surveillance ad would outperform a context ad, delivering more sales for advertisers and more revenue for publishers, the monopolistic tendency of ad-tech means that publishers earn less from surveillance ads (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher commissions), and advertisers see fewer sales from them (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher prices). Context ads, meanwhile, are always going to give power to publishers, because publishers will always understand the materials they publish better than any ad-tech platform could. Commissioning, editing and publishing an article, podcast or video gives a publisher unique and inalienable insight into that material. Surveillance data about audiences is a kind of ambient vapor floating around websites and places and payments that has to be condensed through a heroic and expensive effort that gives power to whichever company can muster the capital and infrastructure to do so. Meanwhile, information about the content of publishers' offerings is already refined into ingots that are already in publishers' own possession. It's possible to run "programmatic ads" without surveillance. Rather than building an ad-tech stack through which publishers transmit sensitive information about their audiences ("Who will pay me to advertise to this 18-34 year old man-child from the outer boroughs who owns an Xbox and has recently researched gonorrhea symptoms?"), we can build systems through which publishers transmit information about their own materials ("Who will advertise to a user with a New York IP address who is reading an article comparing running shoe brands?"). Not only is this possible, but it actually generates more revenues for publishers than the surveillance-based ad-tech stack: https://techcrunch.com/2020/07/24/data-from-dutch-public-broadcaster-shows-the-value-of-ditching-creepy-ads/ On top of that, publishers who don't gather personal information about users also don't need to show their users those awful pop-up ads asking their permission to gather their data. Everyone hates those notices, and they are yet another negative aspect of surveillance advertising that disappears with the switch to context ads. An ad-tech stack for context ads is far less prone to monopolization. Such a stack can be "federated," with multiple "demand-side platforms" (the part of the system that advertisers use to place bids for the right to show their ads) all communicating with the same "supply-side platform" (the part of the system publishers use to transmit opportunities to place ads). This is also in the technopolitics of context ads: they do not tend toward the "efficiencies of scale" that lead to abusive monopolistic middlemen who steal from publishers and advertisers and sell out the public to fascists who want to arrest them and deport them to Salvadoran slave-labor camps. When the ad-tech sector is composed of smaller companies that are more competitive with one another, it is much harder for any of them to collude to rig the market. That fierce competition also means it's harder to create a cozy conspiracy to lobby together to block privacy laws, and it leaves the companies with lower margins and less retained earnings to spend on those lobbying efforts. Surveillance ads also promote all kinds of parasitic businesses. The fact that a publisher can serve ads related to users rather than the subject of their media means that sensationalistic and deceptive websites can sell ads that run against content that's totally unrelated to advertisers' products and services. And because it's cheaper to produce lies and garbage, these publishers can undercut the ad prices demanded by high quality outlets and let advertisers reach the same users. This is the whole reason that "chumboxes" exist: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chumbox Just as nuclear power favors a centralized state, surveillance advertising: favors middlemen over publishers and advertisers; tends toward monopoly; favors low-quality media over high-quality production; impedes the passage of privacy laws; provides authoritarian states with an off-the-books, warrantless source of surveillance data. And just as solar allows for decentralized, anti-authoritarian societies, context advertising: favors publishers over middlemen and advertisers; tends towards pluralism and diversity of voices; favors high-quality media by reserving the lion's share of the rewards to the producers; does not rely on a weak privacy environment; does not militate for "democratizing spying" by issuing every person with a permanent advertising identifier. There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with building systems to tell people about things you want them to know. There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with paying for media with ads. It's possible for both of these things to go awry, but they are not in and of themselves bad. They have contingent technopolitics. But surveillance ads have completely unavoidable, absolutely ghastly technopolitics. Surveillance ads are bad for publishers, for advertisers, and for democracy. We should ban surveillance ads: https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2023/05/save-news-we-must-ban-surveillance-advertising ( Image: Jess , CC BY-SA 4.0 , modified ). The technopolitics of ad-tech (permalink)

"Technopolitics" are the politics embedded in technology. The Ur-text of technopolitics is "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" by the rock critic turned scholar Langdon Winner:

https://faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~beki/cs4001/Winner.pdf

With "Do Artifacts," Winner demands that we move beyond the idea of technologies having "intended consequences" and "unintended consequences" and towards a political economy of tech. In service to this, he divides the politics of artifacts into three categories:

I. Artifacts that have politics embedded in them by their creators, like Robert Moses's infamous bridges over the Long Island parkways. According to Moses biographer Robert Caro, Moses deliberately specified that these bridges must be too low for a city bus to pass under, in a bid to block Black people from traveling from New York City to the beaches he'd developed on Long Island.

Today those bridges are more than a century old, and they are still too low for city buses to pass under them, and this continues to mean that people who don't own private vehicles find it more difficult to get to the beach, and as it's still the case that race is a predictor of low incomes, those are still racist bridges.

II. Artifacts whose politics are accidental but unavoidable. Winner cites a kind of tomato harvester that vastly improved the efficiency of tomato pickers. These harvesters became very popular, which allowed tomato farmers to lay off large numbers of agricultural workers, and also allowed them to price the mechanically harvested tomatoes so cheaply that they crowded out other kinds of tomatoes.

Because these machines created a large pool of unemployed workers, they shifted power from labor to capital, and because these picking machines were too rough for all but the hardest varietals of tomato, they changed the flavor profile of tomatoes in America for the worse, towards a bland, tough tomato.

These picking machines were not designed to make workers poorer, nor were they designed to make tomatoes taste worse, but because of their technical characteristics, this was the unavoidable outcome, the inextricable politics of these machines.

III. Artifacts whose politics are intrinsic to their design. Here, Winner contrasts solar panels with nuclear reactors. Solar panels may require highly centralized industrial systems to produce, but once they are in the field, solar panels are compatible with looser, less coordinated political arrangements. A world of small anarchist communes is fully compatible with solar energy.

Contrast this with nuclear reactors: the prudent ongoing operation of a reactor requires a highly centralized state that is capable of fielding reliable, trustworthy independent inspectors. This state must also be capable of exercising the coercive power to shut down badly maintained or incompetently operated reactors.

The politics of nukes are the politics of a centralized, powerful state; the politics of solar are less determined. Solar is compatible with a wide variety of political systems, including (but not limited to) weak, decentralized states.

(For a further exploration of "Do Artifacts Have Politics?" I highly recommend Ginger Coons' reading guide:)

https://www.not-so-obvious.net/reading-do-artifacts-have-politics/

I really like Winner's framework for exploring technopolitics, but I have my own gloss on it. Winner's framework doesn't explicitly contemplate the idea of technological countermeasures. For example, what if someone were to design a city bus that was low enough to fit under Robert Moses's bridges? At that point, they'd cease to be "racist bridges," and merely become "bridges built by a racist":

https://locusmag.com/feature/commentary-cory-doctorow-technopolitics/

Which brings me to the technopolitics of ad-tech. Lots of people think that advertising is "the original sin of the internet," setting in motion the surveillance dystopia that is closing in on us from all sides today:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/17/mercenary-spyware/#discover-tech

I think this is wrong. I think that finding ways to communicate ideas and pitches to the general public is fine. Without some channel for reaching people with ideas and propositions they may not be familiar with, it would be infinitely harder to reach people for political causes. It would also be harder for new books, movies and music to find new audiences. It would be much harder to get people out to your independent craft fair, your zine show, or your No Kings march.

For me, the internet's original sin isn't advertising, it's surveillance. Contrary to what you have been told – and pax Winner's framework – the internet is fully compatible with privacy:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/31/losing-the-crypto-wars/#surveillance-monopolism

It wasn't the internet's technopolitics that made it a surveillance nightmare. It was just plain politics. Specifically, our politicians decided to stop enacting and enforcing privacy laws. The last consumer privacy law we got in America was a bill that made it illegal for video store clerks to disclose your VHS rentals:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_Privacy_Protection_Act

(As I type these words, the Supreme Court is poised to eliminate even that dried-up old crumb of privacy protection:)

https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2026/10/supreme-court-privacy-rights-case-bork-kavanaugh.html

The widespread phenomenon of ad-tech companies spying on us is the result of the decision to allow them to do so. That decision has had innumerable negative downstream effects, such as skyrocketing "surveillance prices":

https://pluralistic.net/2025/12/11/nothing-personal/#instacartography

And collapsing "surveillance wages":

https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/18/loose-flapping-ends/#luigi-has-a-point

It's created vast surveillance databases that are critical to Trump's racist pogroms, providing dossiers and precise location data on the people ICE kidnaps to Salvadoran slave-labor camps:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/10/ice-tech/#foreseeable-outcomes

Surveillance also promotes oligarchy. Without surveillance, oligarchs must give up more of their fortunes to keep the public happy, because the alternative is spending even more money on guards to keep the public from building guillotines on their lawns. Surveillance lets oligarchs make targeted strikes on restive radicals, which is much cheaper than broad-spectrum policies that make us all better off and neutralize the case for guillotines:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/06/26/autostabilizer/#slicey-bois

These are the technopolitics of surveillance, not advertising. There is nothing about advertising that demands surveillance. For centuries, advertising was not meaningfully linked to surveillance. The decision to fuse surveillance with advertising was just that – a decision, not an inevitability.

Any time we forget this, we let spying tech bosses off the hook. After all, if advertising demands surveillance, then tech bosses are just the avatars of the great forces of history, prisoners of the imperative to spy in order to advertise. By remembering that surveillance advertising is a choice, we put the blame squarely where it belongs: on the guillotineable oligarchs who made that choice, and amassed spectacular fortunes thereby.

Surveillance is political, but surveillance advertising has its own distinct technopolitics, and to understand those technopolitics, we must contrast them with the technopolitics of contextual advertising. Up until a decade or two ago, contextual advertising was simply called "advertising." Contextual advertising is the practice of running refrigerator ads next to articles on cooking and kitchen remodeling; ads for roadside restaurants on highway billboards; ads for Disney vacations in parenting magazines.

Your intuition probably insists that context advertising is less effective than surveillance advertising. After all, surveillance advertising allows a running shoe company to target users who are training for a marathon no matter where they are and no matter what they're doing. Surely this translates into increased "conversions" (clicks and/or purchases, depending on who you're talking to)?

It does, but not by much. Advertisers get about 5% more value from surveillance ads than they do from context ads:

https://weis2019.econinfosec.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2019/05/WEIS_2019_paper_38.pdf

Partly, that's because surveillance ad companies grossly overrate the efficacy of surveillance advertising:

https://peoples-things.ghost.io/youre-doing-it-wrong-notes-on-criticism-and-technology-hype/

But surveillance advertising's anemic returns to advertisers are down to another aspect of the system: its tendency towards monopolization:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_v._Google_LLC_(2023)

Surveillance is a capital-intensive activity: spying on billions of people as they move through the digital and physical world is incredibly expensive. That is a good part of the reason that online advertising has collapsed into the Meta/Google duopoly, who control about 80% of display advertising.

The harms of surveillance monopolies have a severely distorting effect on policy debates. For example, it's led some anti-monopolists to call for government-issued surveillance identifiers that follow us from birth to death in order to facilitate commercial spying to foster more competition in surveillance:

https://www.thesling.org/what-to-do-about-googles-dominance-of-online-advertising/

Here's the thing about monopolists: they cheat. Google and Meta have an illegal, collusive arrangement to rig the advertising market, overcharging advertisers and underpaying publishers:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jedi_Blue

The ad-tech giants have taken in hundreds of billions that they simply can't account for. It's disappeared down a fraud-hole:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/05/25/lying-spies/#spying-liars

All of this has driven the majority of web users to install a privacy-blocker (like EFF's Privacybadger.org), meaning that surveillance ads are disproportionately likely to not even show up in a reader's browser:

https://doc.searls.com/2023/11/11/how-is-the-worlds-biggest-boycott-doing/

So while it's possible that, in a state of nature, a surveillance ad would outperform a context ad, delivering more sales for advertisers and more revenue for publishers, the monopolistic tendency of ad-tech means that publishers earn less from surveillance ads (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher commissions), and advertisers see fewer sales from them (because more users block them, and because monopolistic ad-tech platforms extract higher prices).

Context ads, meanwhile, are always going to give power to publishers, because publishers will always understand the materials they publish better than any ad-tech platform could. Commissioning, editing and publishing an article, podcast or video gives a publisher unique and inalienable insight into that material.

Surveillance data about audiences is a kind of ambient vapor floating around websites and places and payments that has to be condensed through a heroic and expensive effort that gives power to whichever company can muster the capital and infrastructure to do so. Meanwhile, information about the content of publishers' offerings is already refined into ingots that are already in publishers' own possession.

It's possible to run "programmatic ads" without surveillance. Rather than building an ad-tech stack through which publishers transmit sensitive information about their audiences ("Who will pay me to advertise to this 18-34 year old man-child from the outer boroughs who owns an Xbox and has recently researched gonorrhea symptoms?"), we can build systems through which publishers transmit information about their own materials ("Who will advertise to a user with a New York IP address who is reading an article comparing running shoe brands?").

Not only is this possible, but it actually generates more revenues for publishers than the surveillance-based ad-tech stack:

https://techcrunch.com/2020/07/24/data-from-dutch-public-broadcaster-shows-the-value-of-ditching-creepy-ads/

On top of that, publishers who don't gather personal information about users also don't need to show their users those awful pop-up ads asking their permission to gather their data. Everyone hates those notices, and they are yet another negative aspect of surveillance advertising that disappears with the switch to context ads.

An ad-tech stack for context ads is far less prone to monopolization. Such a stack can be "federated," with multiple "demand-side platforms" (the part of the system that advertisers use to place bids for the right to show their ads) all communicating with the same "supply-side platform" (the part of the system publishers use to transmit opportunities to place ads).

This is also in the technopolitics of context ads: they do not tend toward the "efficiencies of scale" that lead to abusive monopolistic middlemen who steal from publishers and advertisers and sell out the public to fascists who want to arrest them and deport them to Salvadoran slave-labor camps.

When the ad-tech sector is composed of smaller companies that are more competitive with one another, it is much harder for any of them to collude to rig the market. That fierce competition also means it's harder to create a cozy conspiracy to lobby together to block privacy laws, and it leaves the companies with lower margins and less retained earnings to spend on those lobbying efforts.

Surveillance ads also promote all kinds of parasitic businesses. The fact that a publisher can serve ads related to users rather than the subject of their media means that sensationalistic and deceptive websites can sell ads that run against content that's totally unrelated to advertisers' products and services. And because it's cheaper to produce lies and garbage, these publishers can undercut the ad prices demanded by high quality outlets and let advertisers reach the same users. This is the whole reason that "chumboxes" exist:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chumbox

Just as nuclear power favors a centralized state, surveillance advertising:

  • favors middlemen over publishers and advertisers;

  • tends toward monopoly;

  • favors low-quality media over high-quality production;

  • impedes the passage of privacy laws;

  • provides authoritarian states with an off-the-books, warrantless source of surveillance data.

And just as solar allows for decentralized, anti-authoritarian societies, context advertising:

  • favors publishers over middlemen and advertisers;

  • tends towards pluralism and diversity of voices;

  • favors high-quality media by reserving the lion's share of the rewards to the producers;

  • does not rely on a weak privacy environment;

  • does not militate for "democratizing spying" by issuing every person with a permanent advertising identifier.

There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with building systems to tell people about things you want them to know. There's nothing (necessarily) wrong with paying for media with ads. It's possible for both of these things to go awry, but they are not in and of themselves bad. They have contingent technopolitics.

But surveillance ads have completely unavoidable, absolutely ghastly technopolitics. Surveillance ads are bad for publishers, for advertisers, and for democracy. We should ban surveillance ads:

https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2023/05/save-news-we-must-ban-surveillance-advertising

(Image: Jess, CC BY-SA 4.0, modified).

items.title: Google Unveils New Android AI Protections to Block Scam Calls, Phishing Links and OTP Theft
items.summary: Google has announced a new set of Android security protections designed to stop mobile scams across calls, text messages, chat apps, web links, and account verification codes. The update comes as criminals increasingly use spoofed phone numbers, fake bank alerts, phishing pages, remote screen sharing, and AI-generated voices to trick users into giving up money or login details. Google said its existing AI-powered scam detection tools in Phone by Google and Google Messages already identify more than five million suspected scam calls and texts each month. The new protections focus on preventing users from reaching the most dangerous stage of a scam. Instead of only blocking known malicious links or spam numbers. Android will use a mix of on-device AI, cloud-based analysis, privacy protections, and real-time checks to identify suspicious behavior before victims share passwords, payment data, or one-time passcodes. A key addition is an opt-in Enhanced Protection mode in Google Messages. Google said the setting will roll out in the coming weeks and will activate stronger protections for complex messaging scams. multi-layered protections across Google Messages (Source: Google) This includes expanded Scam Detection using Google’s Private AI Compute platform, which allows Gemini models to review the context of a conversation with an unknown sender. Google Unveils New Android AI Protections The aim is to spot slow-moving social engineering scams where criminals build trust over several messages before sending a fraudulent request or link. Google said the analysis occurs in an encrypted environment that Google employees cannot access. Enhanced Protection will also strengthen link checks in Google Messages. Scammers frequently create new phishing domains that have not yet been added to threat blocklists, which can make standard URL filtering less effective. Google said Gemini Nano, its on-device AI model, will combine real-time web signals with local analysis to assess unfamiliar links before a user opens them. Scam Detection in chat notifications (Source: Google) Android will also show redesigned warnings for links from numbers not saved in the user’s contacts. This provides an extra checkpoint before users visit a potential phishing page. The company is also expanding scam alerts from Pixel devices to a wider Android ecosystem. Scam Detection in chat notifications can flag suspicious messages from supported chat apps directly in the notification panel, allowing users to see a warning before opening the message. Google is working with Android device makers to bring the on-device feature to hundreds of millions of additional users later this year. Google’s update also targets phone-based social engineering scams, particularly cases where criminals persuade victims to share their screen or redirect incoming calls. Android will now automatically hide login fields and payment screens during active screen-sharing sessions in Chrome and Android WebView. The Protection is designed to stop fraudsters from viewing passwords, card details, and other sensitive information while guiding a victim through a fake support or banking process. Proactive call-forwarding protection (Source: Google) Another major safeguard addresses OTP theft through call forwarding . Threat actors may trick a user into entering a call-forwarding code, redirecting incoming calls containing verification codes to a criminal-controlled number. Android will block apps from silently enabling call forwarding in the background and warn users before a manually entered MMI forwarding code takes effect. Security teams can also review related account takeover risks and prevention steps in Cyber Security News coverage of OTP bypass and MFA phishing campaigns and mobile banking malware . Google is also expanding verified financial calls, a feature built with banks including Banco do Brasil and Itaú Unibanco. The system checks whether the bank’s official app actually initiated a call claiming to come from a bank. Built-in scam defenses across Android and iOS (Source: Google) If verification fails, Android can end the call and alert the user. Google said the feature has blocked more than three million spoofed calls involving the two Brazilian banks since its June launch. The announcement shows mobile security shifting from simple spam filtering to behavior-based fraud prevention. Users should still avoid sharing passwords, card information, recovery codes, or OTPs over calls and messages, even when the caller appears legitimate. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .
