items.title: Hackers Exploiting Plex Vulnerabilities in the Wild to Deploy Cryptominer Malware
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting flaws in Plex Media Server to install cryptocurrency mining malware, with a researcher recording successful attacks against a honeypot on October 17, 2026. The activity follows the release of Plex2Shell, a public exploit that chains four vulnerabilities to run code without logging in. Later observations also revealed proxy software running alongside the miner. The findings from Boredhackerblog show active exploitation of an exposed test server, rather than scanning alone. However, the available evidence does not establish how many real servers have been compromised or identify the attackers behind the activity. The researcher also warned that restrictions on outbound traffic initially prevented collection of some payloads. How the Plex2Shell Exploit Works Plex announced security updates on September 1, urging users to install Plex Media Server 1.43.3 and Plex Desktop 1.115.0. Its official security notice warned that NAS users might need to install updates manually. Cyber Security News previously covered the Plex security update and affected releases . The exploit combines CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. According to the Plex2Shell repository , the chain starts with server-side request forgery, which tricks Plex into sending requests chosen by an attacker. It then reaches internal functions, gains access to owner-authorized requests, and writes a file to an attacker-selected location. The final stage abuses the loading of an unsigned codec to execute code. The repository identifies versions before 1.43.3.10828 as vulnerable and lists 1.43.3.10861 as fixed. Although the exploit supports Linux and Windows targets, the reported honeypot activity involved a Linux-based Plex deployment running in Docker. Honeypot Captures Miner and Proxy Activity In the researcher’s report , the first exploitation attempt came from 45.194.92[.]222. Further attempts involved 91.92.40[.]202 and 176.65.139[.]228. Recorded requests targeted /player/timeline/subscribe and included references to internal Plex services, an sslip.io hostname, and the Python-urllib/3.10 user agent. After outbound access was enabled, the researcher observed downloads from 217.60.194[.]116 involving files named docker and x . Published artifacts included packed and unpacked samples, followed by an XMRig miner. Similar misuse of XMRig has appeared in other campaigns, including attacks against exposed Redis servers . An update also reported a process named myawesomeproxy and traffic involving proxystream[.]st. The program displayed a message about external use of the device’s internet traffic. These observations raise concerns about proxy abuse, but they do not establish who operates this Plex campaign or prove a connection to a specific botnet. Administrators should install the latest Plex release and verify the running version, particularly on NAS systems and Docker deployments. On Linux, review the Plex process tree for unexpected child processes, suspicious downloads, and unfamiliar mining or proxy programs. The researcher recommends examining processes with ps axjf . Defenders can use the published packet captures to develop detections. Files marked “lab” come from controlled tests, not live attacks. items.title: Microsoft Confirms October Windows Updates Can Break Exchange Server Email Services
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed that Windows Server security updates released on October 13, 2026, can disrupt Exchange Server email services, blocking webmail access and leaving messages undelivered. The issue affects some on-premises systems running Exchange Server 2016, Exchange Server 2019, and Exchange Server Subscription Edition. Microsoft has published a workaround and advises administrators not to uninstall the Windows updates. The failures stem from changes in Windows Server, not the separate October Exchange Server security updates. Servers can experience problems even without installing the latest Exchange patches, making the underlying operating system update the key factor when investigating these outages. Affected Updates and Exchange Server Symptoms Microsoft identified four Windows updates linked to the failures. These are KB5126646 for Windows Server 2025, KB5126655 for Windows Server 2022, KB5126651 for Windows Server 2019, and KB5126868 for Windows Server 2016. The impact depends on server workload, and some systems may never develop symptoms. Users may be unable to sign in to Outlook on the web, while messages sent through Outlook remain stuck in the Outbox. Administrators may notice growing mail queues, failed mailbox access during replication, or problems with Database Availability Group members reaching quorum. Restarting an affected server may restore service temporarily. One error administrators should watch for is MapiExceptionMdbOffline: Unable to make connection to the server. (hr=0x80004005, ec=1142) . Affected systems may also record Event ID 1006 in the Application log, providing a useful sign when checking whether an outage matches Microsoft’s report. According to Microsoft’s Windows release health notice , the October updates introduced a default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls. This limit controls memory use by Endpoint Mapper, a Windows component involved in remote procedure call communications. Heavy Exchange workloads can exceed the default allowance. Increasing the limit allows Endpoint Mapper to use more memory to handle these calls. Microsoft currently lists the issue as mitigated rather than resolved and says its investigation remains ongoing. An additional mitigation is available through Microsoft Support for affected organizations. Microsoft’s Registry Workaround Microsoft’s Exchange Team advisory instructs administrators to open an elevated Command Prompt on the Exchange server and run reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc" /v EpmapSavedContextCap /t REG_DWORD /d 65536 /f . The server must then be restarted. After the reboot, administrators should monitor the environment for recurring failures. Microsoft says the limit should be raised further if problems return, although its advisory does not specify a second value. The company reports that this approach has resolved the issue in customer cases it has handled. Keeping security updates installed remains important. Cybersecurity News recently covered Microsoft’s reissued Exchange Server security update , highlighting the continuing need for supported patches. The disruption also arrives as Exchange 2016 and 2019 approach the end of their final paid update period. Following earlier reporting on out-of-support Exchange servers , Microsoft says October 2026 marks their last scheduled ESU security release, with future updates limited to Subscription Edition. items.title: 5 signs that standing privileges are putting systems at risk
items.summary: In most organizations, standing privileges don’t show up all at once. They accumulate quietly. A role is added “temporarily.” A contractor needs broad access to finish a project. A service account gets oversized permissions because no one has time to fine-tune them. None of these choices seem harmful in the moment, but over time they build into a privilege surface that’s far too large to monitor and far too easy to misuse. The challenge is that standing privileges often look harmless until something finally goes wrong. The indicators are visible long before the incident, but only if you know where to look. Top indicators of standing privileges Here are five of the clearest signs that your environment is carrying more access risk than it should. 1. You have more admins than your environment actually needs Admin creep happens naturally. In fast-moving environments, the easiest way to unblock a task is to give someone full access. It works, it’s quick, and that access is rarely revisited. Multiply that across cloud accounts, SaaS tools, Kubernetes clusters, and databases, and you end up with dozens or even hundreds of identities that hold far more privilege than they need. The problem isn’t just security. Admin sprawl amplifies operational fragility. A single mistake or a single malicious action can ripple far beyond its intended scope; the blast radius from an incident expands because privileges were broader than they needed to be. If you can’t articulate why every admin in your environment truly needs that level of access, that’s a strong indicator that standing privileges have taken root. 2. Long-lived keys and credentials are still everywhere API keys, service account tokens, SSH keys, and automation secrets are some of the easiest paths into a cloud environment. They’re also some of the least governed. Many businesses have: Credentials that never expire Keys embedded in pipelines or code Secrets used across multiple systems, including by AI agents Tokens with full read/write access to production resources Long-lived credentials aren’t the result of bad people making bad decisions. They’re created by busy teams trying to keep workflows productive, rather than having to spin up a new credential every time they ask an agent to perform a task, for instance. The problem is that long-lived credentials become high-value targets, as we saw during the AWS incident involving compromised IAM credentials. Whether the threat is external or internal, a persistent key with broad permissions is often the fastest route to sensitive resources. If a service account can do more than its exact task, and keep doing it indefinitely, that’s an indicator of standing privilege risk. 3. Privileges don’t match what identities actually use Privilege sprawl is often a visibility problem. Teams don’t know what rights are being used, so they over-grant “just in case.” Over time, roles accumulate hundreds of permissions, most of which are never touched. Common examples include: IAM roles with wildcard permissions CI/CD pipelines that can modify infrastructure far beyond their workload Databases where read/write permissions aren’t separated Kubernetes service accounts with full cluster-admin rights AI agents and NHIs with cross-environment access because it was simpler than scoping When permissions are broader than their real usage, the organization isn’t just exposed to attackers. It’s exposed to insider mistakes, misconfigurations, and accidental changes in sensitive systems. If your team doesn’t regularly compare “granted” versus “used,” standing privileges are almost certainly accumulating. 4. Sensitive actions don’t require enough friction Some operations should not be immediately available to any identity, no matter how trusted: Resetting large numbers of passwords Editing IAM policies Disabling security controls Modifying production data Creating new users or access keys Stopping backup or logging services These actions should require either approvals, elevated just-in-time access, or automated guardrails that constrain when and how they can be performed. In environments without enough friction, sensitive actions can be executed accidentally or misused maliciously. This is how attackers using valid RDP credentials can disable security tools instantly, or how AI agents can misinterpret commands in such a way that it deletes an entire production database . If sensitive actions feel too easy, that’s an indicator that standing privileges are enabling more reach than intended. 5. You can’t easily answer who has access to what Standing privileges thrive in environments where visibility is fragmented. Cloud, SaaS, identity providers, CI/CD, Kubernetes, and databases all have their own privilege models. Without unified visibility, organizations rely on: Spreadsheets for access reviews Outdated role definitions Tribal knowledge Manual investigations Multiple admin consoles This fragmentation makes it nearly impossible to catch privilege drift or identify when service accounts, contractors, or AI agents have more access than expected. When an incident does happen, response time is delayed because teams don’t have an easy way of knowing who had the ability to take a specific action. This is one of the biggest and most overlooked indicators that standing privileges have become ingrained. How zero standing privileges addresses these indicators Zero standing privileges (ZSP) focuses on removing permanent access and replacing it with temporary, scoped, and auditable elevation. Under ZSP: Access is granted just-in-time Privileges match the specific task Access expires automatically Sensitive actions require deliberate elevation ZSP reduces the opportunity for malicious insiders, limits the surface attackers can abuse with stolen credentials, prevents accidental actions from impacting production systems, and enables teams to safely use AI agents to perform tasks. It directly addresses all five indicators by keeping privilege surfaces small and access intentional. How 1Password Privileged Access helps you reduce standing privilege risk 1Password Privileged Access makes zero standing privileges default across cloud, databases, SaaS, Kubernetes, and hybrid environments. It helps teams: Automate just-in-time elevation without slowing users down Quarantine risky privileges without breaking workflows Rightsize access based on real usage and risk data Remove standing access for humans and NHIs Log and audit all elevations and admin actions Detect unusual privilege behavior early Across cloud and hybrid environments, Privileged Access introduces guardrails that make access safer and more predictable. items.summary_html:
In most organizations, standing privileges don’t show up all at once. They accumulate quietly. A role is added “temporarily.” A contractor needs broad access to finish a project. A service account gets oversized permissions because no one has time to fine-tune them. None of these choices seem harmful in the moment, but over time they build into a privilege surface that’s far too large to monitor and far too easy to misuse.

The challenge is that standing privileges often look harmless until something finally goes wrong. The indicators are visible long before the incident, but only if you know where to look.

Top indicators of standing privileges

Here are five of the clearest signs that your environment is carrying more access risk than it should.

1. You have more admins than your environment actually needs

Admin creep happens naturally. In fast-moving environments, the easiest way to unblock a task is to give someone full access. It works, it’s quick, and that access is rarely revisited. Multiply that across cloud accounts, SaaS tools, Kubernetes clusters, and databases, and you end up with dozens or even hundreds of identities that hold far more privilege than they need.

The problem isn’t just security. Admin sprawl amplifies operational fragility. A single mistake or a single malicious action can ripple far beyond its intended scope; the blast radius from an incident expands because privileges were broader than they needed to be.

If you can’t articulate why every admin in your environment truly needs that level of access, that’s a strong indicator that standing privileges have taken root.

2. Long-lived keys and credentials are still everywhere

API keys, service account tokens, SSH keys, and automation secrets are some of the easiest paths into a cloud environment. They’re also some of the least governed.

Many businesses have:

  • Credentials that never expire

  • Keys embedded in pipelines or code

  • Secrets used across multiple systems, including by AI agents

  • Tokens with full read/write access to production resources

Long-lived credentials aren’t the result of bad people making bad decisions. They’re created by busy teams trying to keep workflows productive, rather than having to spin up a new credential every time they ask an agent to perform a task, for instance.

The problem is that long-lived credentials become high-value targets, as we saw during the AWS incident involving compromised IAM credentials. Whether the threat is external or internal, a persistent key with broad permissions is often the fastest route to sensitive resources.

If a service account can do more than its exact task, and keep doing it indefinitely, that’s an indicator of standing privilege risk.

3. Privileges don’t match what identities actually use

Privilege sprawl is often a visibility problem. Teams don’t know what rights are being used, so they over-grant “just in case.” Over time, roles accumulate hundreds of permissions, most of which are never touched.

Common examples include:

  • IAM roles with wildcard permissions

  • CI/CD pipelines that can modify infrastructure far beyond their workload

  • Databases where read/write permissions aren’t separated

  • Kubernetes service accounts with full cluster-admin rights

  • AI agents and NHIs with cross-environment access because it was simpler than scoping

When permissions are broader than their real usage, the organization isn’t just exposed to attackers. It’s exposed to insider mistakes, misconfigurations, and accidental changes in sensitive systems.

If your team doesn’t regularly compare “granted” versus “used,” standing privileges are almost certainly accumulating.

4. Sensitive actions don’t require enough friction

Some operations should not be immediately available to any identity, no matter how trusted:

  • Resetting large numbers of passwords

  • Editing IAM policies

  • Disabling security controls

  • Modifying production data

  • Creating new users or access keys

  • Stopping backup or logging services

These actions should require either approvals, elevated just-in-time access, or automated guardrails that constrain when and how they can be performed.

In environments without enough friction, sensitive actions can be executed accidentally or misused maliciously. This is how attackers using valid RDP credentials can disable security tools instantly, or how AI agents can misinterpret commands in such a way that it deletes an entire production database.

If sensitive actions feel too easy, that’s an indicator that standing privileges are enabling more reach than intended.

5. You can’t easily answer who has access to what

Standing privileges thrive in environments where visibility is fragmented. Cloud, SaaS, identity providers, CI/CD, Kubernetes, and databases all have their own privilege models. Without unified visibility, organizations rely on:

  • Spreadsheets for access reviews

  • Outdated role definitions

  • Tribal knowledge

  • Manual investigations

  • Multiple admin consoles

This fragmentation makes it nearly impossible to catch privilege drift or identify when service accounts, contractors, orAI agents have more access than expected.

When an incident does happen, response time is delayed because teams don’t have an easy way of knowing who had the ability to take a specific action. This is one of the biggest and most overlooked indicators that standing privileges have become ingrained.

How zero standing privileges addresses these indicators

Zero standing privileges (ZSP) focuses on removing permanent access and replacing it with temporary, scoped, and auditable elevation. Under ZSP:

  • Access is granted just-in-time

  • Privileges match the specific task

  • Access expires automatically

  • Sensitive actions require deliberate elevation

ZSP reduces the opportunity for malicious insiders, limits the surface attackers can abuse with stolen credentials, prevents accidental actions from impacting production systems, and enables teams to safely use AI agents to perform tasks.

It directly addresses all five indicators by keeping privilege surfaces small and access intentional.

How 1Password Privileged Access helps you reduce standing privilege risk

1Password Privileged Access makes zero standing privileges default across cloud, databases, SaaS, Kubernetes, and hybrid environments. It helps teams:

  • Automate just-in-time elevation without slowing users down

  • Quarantine risky privileges without breaking workflows

  • Rightsize access based on real usage and risk data

  • Remove standing access for humans and NHIs

  • Log and audit all elevations and admin actions

  • Detect unusual privilege behavior early

Across cloud and hybrid environments, Privileged Access introduces guardrails that make access safer and more predictable.

Putting better guardrails around access

Standing privileges rarely feel dangerous until they’re misused. But the indicators show up long before the incident happens. items.title: A path to user verification in 1Password
items.summary: At 1Password, we believe strong security should feel like part of the workflow, not an interruption. That is the goal behind our work on user verification (UV) for passkeys . UV is a local identity check a website can require as part of a passkey action, to confirm the person approving the action is the person authorized to do so. This decision belongs to the website, not 1Password, as the site will validate UV occurred before accepting the operation. A useful analogy is paying with a bank card. For some transactions, tapping the card is enough. For higher-risk transactions, the terminal asks for a PIN. The card shows the credential is present, and the PIN adds confidence that the authorized cardholder is using it. Passkeys have a similar distinction; when stronger assurance is needed, UV asks for a fingerprint, face scan, device PIN, or password. If someone can add or use a passkey without proving they are authorized, a hijacked browser interaction or temporary access to an unlocked session could become lasting account access. Imagine someone steals your bank card and tries to buy a new TV. In that moment, you want the terminal to ask for a PIN. UV plays the same role for passkeys, ensuring high-impact operations are approved by the right person, not whoever has the computer. Not every passkey flow needs UV, but when a website requests it, we want the experience to be as seamless as possible. The website has the context to decide when stronger assurance is needed, and 1Password’s role is to honor that request and ensure the local verification check is completed. Protecting the user is a shared responsibility between the website and client. User verification for passkeys is now available for mobile and desktop applications As of August 27th, our mobile and desktop apps have prompted for UV whenever a passkey flow requires it. In these supported flows, 1Password can call the native APIs provided by the operating system to trigger a familiar platform prompt, such as biometrics or a device PIN, instead of a more burdensome 1Password account password prompt. We want this experience to feel familiar and to avoid additional account password prompts whenever possible. Please share your feedback about where the experience feels seamless and where it still gets in the way. Share your feedback Your feedback will help us improve the experience and deliver security that feels effortless. What we're building next: a better extension-only experience UV prompting in mobile and desktop apps is only the beginning. The next step is to improve the passkey experience within the 1Password browser extension . Why extension-only flows need a better solution When someone uses both the browser extension and the desktop app, 1Password can hand the passkey request to the native app. The desktop app can then call the operating system's native APIs and show the same biometric, PIN, or device-authentication prompt people already use elsewhere. The challenge appears when the browser extension runs without the desktop app, creating an extension-only setup. Extensions do not have a standard, cross-browser way to call the required native APIs directly. If a website requires UV in an extension-only flow, we are of the opinion that the only viable fallback today is another 1Password account password prompt. If the user needs to type the password instead of using biometrics, the flow is slower, more disruptive, and inconsistent with the native experience available in our apps. The browser community needs a new API that can provide a consistent experience across browser engines. A standards-based path forward: Secure Cache 1Password has drafted a new WebExtensions proposal, browser.secureCache , to solve this problem. The proposed API would give browser extensions a standard way to use platform-backed credential storage and request native user verification where supported. In a UV flow, the operating system can show its familiar biometric, PIN, or device-authentication prompt before allowing access to the protected material. While UV is our flagship use case, Secure Storage addresses a wider browser security gap. Credential managers, secure messaging apps, wallets, and other security-sensitive extensions all need safer ways to protect key material. Secure Cache will reduce dependence on volatile extension memory and native companion apps while giving developers stronger protections for critical data. 1Password will work with the open source community to help move Secure Storage from proposal to implementation targeting Chromium . A working Chromium implementation will create a path for Chrome and all other Chromium-based browsers like Edge. Our end goal is a broadly supported API rather than a browser-specific workaround. Once various browsers ship a suitable Secure Storage API, we will adopt it for extension-only UV in 1Password. Try it today and help shape what comes next Today's release is the first part of the story. The next part is closing the extension-only gap through Secure Cache and broader browser support. This is the kind of work we believe is worth investing in. Rather than implementing a workaround, we can help add a critical browser capability that improves user experience and raises the security bar for the wider community. It follows the same approach as our work with the FIDO Alliance and our support for secure passkey import and export : solve real product problems through open, interoperable standards. User verification is available now User Verification is available now in the latest 1Password mobile and desktop apps. Try it when you create and use passkeys, and tell us how it feels. Share your feedback

UV is a local identity check a website can require as part of a passkey action, to confirm the person approving the action is the person authorized to do so. This decision belongs to the website, not 1Password, as the site will validate UV occurred before accepting the operation. A useful analogy is paying with a bank card. For some transactions, tapping the card is enough. For higher-risk transactions, the terminal asks for a PIN. The card shows the credential is present, and the PIN adds confidence that the authorized cardholder is using it. If someone can add or use a passkey without proving they are authorized, a hijacked browser interaction or temporary access to an unlocked session could become lasting account access. Imagine someone steals your bank card and tries to buy a new TV. In that moment, you want the terminal to ask for a PIN. UV plays the same role for passkeys, ensuring high-impact operations are approved by the right person, not whoever has the computer.

Not every passkey flow needs UV, but when a website requests it, we want the experience to be as seamless as possible. The website has the context to decide when stronger assurance is needed, and 1Password’s role is to honor that request and ensure the local verification check is completed. Protecting the user is a shared responsibility between the website and client.

User verification for passkeys is now available for mobile and desktop applications
As of August 27th, our mobile and desktop apps have prompted for UV whenever a passkey flow requires it.

In these supported flows, 1Password can call the native APIs provided by the operating system to trigger a familiar platform prompt, such as biometrics or a device PIN, instead of a more burdensome 1Password account password prompt. We want this experience to feel familiar and to avoid additional account password prompts whenever possible. Please share your feedback about where the experience feels seamless and where it still gets in the way.

Share your feedback

Your feedback will help us improve the experience and deliver security that feels effortless.

What we're building next: a better extension-only experience

UV prompting in mobile and desktop apps is only the beginning. The next step is to improve the passkey experience within the 1Password browser extension.

Why extension-only flows need a better solution

When someone uses both the browser extension and the desktop app, 1Password can hand the passkey request to the native app. The desktop app can then call the operating system's native APIs and show the same biometric, PIN, or device-authentication prompt people already use elsewhere.

The challenge appears when the browser extension runs without the desktop app, creating an extension-only setup. Extensions do not have a standard, cross-browser way to call the required native APIs directly. If a website requires UV in an extension-only flow, we are of the opinion that the only viable fallback today is another 1Password account password prompt. If the user needs to type the password instead of using biometrics, the flow is slower, more disruptive, and inconsistent with the native experience available in our apps.

The browser community needs a new API that can provide a consistent experience across browser engines.

A standards-based path forward: Secure Cache

1Password has drafted a new WebExtensions proposal, browser.secureCache, to solve this problem. The proposed API would give browser extensions a standard way to use platform-backed credential storage and request native user verification where supported. In a UV flow, the operating system can show its familiar biometric, PIN, or device-authentication prompt before allowing access to the protected material.

While UV is our flagship use case, Secure Storage addresses a wider browser security gap. Credential managers, secure messaging apps, wallets, and other security-sensitive extensions all need safer ways to protect key material. Secure Cache will reduce dependence on volatile extension memory and native companion apps while giving developers stronger protections for critical data.

1Password will work with the open source community to help move Secure Storage from proposal to implementation targeting Chromium. A working Chromium implementation will create a path for Chrome and all other Chromium-based browsers like Edge.

Our end goal is a broadly supported API rather than a browser-specific workaround. Once various browsers ship a suitable Secure Storage API, we will adopt it for extension-only UV in 1Password.

Try it today and help shape what comes next

Today's release is the first part of the story.

The next part is closing the extension-only gap through Secure Cache and broader browser support. This is the kind of work we believe is worth investing in. Rather than implementing a workaround, we can help add a critical browser capability that improves user experience and raises the security bar for the wider community. It follows the same approach as our work with the FIDO Alliance and our support for secure passkey import and export: solve real product problems through open, interoperable standards.

User verification is available now

User Verification is available now in the latest 1Password mobile and desktop apps. Try it when you create and use passkeys, and tell us how it feels.
